abstract: |
  Video game research often treats games as a monolithic category, and single-game or single-platform studies leave open whether findings generalise across the medium. In this registered report, we used multi-platform digital trace data from the Open Play dataset to test whether (H1) total playtime is meaningfully associated with mental wellbeing and (H2) whether this association differs by game genre. The data comprise 6,680 observations from 1,838 UK and US adults whose Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam telemetry, spanning 4,154 distinct titles, was linked to structured genre metadata and to six biweekly wellbeing assessments (SWEMWBS). Bayesian multilevel within-between models evaluated both hypotheses against a pre-registered threshold for practical significance. Total playtime was practically equivalent to zero on both dimensions: wellbeing barely moved in waves when participants played more than their own average, and those who habitually played more reported slightly lower wellbeing, well under the threshold. Contrary to our registered prediction that genres would diverge in sign and strength, genre differences fell below the threshold across three model specifications, including a multi-membership model for games carrying multiple genre labels. Genres proved statistically distinguishable but practically interchangeable, and person-to-person variation in the playtime association was similarly bounded. An exploratory extension to the study's daily-diary component reproduced both conclusions at the daily timescale: a small positive within-person trend far below practical significance, and between-person contrasts leaning negative within the equivalence region, echoing the registered pattern. The playtime–wellbeing null thus survives its strictest test to date and generalises across genres, with heterogeneity bounded below any practically meaningful magnitude rather than merely undetected. Genre differences appear to be the wrong place to look for gaming's wellbeing effects; genre labels are too coarse a proxy for the psychological experiences that plausibly drive them, which directs attention towards finer-grained characterisations of play.
categories: [video games, wellbeing, genres, digital trace data, registered report]

# Introduction

Video game effects research utilising digital trace data often focuses on a single game or a handful of games to understand the psychological processes and outcomes of digital play [@bruhlmannMotivationalProfilingLeague2020; @JohannesEtAl2021video; @larrieuHowGamingMotives2023; @ballouPerceivedValueVideo2025]. While understandable given the limited resources and lack of objective data available to independent researchers, it has left the field guessing whether identified relationships are unique to the studied titles or whether they apply universally across games. This limitation has restricted researchers' abilities to estimate the true prevalence of any found effects, leading to assumptions of generalisability and the formation of theories that fail to capture the diversity of the medium. Potential overgeneralisation of findings has been well-documented in psychological research and is particularly pertinent to research on video games [@yarkoniGeneralizabilityCrisis2019].

With more than 10,000 new games released each year [@notisYoureRightThere2021], an accessible classification system is essential for studying and comparing video games at scale. Genres, while defined by convention and neither exclusive nor exhaustive as labels [@clarkeWhyVideoGame2017; @ballouHowVideoGames2025; @vargas-iglesiasMakingSenseGenre2020], remain the most pragmatic means of categorising video games, providing utility for researchers, players, industry, and policymakers alike. Psychologists have been trying to classify game genres for decades [@griffithsAreComputerGames1993; @wolf6GenreVideo2002], but must negotiate challenges in definition, overlaps between genres, and the continuous evolution of genres as new games are released. Genres are therefore best treated not as definitive taxonomical statements but as crude yet practical tools for organising a growing and diversifying library.

Studies have documented marked differences between video game genres in terms of their playtime and their effects on player behaviour, cognition, and wellbeing [@andreRelationshipGameGenre2024; @dobrowolskiCognitiveEnhancementVideo2015; @raithMassivelyMultiplayerOnline2021; @hazelExploringPossibleMental2022]. Action games have been linked to increased visual attention [@palausNeuralBasisVideo2017], cognitive and attentional control [@angueraVideoGameTraining2013; @bavelierEnhancingAttentionalControl2019], and working memory [@blackerEffectsActionVideo2014]. Massively multiplayer online role-playing games (MMORPGs), first-person shooters, real-time strategy games (RTS), and Multiplayer Online Battle Arena (MOBA) games have been associated with higher gaming disorder (GD) symptoms [@elliottContributionGameGenre2012; @rehbeinContributionGameGenre2021]. At the same time, randomised controlled trials have employed genres like casual games and exergames to induce positive moods and reduce stress [@huangImpactPlayingExergames2017; @russonielloEffectivenessCasualVideo2009]. These findings suggest that the effects of video games are not uniform and that genre helps shape both gaming behaviour and its impact on wellbeing.

A recent systematic review, however, documented inconsistencies in how genres are classified across psychological research [@starostaTangledWaysClassify2024]. Of 96 examined articles, only 50 (52%) employed an existing genre classification; 46 (48%) used a unique classification, and 18 (19%) failed to specify the basis or definitions of their genre categorisations altogether. Genre classifications were typically self-reported by participants or assigned by authors, and the same games are habitually classified into different genres across studies. This subjectivity undermines the validity of existing self-report or researcher-ascribed genre taxonomies.

Structured, crowd-sourced metadata repositories such as SteamDB, The Games Database, and the Internet Games Database (IGDB) offer a more reliable alternative, involving both game developers and large player samples in collaboratively maintaining genre labels [@liPreliminaryNetworkAnalysis2020; @starostaTangledWaysClassify2024; @leeEmpiricalEvaluationMetadata2015]. This approach accommodates the fluidity of genres over time [@cohenHistoryGenre1986] and enables comparative research at scale. Yet several methodological obstacles have prevented genre-level research using digital trace data. Data access is fragmented: digital trace data are siloed within individual platform holders, and no cross-platform standard exists for recording or sharing gameplay telemetry [@zendle2023challenges]. The choice of taxonomy is also not neutral: genre labels conflate distinct facets of games, such as gameplay style, purpose, and mood [@leeFacetAnalysisVideo2014]; treating players as pure-genre versus acknowledging multi-genre play alters conclusions about player characteristics [@aziziExperienceMultigenreVideo2018], and factor-analytic decompositions of crowd-sourced game tags produce genre structures that diverge from conventional labels [@liFactororientedUnderstandingVideo2020].

## The Present Study

In sum, one portion of the literature has shown that playtime undifferentiated by genre is not a meaningful predictor of wellbeing, using data from both specific games [@larrieuHowGamingMotives2023] and platforms [@ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024; @ballouPerceivedValueVideo2025]. This relationship, however, has not yet been tested using comprehensive multi-platform play data. Furthermore, multiple mechanisms have been proposed to explain why aggregate playtime is poorly predictive of wellbeing, including displacement of beneficial activities, satisfaction or frustration of basic psychological needs, and selection effects whereby individuals with lower wellbeing play more [@ballouHowVideoGames2025]. Most proposed mechanisms operate at the level of game features or player experience rather than at the level of total time spent; playtime is, at best, a moderator [@ballouHowVideoGames2025]. The only causal evidence to date, exploiting console lotteries as a natural experiment, found positive effects of gaming on wellbeing, with heterogeneous effects by console type [@egami2024causal], suggesting that observational null findings may reflect confounding rather than absence of effect. Thus, our first hypothesis predicts the absence of a meaningful relationship, this time with digital trace data across several platforms and thousands of games:

**H1.** Total cross-platform playtime is not meaningfully associated with fluctuations in general mental wellbeing over a 2-week period (**H1a**, "within-person") or with average wellbeing over the full study period (**H1b**, "between-person").

We test this via a Bayesian ROPE analysis with equivalence bounds of ±0.06 SWEMWBS item-mean points per hour/day, matching the SESOI used by @ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024. In practical terms, H1a asks whether playing more than one's own average in a given two-week wave is associated with a shift in wellbeing, while H1b asks whether individuals who habitually play more report different average wellbeing than those who play less. The within-person component isolates the effect of playtime fluctuations from stable individual differences; the between-person component captures the cross-sectional association, which is inherently more vulnerable to confounding by self-selection.

Consistent null findings for the effects of playtime on wellbeing have generated calls for the unpacking of raw decontextualised playtime into more informative measures that consider games' varied characteristics and affordances [@ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024]. Game genres offer a structured way to differentiate between video games and their corresponding play experiences [@starostaTangledWaysClassify2024]. While genre differences are widely established [@aziziExperienceMultigenreVideo2018; @dobrowolskiCognitiveEnhancementVideo2015; @johnsonMotivationsVideogamePlay2016; @rehbeinContributionGameGenre2021], the effects of genre-level playtime on wellbeing are yet to be studied using digital trace data. Following previous literature, we predict that genres vary in their relation to wellbeing, with some potentially positive and others potentially negative, varying in strength. Put more formally:

**H2.** Genres differ in how playtime relates to fluctuations in general mental wellbeing over a 2-week period (**H2a**, "within-person") and to average wellbeing over the full study period (**H2b**, "between-person").

H2a asks: when a participant plays more than their own average this wave, does it matter what genres that extra playtime is in? H2b asks the between-person complement: among people who play more overall, does it matter whether that habitual extra playtime is concentrated in RPGs versus Shooters versus other genres? If H2 is supported, and genre-specific associations differ from one another, it would provide a candidate explanation for the consistent null aggregate findings: undifferentiated playtime measures may average over heterogeneous genre effects that cancel in aggregate. H2 thus tests whether it is justified to generalise video game effects across genres, testing the generalisability that single-title studies must assume [@yarkoniGeneralizabilityCrisis2019]. Taken together, the two hypotheses form a single generalisability test rather than two separate null results: H1 establishes whether an aggregate association exists, and H2 establishes whether that aggregate conceals genre-level associations that offset one another. The generalisability critique is widely cited but rarely operationalised as a quantity a study can estimate; here it is the quantity being estimated.

Beyond the registered hypotheses, we report one unregistered extension. The biweekly window aggregates many individual play sessions into a single retrospective judgement, so the registered tests leave open whether associations operating on shorter timescales are hidden by aggregation; the daily-diary component of the Open Play study allows both hypotheses to be re-examined at the daily level. This extension was specified after the registered analyses were complete and is reported as exploratory throughout (see Exploratory Daily-Timescale Analysis in Methods).

```{r}
platform_ranges <- map_dfr(names(telemetry_files), function(p) {
  tibble(
    platform = p,
    min_date = min(telemetry_files[[p]]$date, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_date = max(telemetry_files[[p]]$date, na.rm = TRUE)

  mutate(range_text = glue("{format(min_date, '%b %Y')} to {format(max_date, '%b %Y')}"))

telemetry_range_sentence <- platform_ranges |>
  mutate(platform_range = glue("{platform} ({range_text})")) |>
  pull(platform_range) |>
  paste(collapse = ", ")

intake_range <- intake_raw |>
  summarise(
    min_date = min(date, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_date = max(date, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

intake_range_sentence <- glue(
  "{format(intake_range$min_date, '%b %Y')} and {format(intake_range$max_date, '%b %Y')}"
)
```

## Data Source and Participants

The analyses reported here are part of a Stage 1 Registered Report [@ballou2024psychological] and utilise data from the Open Play dataset [@ballou2025openplay], a longitudinal study that collected multi-platform video game digital trace data alongside psychological measures from adult gamers in the UK and US over a three-month period. Intake surveys were completed between `r intake_range_sentence`. Digital trace data span the following periods: `r telemetry_range_sentence`. The study combined objective behavioural telemetry from gaming platforms with repeated self-report surveys administered biweekly across six waves. Genre-level analyses (H2) use data from Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam, as these provide session-level (Nintendo, Xbox) or near session-level (Steam) temporal granularity and video game title or genre metadata. The pre-registration specified that H2 would include "all platforms but iOS"; however, Android data collection was modified from the planned ActivityWatch session-level exports to Digital Wellbeing screenshot-based daily aggregates (see @ballou2025openplay for details), yielding only daily total gaming minutes without game-level metadata. Android is therefore excluded from H2 alongside iOS. For H1, which examines total playtime regardless of genre, total playtime is computed from Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam only; iOS and Android provide daily aggregate gaming minutes without game-level metadata and enter solely through the pre-registered all-platform sensitivity analysis reported in the supplementary materials (Appendix B, Deviation D6). The Open Play study received ethical approval from the Social Sciences and Humanities Inter-Divisional Research Ethics Committee at the University of Oxford (OII_CIA_23_107); all participants provided informed consent at the start of the study, including consent to their data being shared openly for reanalysis [@ballou2025openplay].

```{r}
#| label: build-demographics
#| include: false

# The analytic sample is defined by the models: all participants with at
# least one valid SWEMWBS response in the biweekly survey. Telemetry-based
# playtime is zero for participants/waves without recorded play.
analysis_pids <- read_csv(here("data/clean/survey_biweekly.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(wave >= 1, wave <= 6) |>
  mutate(wemwbs = rowMeans(across(starts_with("wemwbs_")), na.rm = FALSE)) |>
  filter(!is.na(wemwbs)) |>
  distinct(pid) |>
  pull(pid)

n_model <- length(analysis_pids)

genre_matched_pids <- read_csv(here("data/processed/genre_wave_long.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  distinct(pid) |>
  pull(pid)

n_genre_matched <- length(intersect(analysis_pids, genre_matched_pids))

daily_telemetry <- bind_rows(
  read_csv(here("data/clean/xbox.csv.gz"),     show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "Xbox"),
  read_csv(here("data/clean/steam.csv.gz"),    show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "Steam"),
  read_csv(here("data/clean/nintendo.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "Nintendo"),
  read_csv(here("data/clean/ios.csv.gz"),      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "iOS"),
  read_csv(here("data/clean/android.csv.gz"),  show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(pid) |> mutate(platform = "Android")
) |>
  distinct(pid, platform)

demographics <- intake |>
  filter(qualified) |>
  mutate(
    pid = as.character(pid),
    age_group = cut(
      age,
      breaks = c(17, 24, 30, 35, 40),
      labels = c("18-24", "25-30", "31-35", "36-40")
    ),
    gender = case_when(
      gender %in% c("Man", "Male")     ~ "Man",
      gender %in% c("Woman", "Female") ~ "Woman",
      gender == "Prefer not to say"    ~ NA_character_,
      is.na(gender)                    ~ NA_character_,
      TRUE                             ~ "Non-binary/Other"
    ),
    ethnicity = case_when(
      ethnicity %in% c("White", "White alone")                                          ~ "White",
      ethnicity %in% c("Asian", "Asian alone", "Asian or Asian British")                ~ "Asian",
      ethnicity %in% c("Black", "Black or African American alone",
                       "Black, African, Caribbean or Black British")                    ~ "Black",
      ethnicity %in% c("Mixed", "Mixed or multiple ethnic groups", "Two or More Races") ~ "Mixed/Multiple",
      ethnicity == "Prefer not to say"                                                  ~ NA_character_,
      is.na(ethnicity)                                                                  ~ NA_character_,
      TRUE                                                                              ~ "Other"
    )
  ) |>
  select(pid, country, age, age_group, gender, ethnicity)

analytic_sample <- demographics |>
  filter(pid %in% analysis_pids, !is.na(age_group))

n_total <- nrow(analytic_sample)
n_us    <- sum(analytic_sample$country == "US", na.rm = TRUE)
n_uk    <- sum(analytic_sample$country == "UK", na.rm = TRUE)

n_intake_total <- nrow(intake)
n_qualified    <- sum(intake$qualified, na.rm = TRUE)
```

From `r formatC(n_intake_total, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` participants who completed the intake survey, `r formatC(n_qualified, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` met the pre-registered screening and linking criteria. The analytic sample comprises the `r formatC(n_model, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` participants who provided valid SWEMWBS responses in at least one biweekly survey wave. Playtime for these participants is measured from their linked Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam accounts; participants and waves without recorded play on these platforms contribute zero hours, and `r formatC(n_genre_matched, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` participants (`r round(100 * n_genre_matched / n_model)`%) had at least one genre-matched gameplay session. The demographic sensitivity analysis uses the `r formatC(n_total, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` participants with a matching qualified intake record and age within the 18–40 screening range (`r formatC(n_us, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` US, `r formatC(n_uk, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` UK; mean age `r round(mean(analytic_sample$age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` years, `r round(100 * mean(analytic_sample$gender == "Man", na.rm = TRUE))`% men); `r formatC(n_model - n_total, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` analytic-sample participants are excluded from that subset (`r sum(!(analysis_pids %in% demographics$pid))` without a matching intake record, `r sum(demographics$age[demographics$pid %in% analysis_pids] > 40, na.rm = TRUE)` aged over 40). Full demographic characteristics, including country-level breakdowns, are reported in @tbl-demographics.

```{r}
#| label: genre-metadata-stats
#| include: false

# --- Raw IGDB label statistics (game_metadata.csv.gz) -----------------------
meta_raw_gm   <- read_csv(here("data/clean/game_metadata.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)
meta_labelled <- meta_raw_gm |> filter(!is.na(genres), nchar(genres) > 0)
raw_label_list      <- map(str_split(meta_labelled$genres, ","), str_trim)
raw_labels_distinct <- sort(unique(unlist(raw_label_list)))
n_raw_genre_labels  <- length(raw_labels_distinct)
n_labels_per_game   <- lengths(raw_label_list)
max_raw_labels      <- max(n_labels_per_game)
pct_games_gt3_labels <- 100 * mean(n_labels_per_game > 3)

# Genre count under the PRE-REGISTERED collapsing (for Appendix A)
prereg_collapse <- function(g) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    g == "Hack and slash/Beat 'em up" ~ "Action",
    g %in% c("Turn-based strategy (TBS)", "Real Time Strategy (RTS)", "Tactical") ~ "Strategy",
    g %in% c("Point-and-click", "Visual Novel") ~ "Adventure",
    g == "Quiz/Trivia" ~ "Puzzle",
    TRUE ~ g
  )
}
n_prereg_genres <- n_distinct(prereg_collapse(raw_labels_distinct))

# --- Xbox genre rescue (Deviation U1): coverage before/after the local fix --
meta_fixed_gm <- populate_xbox_genres(meta_raw_gm)
xb_has <- function(meta) meta |> filter(platform == "Xbox") |>
  transmute(original_name, has = !is.na(genres) & nchar(genres) > 0)
xbox_cov <- telemetry_files$Xbox |>
  left_join(xb_has(meta_raw_gm),   by = c("title_id" = "original_name")) |>
  rename(has_before = has) |>
  left_join(xb_has(meta_fixed_gm), by = c("title_id" = "original_name")) |>
  rename(has_after = has) |>
  summarise(
    total_min  = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_before = sum(duration[replace_na(has_before, FALSE)], na.rm = TRUE),
    min_after  = sum(duration[replace_na(has_after,  FALSE)], na.rm = TRUE)
  )
xbox_pct_before  <- 100 * xbox_cov$min_before / xbox_cov$total_min
xbox_pct_after   <- 100 * xbox_cov$min_after  / xbox_cov$total_min
xbox_min_rescued <- xbox_cov$min_after - xbox_cov$min_before

# --- In-study (waves 1-6) sessions, from the already-loaded telemetry -------
survey_ms   <- load_survey_data() |> filter(wave >= 1, wave <= 6)
sessions_ms <- bind_rows(
  telemetry_files$Nintendo |> transmute(pid, platform = "Nintendo", title_id, date, duration),
  telemetry_files$Xbox     |> transmute(pid, platform = "Xbox",     title_id, date, duration),
  telemetry_files$Steam    |> transmute(pid, platform = "Steam",    title_id, date, duration = minutes)
)
sessions_instudy <- add_waves(sessions_ms, survey_ms)

# Genre coverage of in-study playtime and platform composition (for Methods
# and Limitations): share of minutes matched to >= 1 study genre
matched_keys_ms <- load_game_metadata_long() |> distinct(original_name, platform)
cov_by_platform <- sessions_instudy |>
  left_join(matched_keys_ms |> mutate(matched = TRUE),
            by = c("title_id" = "original_name", "platform")) |>
  mutate(matched = replace_na(matched, FALSE)) |>
  group_by(platform) |>
  summarise(minutes = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
            pct_matched = 100 * sum(duration[matched], na.rm = TRUE) / minutes,
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(share = 100 * minutes / sum(minutes))
genre_cov_overall <- with(cov_by_platform, 100 * sum(minutes * pct_matched / 100) / sum(minutes))
cov_get   <- function(p) cov_by_platform$pct_matched[cov_by_platform$platform == p]
share_get <- function(p) cov_by_platform$share[cov_by_platform$platform == p]

# --- Telemetry history depth and wave-1 behaviour/availability --------------
# All rates below use the analytic sample as their basis: play rates are
# per analytic-sample participant; availability is per analytic-sample
# participant with any telemetry on the platform.
first_dates_ms <- sessions_ms |>
  filter(pid %in% analysis_pids) |>
  group_by(pid, platform) |>
  summarise(first_date = min(date, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  inner_join(survey_ms |> distinct(pid, baseline_date), by = "pid") |>
  mutate(days_before = as.numeric(baseline_date - first_date))
med_days <- first_dates_ms |>
  group_by(platform) |>
  summarise(median_days = median(days_before), .groups = "drop") |>
  (\(d) setNames(d$median_days, d$platform))()

w1_played <- sessions_instudy |>
  filter(wave == 1, pid %in% analysis_pids) |>
  distinct(pid, platform)
w1_rate   <- function(p) 100 * sum(w1_played$platform == p) / n_model
# Availability: telemetry history covers the full wave-1 window
w1_avail <- first_dates_ms |>
  mutate(covers_w1 = days_before >= 14) |>
  group_by(platform) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(covers_w1), .groups = "drop") |>
  (\(d) setNames(d$pct, d$platform))()

# Guard for the fixed prose: full-window telemetry availability is high on
# every platform among linked participants.
stopifnot(all(w1_avail[c("Nintendo", "Xbox", "Steam")] >= 80))
```

```{r}
#| label: load-mobile
#| include: false

survey <- load_survey_data()
baselines <- survey |> distinct(pid, baseline_date)

ios     <- read_csv(here("data/clean/ios.csv.gz"),     show_col_types = FALSE)
android <- read_csv(here("data/clean/android.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)

mobile <- bind_rows(ios, android) |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(day_local)) |>
  group_by(pid, date) |>
  summarise(minutes = sum(minutes, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(baselines, by = "pid") |>
  filter(!is.na(baseline_date)) |>
  mutate(wave = assign_wave_vec(date, baseline_date)) |>
  filter(!is.na(wave), wave >= 1, wave <= 6) |>
  group_by(pid, wave) |>
  summarise(mobile_hours_per_day = sum(minutes, na.rm = TRUE) / 60 / 14,
            .groups = "drop")

# Merge mobile into total_playtime (no double-counting; console/PC side comes
# from raw sessions via 01_preprocess.R)
total_playtime <- total_playtime |>
  left_join(mobile, by = c("pid", "wave")) |>
  mutate(
    mobile_hours_per_day     = replace_na(mobile_hours_per_day, 0),
    total_time_all_platforms = total_hours_per_day + mobile_hours_per_day
  ) |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  mutate(
    total_time_all_platforms_within  = total_time_all_platforms - mean(total_time_all_platforms, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_time_all_platforms_between = mean(total_time_all_platforms, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{r}
#| label: build-aggregated-playtime
#| include: false

# Build wide-format aggregated_playtime and genre variable vectors from the
# new long-format pipeline (genre_wave_long + total_playtime + survey).
#
# Sanitize genre names to valid R column names, e.g.:
#   "Action & Adventure"  → "time_action_adventure"
#   "Role-playing (RPG)"  → "time_role_playing_rpg"
#   "Shooter"             → "time_shooter"
genre_to_col <- function(g) {
  col <- gsub("[^a-z0-9]+", "_", tolower(g))
  col <- gsub("^_+|_+$", "", col)
  paste0("time_", col)
}

# Pivot genre_wave_long wide: one time_{genre} column per genre per pid × wave.
# values_fill = 0 handles genre × wave combos with no play.
genre_wide <- genre_wave_long |>
  mutate(col = genre_to_col(genre)) |>
  select(pid, wave, col, hours_per_day) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = col, values_from = hours_per_day, values_fill = 0)

genre_vars <- sort(setdiff(names(genre_wide), c("pid", "wave")))

# Build aggregated_playtime starting from the full survey (includes 0-play waves).
# Left-joining telemetry ensures participants who skipped gaming in a wave get 0.
aggregated_playtime <- survey |>
  select(pid, wave, wemwbs, self_reported_biweekly_play) |>
  left_join(
    total_playtime |> select(pid, wave, total_hours_per_day,
                             mobile_hours_per_day, total_time_all_platforms),
    by = c("pid", "wave")
  ) |>
  left_join(genre_wide, by = c("pid", "wave")) |>
  mutate(
    total_time_all_genres    = replace_na(total_hours_per_day, 0),
    mobile_hours_per_day     = replace_na(mobile_hours_per_day, 0),
    total_time_all_platforms = replace_na(total_time_all_platforms, 0),
    across(all_of(genre_vars), ~ replace_na(.x, 0))
  ) |>
  select(-total_hours_per_day) |>
  # Within/between decompose over ALL survey waves (including 0-play waves)
  group_by(pid) |>
  mutate(
    total_time_all_platforms_within  =
      total_time_all_platforms - mean(total_time_all_platforms, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_time_all_platforms_between =
      mean(total_time_all_platforms, na.rm = TRUE),
    across(
      all_of(genre_vars),
      list(
        within  = ~ .x - mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        between = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
      ),
      .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

genre_within_vars  <- paste0(genre_vars, "_within")
genre_between_vars <- paste0(genre_vars, "_between")
genre_vars_demean  <- c(genre_within_vars, genre_between_vars)
```

```{r}
    display_name = iconv(display_name, to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT"),

# Per-genre stats: n_games, total_minutes, mean_min_per_day, top 5 titles with % of genre playtime

    total_minutes = first(genre_total),
```

## Measures

The distributions and structure of the key variables are visualised in @fig-descriptives.

**Wellbeing.** Wellbeing was assessed using the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale [SWEMWBS; @tennant2007warwick], a 7-item short form of the WEMWBS covering psychological functioning and subjective wellbeing over the past 2 weeks, with responses on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from "None of the time" to "All of the time." Scores are computed as the arithmetic mean of the 7 items (range: 1–5), not the conventional summed 7–35 scale. All reported coefficients, priors, and the pre-registered SESOI are defined on this item-mean scale.

**Video game playtime.** Digital trace data from Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam provide session-level records (per-title start and end timestamps), while iOS and Android contribute only daily aggregate minutes (no game-level metadata). Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam therefore contribute to both H1 (total playtime) and H2 (genre-specific playtime); iOS and Android contribute only to the pre-registered all-platform sensitivity analysis (Appendix B, Deviation D6). Total playtime is computed from raw sessions without multi-genre duplication (see Game genre classification below).

**Game genre classification.** Game genre for Nintendo and Steam is obtained by cross-referencing game titles in the digital trace data with the Internet Games Database (igdb.com); `r n_raw_genre_labels` distinct raw IGDB genre labels appear in the study's game metadata (e.g., Platform, Role-playing (RPG), Simulator). IGDB is, to our knowledge, the only database with complete metadata coverage of games across platforms that offers an API for programmatic data retrieval. The platform is crowd-sourced; community members can submit contributions (e.g., a new game or alternative categorisation), which are vetted by admins and moderators before appearing in the database. Genre labels used are those recorded in the Open Play dataset at the time of data collection [@ballou2025openplay]. For Xbox, genre labels provided by the Xbox store are mapped onto the IGDB taxonomy (see Appendix A); Xbox titles are anonymised and cannot be matched by name. A string-formatting issue in the upstream mapping pipeline had left approximately `r round(100 - xbox_pct_before)`% of Xbox playtime unmapped; we corrected this locally using the `xbox_primary_genre` and `xbox_subgenre` metadata fields, increasing Xbox genre coverage from `r round(xbox_pct_before)`% to `r round(xbox_pct_after)`% of playtime (see Appendix B, Deviation U1). We do not consider IGDB "themes" or other metadata fields. Overall, `r round(genre_cov_overall, 1)`% of in-study playtime is matched to at least one study genre (Steam `r round(cov_get("Steam"), 1)`%, Nintendo `r round(cov_get("Nintendo"), 1)`%, Xbox `r round(cov_get("Xbox"), 1)`%); unmatched playtime counts towards total playtime but towards no genre.

IGDB's raw genres were collapsed into 14 study-level categories: **Strategy** subsumes Turn-Based Strategy (TBS), Real-Time Strategy (RTS), Tactical, and MOBA; **Puzzle** subsumes Card & Board Game and Quiz/Trivia; **Arcade** subsumes Pinball and Music; **Indie** is excluded. The remaining genres (Adventure, Shooter, Role-playing (RPG), Simulator, Sport, Racing, Platform, Fighting, Hack-and-slash/Beat-'em-up, Point-and-click, and Visual Novel) are retained as distinct categories. (IGDB does not include a top-level "Action" category; what is colloquially called "action" is distributed across Shooter, Hack-and-slash, Fighting, and Platform.) A complete mapping table is in Appendix A.

**Multi-genre attribution.** The pre-registration specified using only each game's primary (first) IGDB genre. Because many games genuinely span multiple genres, the main analysis instead uses full attribution: a session of a game carrying $k$ genre labels contributes its full duration to each of the $k$ genres (see Appendix B, Deviation D1). We treat genre as an attribute of the play experience rather than as a partition of time; a 60-minute session of an Adventure-RPG (such as *Elden Ring* or *Skyrim*) contributes 60 minutes to Adventure and, simultaneously, 60 minutes to RPG. Dividing the hour between the two labels would understate exposure to both, and using only the first-listed label would discard meaningful classification information while depending on IGDB's arbitrary label ordering. One consequence must be kept in mind throughout: exposures are not additive across genres. Each genre's exposure is bounded by real playtime, but the sum across genres exceeds time played, and no analysis interprets that sum; total playtime for H1 is therefore computed separately from the raw sessions, and no double counting enters it. Each genre coefficient estimates the association between exposure to games carrying that label and wellbeing, not the effect of that genre in isolation. The pre-registered primary-genre analysis is reported in supplementary materials.

```{r}
#| label: genre-upset-data
#| include: false

# Filter to only games played by participants in the analysis.
# telemetry_genre (loaded above) contains wave-assigned sessions for study
# participants; semi_join restricts meta_long_full to those title_ids only.
relevant_games <- telemetry_genre |> distinct(title_id, platform)

# Build combination labels and playtime per game-platform pair
game_combos <- meta_long_full |>
  semi_join(relevant_games, by = c("original_name" = "title_id", "platform")) |>
  distinct(original_name, platform, genre) |>
  group_by(original_name, platform) |>
  summarise(combination = paste(sort(genre), collapse = " + "), .groups = "drop")

n_total_games <- nrow(game_combos)

# Total playtime per game-platform pair.
# telemetry_genre is genre-long (one row per session x genre label), so a
# k-genre game's sessions appear k times; divide by the game's label count
# to recover true playtime. Within a game the label set is constant.
game_hours <- telemetry_genre |>
  group_by(title_id, platform) |>
  summarise(
    total_hours = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE) / 60 / n_distinct(genre),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Summary statistics for the co-occurrence prose in Measures
cooc_stats <- game_combos |>
  left_join(game_hours, by = c("original_name" = "title_id", "platform")) |>
  mutate(
    total_hours = replace_na(total_hours, 0),
    multi = str_detect(combination, fixed(" + "))
  ) |>
  summarise(
    n_combinations       = n_distinct(combination),
    pct_multigenre_games = 100 * mean(multi),
    pct_multigenre_hours = 100 * sum(total_hours[multi]) / sum(total_hours)
  )
n_combinations       <- cooc_stats$n_combinations
pct_multigenre_games <- cooc_stats$pct_multigenre_games
pct_multigenre_hours <- cooc_stats$pct_multigenre_hours

# --- Data for playtime-weighted UpSet plot (exact hours) ---
# Compute exact total hours per genre intersection
int_hours <- game_combos |>
  left_join(game_hours, by = c("original_name" = "title_id", "platform")) |>
  mutate(total_hours = replace_na(total_hours, 0)) |>
  group_by(combination) |>
  summarise(hours = sum(total_hours), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(hours)) |>
  slice_head(n = 40) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number())

# Parse each combination into its constituent genres
int_genres <- int_hours |>
  mutate(genres_list = str_split(combination, " \\+ ")) |>
  unnest(genres_list) |>
  rename(genre = genres_list)

# All genres appearing in the top intersections (ordered by total hours across
# all games, ascending so the most common genre appears at the top of the matrix)
genre_totals <- game_combos |>
  left_join(game_hours, by = c("original_name" = "title_id", "platform")) |>
  mutate(total_hours = replace_na(total_hours, 0)) |>
  mutate(genres_list = str_split(combination, " \\+ ")) |>
  unnest(genres_list) |>
  group_by(genre = genres_list) |>
  summarise(genre_hours = sum(total_hours), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(genre_hours)

genre_order <- genre_totals$genre

# Dot matrix: which genres are active for each intersection
dot_df <- expand_grid(rank = int_hours$rank, genre = genre_order) |>
  left_join(int_genres |> select(rank, genre) |> mutate(active = TRUE),
            by = c("rank", "genre")) |>
  mutate(active = replace_na(active, FALSE),
         genre = factor(genre, levels = genre_order))

# Connecting segments between active dots in multi-genre intersections
seg_df <- int_genres |>
  mutate(ypos = match(genre, genre_order)) |>
  group_by(rank) |>
  filter(n() > 1) |>
  summarise(
    ymin = genre_order[min(ypos)],
    ymax = genre_order[max(ypos)],
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
# Compose: left genre bars aligned with the dot matrix; bars on top

p_spacer <- plot_spacer()

p_spacer + p_bars + p_genre + p_matrix +
```
