:::

**Composition weights and display conventions.** Two further quantities derive from the same attribution scheme. The first is the composition weight used by the multi-membership model: each wave's weights are the shares of its attributed playtime that fall in each genre, normalised to sum to one, and the model distributes the wave's true total playtime across genres according to these weights. Because games with more labels contribute to more shares, such games receive slightly more weight than an equal division of each session's time would give them, which is consistent with the exposure construct. The second is a display convention: figures that present genres one at a time report full-attribution exposures, matching the model inputs, whereas the one display that stacks genres into a daily total (@fig-descriptives, panel D) divides each session's time equally across its labels, so that the stacked bars represent clock time.

**Genre co-occurrence.** Because full attribution makes genre exposures non-exclusive, the structure of genre co-occurrence matters for interpreting every genre-level estimate: each genre coefficient describes exposure to a label in the company that label keeps. Multi-label games dominate the present data: `r round(pct_multigenre_games)`% of genre-matched titles and `r round(pct_multigenre_hours)`% of genre-matched playtime involve games carrying more than one label, across `r n_combinations` distinct observed combinations. @fig-genre-upset shows the playtime-weighted co-occurrence structure across these combinations, and @tbl-genre-cooccurrence lists the fifteen most-played combinations with their top titles, making concrete which games drive each pairing.

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-genre-cooccurrence
#| tbl-cap: "Top 15 genre combinations by total playtime. Multi-genre rows join labels with ' + '. Total hours = playtime for games with that combination; % of playtime = share of all genre-matched playtime; n games = unique game-platform pairs. Xbox titles anonymised."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| echo: false

# Session-level stats per combination.
# telemetry_genre already has display_name from the genre-descriptives-extended chunk.
# Deflate genre-long rows by each game's label count (see game_hours above)
# so per-title minutes count each session once.
title_min <- telemetry_genre |>
  left_join(game_combos, by = c("title_id" = "original_name", "platform")) |>
  filter(!is.na(combination)) |>
  group_by(combination, title_id, display_name) |>
  summarise(total_min = sum(duration, na.rm = TRUE) / n_distinct(genre),
            .groups = "drop")

total_matched_minutes <- sum(title_min$total_min)

combo_stats <- title_min |>
  group_by(combination) |>
  mutate(
    combo_total = sum(total_min),
    pct_title   = round(100 * total_min / combo_total, 1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_min)) |>
  summarise(
    n_games          = n(),
    total_minutes    = first(combo_total),
    mean_min_per_day = first(combo_total) / total_person_days,
    top_5 = paste(
      paste0(display_name[1:min(5, n())], " [", pct_title[1:min(5, n())], "%]"),
      collapse = ", "
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_minutes)) |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  mutate(
    `% of playtime` = round(100 * total_minutes / total_matched_minutes, 1)
  ) |>
  transmute(
    `Genre combination` = gsub("[()]", "", combination),
    `Total hours`       = round(total_minutes / 60, 1),
    `% of playtime`,
    `n games`           = n_games,
    `Mean min/day`      = round(mean_min_per_day, 1),
    `Top 5 titles`      = replace_na(top_5, "")
  )

combo_stats |>
  tt(width = c(0.20, 0.09, 0.10, 0.08, 0.09, 0.44)) |>
  format_tt(digits = 1) |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.8) |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)
```
:::

**Demographics.** Age, gender, ethnicity, country, and employment were collected at baseline via self-report. Full demographic characteristics are reported in @tbl-demographics.

@fig-descriptives introduces the measures the models work with: the outcome's distribution at each biweekly wave (A), the distribution of the daily-playtime dose (B), the platform composition of the recorded play (C), and the day-to-day course of playtime, genre composition, and wellbeing for one participant with above-average playtime (D). Panel D makes the modelling problem concrete: within an individual, playtime, genre mix, and wellbeing all fluctuate from wave to wave, and their relationship is not discernible by eye. This is the situation that the within-between decomposition and the multi-membership specification below are designed to handle.

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-descriptives
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("*Distributions, Composition, and Raw Structure of the Study Measures.* (A) SWEMWBS by wave: density, raw person-wave observations, and median box, fill lightening from wave 1 to 6. (B) Average daily playtime across person-waves with recorded play (15-minute bins; dashed line: median; x-axis truncated at the 99th percentile); ", round(pct_zero_pw), "% of person-waves have no recorded play. (C) Platform share of recorded playtime across study days 1\u201384. (D) Raw measures for one participant at the 75th percentile of playtime (ID ", p75_pid, "): daily playtime coloured by genre, with multi-genre time split equally across labels so bar heights are clock time (analysis exposures use full attribution; Appendix B, Deviation D1). Biweekly SWEMWBS is the purple line, read against the right axis.")'
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 9.5
#| echo: false

desc_svy <- survey |> filter(pid %in% analysis_pids)

pw <- desc_svy |>
  select(pid, wave, wemwbs) |>
  left_join(total_playtime |> select(pid, wave, total_hours_per_day),
            by = c("pid", "wave")) |>
  mutate(total_hours_per_day = replace_na(total_hours_per_day, 0))
pct_zero_pw <- 100 * mean(pw$total_hours_per_day == 0)

# Panel A: SWEMWBS by wave (raincloud: density + raw points + median box),
# fill lightening across waves 1-6.
panel_a <- desc_svy |>
  filter(!is.na(wemwbs)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(wave), y = wemwbs, fill = factor(wave))) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.8, width = 0.6, justification = -0.25,
                       .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.06, alpha = 0.04, size = 0.4, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, fill = NA, colour = "grey20",
               linewidth = 0.35) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colorRampPalette(c("#5E3C99", "#D8CFEA"))(6),
                    guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1, 5)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title = "Wellbeing by Wave",
       subtitle = "SWEMWBS distributions per biweekly wave",
       x = "Wave", y = "SWEMWBS (1\u20135)")

# Panel B: distribution of the playtime dose (15-minute bins; median marked)
pw_pos <- pw |> filter(total_hours_per_day > 0)
med_dose <- median(pw_pos$total_hours_per_day)
panel_b <- ggplot(pw_pos, aes(x = total_hours_per_day)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0, fill = "#E69F00",
                 colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = med_dose, linetype = 2, colour = "grey20") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, quantile(pw_pos$total_hours_per_day, 0.99))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title = "Playtime Dose",
       subtitle = "Average daily hours per person-wave with play",
       x = "Average daily playtime (hours)", y = "Person-waves")

# Panel C: platform share of recorded playtime across study days
study_starts <- survey |>
  distinct(pid, baseline_date) |>
  filter(!is.na(baseline_date)) |>
  transmute(pid, study_start = as.Date(baseline_date))

plat_daily <- bind_rows(
  telemetry_files$Nintendo |> transmute(pid, date, platform = "Nintendo", minutes = duration),
  telemetry_files$Xbox     |> transmute(pid, date, platform = "Xbox",     minutes = duration),
  telemetry_files$Steam    |> transmute(pid, date, platform = "Steam",    minutes = minutes)
) |>
  filter(pid %in% analysis_pids) |>
  inner_join(study_starts, by = "pid") |>
  mutate(study_day = as.integer(date - study_start) + 1L) |>
  filter(study_day >= 1, study_day <= 84) |>
  count(study_day, platform, wt = minutes, name = "minutes") |>
  group_by(study_day) |>
  mutate(prop = minutes / sum(minutes)) |>
  ungroup()

panel_c <- ggplot(plat_daily, aes(x = study_day, y = prop, fill = platform)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Nintendo = "#D55E00", Steam = "#0072B2", Xbox = "#009E73")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 84, 14)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title = "Platform Composition",
       subtitle = "Share of recorded playtime per study day",
       x = "Study day", y = "Share of playtime", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# Panel D: raw measures for the 75th-percentile participant.
# Stacked bars must sum to clock time, so for DISPLAY each session's minutes
# are split equally across its genre labels (a 1 h Shooter+Strategy session
# shows as 30 min of each). This mirrors the multi-membership model's view:
# true total time distributed by genre composition. The analysis exposures
# themselves use full attribution (Appendix B, Deviation D1) and are shown
# per genre, unstacked, in the co-occurrence figure.
daily_genre_telemetry <- load_genre_sessions(meta_long_full) |>
  group_by(pid, platform, title_id, date) |>
  mutate(n_labels = n_distinct(genre)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(minutes_split = duration / n_labels) |>
  group_by(pid, date, genre) |>
  summarise(minutes = sum(minutes_split, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  rename(day_local = date) |>
  mutate(genre_display = if_else(genre %in% names(raw_to_display),
                                 unname(raw_to_display[genre]), genre))

dgs <- daily_genre_telemetry |>
  inner_join(study_starts, by = "pid") |>
  mutate(study_day = as.integer(day_local - study_start) + 1L) |>
  filter(study_day >= 1, study_day <= 84)

eligible_cs <- desc_svy |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  summarise(n_surveys = sum(!is.na(wemwbs)), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_surveys >= 3)

tot_by_pid <- dgs |>
  semi_join(eligible_cs, by = "pid") |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  summarise(total_minutes = sum(minutes),
            n_genres = n_distinct(genre), .groups = "drop")

# 75th-percentile target; prefer the most genre-diverse participant within 10%
p75_target <- quantile(tot_by_pid$total_minutes, 0.75)
p75_cand <- tot_by_pid |>
  mutate(d = abs(total_minutes - p75_target)) |>
  filter(d <= pmax(p75_target * 0.10, 60)) |>
  arrange(desc(n_genres), d)
p75_pid <- if (nrow(p75_cand) > 0) p75_cand$pid[1] else
  tot_by_pid |> slice_min(abs(total_minutes - p75_target), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |> pull(pid)

cs_grid <- dgs |>
  filter(pid == p75_pid) |>
  count(study_day, g = genre_display, wt = minutes, name = "minutes") |>
  right_join(expand_grid(study_day = 1:84, g = rank14),
             by = c("study_day", "g")) |>
  mutate(minutes = replace_na(minutes, 0),
         g = factor(g, levels = rank14))

cs_wb <- desc_svy |>
  filter(pid == p75_pid, !is.na(wemwbs)) |>
  inner_join(study_starts, by = "pid") |>
  mutate(study_day = as.integer(as.Date(date) - study_start) + 1L) |>
  select(study_day, wemwbs)

# Split attribution makes stacked daily totals clock time; guard the bound.
stopifnot(max(tapply(cs_grid$minutes, cs_grid$study_day, sum)) <= 24 * 60)
coeff_cs <- max(tapply(cs_grid$minutes, cs_grid$study_day, sum)) / 4

panel_d <- ggplot() +
  geom_col(data = cs_grid, aes(x = study_day, y = minutes, fill = g), width = 1) +
  geom_line(data = cs_wb, aes(x = study_day, y = (wemwbs - 1) * coeff_cs),
            colour = "#5E3C99", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = cs_wb, aes(x = study_day, y = (wemwbs - 1) * coeff_cs),
             colour = "#5E3C99", size = 2.3, shape = 15) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal_genre, name = NULL) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 84, 14), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    "Daily playtime (minutes)",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / coeff_cs + 1, name = "SWEMWBS", breaks = 1:5)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title = "One Participant in Full",
       subtitle = "Daily playtime by genre composition, with biweekly wellbeing overlaid (right axis)",
       x = "Study day") +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.size = unit(4.5, "mm"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title.y.right = element_text(colour = "#5E3C99"),
    axis.text.y.right  = element_text(colour = "#5E3C99"),
    axis.ticks.y.right = element_line(colour = "#5E3C99")
  )

p_descriptives <- ((panel_a | panel_b | panel_c) / panel_d) +
  patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.1)) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9.5, colour = "grey35"))

p_descriptives
```
:::

## Analytic Approach

SWEMWBS asks participants to reflect on their wellbeing "over the past 2 weeks." The wave 1 survey was completed on the baseline day itself, so the two weeks it describes lie before baseline. Each playtime window is therefore aligned retrospectively to the survey it accompanies: wave 1 playtime covers days −14 to −1, wave 2 covers days 0–13, and so on through wave 6 (days 56–69; Deviation D3). This alignment is possible because participants linked their gaming accounts at intake, which provides telemetry from before the study formally began. Recorded histories covered the full wave 1 window for `r round(w1_avail["Steam"])`% (Steam), `r round(w1_avail["Nintendo"])`% (Nintendo), and `r round(w1_avail["Xbox"])`% (Xbox) of linked participants; Nintendo and Xbox histories extend a median of `r round(med_days["Nintendo"] / 365.25, 1)` and `r round(med_days["Xbox"] / 365.25, 1)` years before baseline, and Steam a median of `r round(med_days["Steam"])` days. During the wave 1 window, `r round(w1_rate("Steam"))`%, `r round(w1_rate("Nintendo"))`%, and `r round(w1_rate("Xbox"))`% of analytic-sample participants had recorded play on Steam, Nintendo, and Xbox respectively; these rates reflect which platforms participants use rather than gaps in data availability.

All models use a within-between decomposition of playtime, which we explain here once. Each playtime variable is separated into two components: a between-person component, defined as the participant's average across the study, and a within-person component, defined as the deviation of a given wave from that personal average. The two components answer different questions. The within-person coefficient describes whether a participant's wellbeing changes in waves in which they play more than they usually do; because each participant serves as their own comparison, this coefficient is unaffected by stable differences between people. The between-person coefficient describes whether participants who habitually play more report different average wellbeing than participants who habitually play less; this comparison is made across people and is therefore vulnerable to confounding by stable individual differences. Every model estimates both coefficients.

We fit four Bayesian multilevel models. M0 includes total playtime only and addresses H1. M1, M2, and M3 add genre-specific terms and address H2. The three genre models differ in how much information the estimate for one genre shares with the estimates for the others: M1 estimates each genre's coefficients independently (the pre-registered structure), M2 places a common prior distribution over the genre coefficients and estimates its standard deviation (partial pooling), and M3 assigns each wave to the genres it contains in proportion to their playtime shares (multi-membership). Deviations from the pre-registered plan are catalogued in Appendix B and are flagged below where they affect interpretation.

### M0: Total Playtime

M0 addresses H1: is total playtime across Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam associated with wellbeing? The model is a random-effects within-between (REWB) regression and returns the two coefficients defined above, $\beta_W$ for within-person fluctuations and $\beta_B$ for habitual between-person differences. Each participant receives a random intercept, because people differ in baseline wellbeing, and a random slope for within-person playtime, because the association need not be identical for everyone; the spread of these person-specific slopes is used later to bound individual susceptibility. Mobile platforms are excluded so that total playtime is defined identically in M0 and in the genre models, which cannot include them (Deviation D6; the pre-registered supplement retains the all-platform total). Priors are calibrated to the 1–5 outcome scale: the intercept prior is centred on the scale midpoint, and the coefficient priors are weakly informative, leaving effects up to roughly 1 point per hour/day plausible while regularising implausibly large values.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\
\mu_{ij} &= \alpha + \beta_W \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} + \beta_B \text{Time}_{\text{between},j} + u_{0j} + u_{1j} \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} \\
\begin{pmatrix} u_{0j} \\ u_{1j} \end{pmatrix} &\sim \text{Normal}\left(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right) \\
\alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 3, 2) \\
\beta_W, \beta_B &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 0, 0.5)
\end{aligned}$$

### M1: Pre-Registered Fixed-Effects

M1 is the pre-registered specification for H2. Each of the 14 genres receives its own within-person and between-person coefficient, estimated independently, with a random intercept per participant. Independent estimation has a benefit and a cost. The benefit is that the model imposes no assumptions about how similar genres are to one another. The cost is that rarely played genres are estimated from little data and therefore receive wide credible intervals; this is the problem that M2 and M3 address. Because genre exposures are non-exclusive, they cannot be summed to recover total playtime, and M1 therefore contains no separate total-playtime term. Two departures from the registered specification should be noted: exposures use full attribution rather than primary-genre labels (Deviation D1), and the registered random slopes for all genre terms (28 additional parameters) proved near-singular, so we followed the pre-registered contingency plan and retained the random intercept only.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\
\mu_{ij} &= \alpha + \sum_{g=1}^{G}\bigl(\beta_{W,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{within},g,ij} + \beta_{B,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{between},g,j}\bigr) + u_{0j} \\
u_{0j} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau_{\text{pid}}) \\
\alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 3, 2) \\
\beta_{W,g}, \beta_{B,g} &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 0, 0.5)
\end{aligned}$$

### M2: Hierarchical Prior

M2 keeps M1's structure but changes how the genre coefficients are estimated, and this change yields a direct answer to H2. Rather than treating the 14 coefficients as unrelated, M2 assumes that they are drawn from a common normal distribution centred at zero and estimates the standard deviation of that distribution, τ~genre~, separately for the within-person and between-person dimensions. τ~genre~ is therefore an estimate of exactly the quantity H2 asks about: how much the genre coefficients differ from one another, expressed in outcome units per hour of play. The shared distribution also produces partial pooling. Estimates for rarely played genres are pulled towards the common centre, which stabilises them; genres with ample data retain estimates close to their independent values.

The Half-Normal(0, 0.1) hyperprior on τ is matched to the outcome scale. Genre coefficients are expressed in SWEMWBS points per hour/day, and the smallest effect size of interest is 0.06 on that scale, so a much wider hyperprior would place substantial prior mass on heterogeneity far larger than any effect considered plausible. The sensitivity of the results to halving and doubling this scale is examined in Appendix D. Sampling near τ = 0 is numerically difficult, so we use conservative sampler settings and report divergence counts and R-hat diagnostics for every model alongside the results.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\
\mu_{ij} &= \alpha + \sum_{g=1}^{G}\bigl(\beta_{W,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{within},g,ij} + \beta_{B,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{between},g,j}\bigr) + u_{0j} \\
u_{0j} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau_{\text{pid}}) \\
\beta_{W,g} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau_{\text{within}}) \\
\beta_{B,g} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau_{\text{between}}) \\
\tau_{\text{within}}, \tau_{\text{between}} &\sim \text{Half-Normal}(0, 0.1) \\
\alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 3, 2)
\end{aligned}$$

### M3: Multi-Membership

M3 represents each wave the way panel D of @fig-descriptives displays it: as a total amount of playtime with a genre composition. The model retains total playtime as the predictor, inheriting M0's structure including the overall $\beta_W$ and $\beta_B$, and allows the composition of that playtime to modify the playtime slope. Formally, this is a multi-membership structure, originally developed for settings in which one observation belongs to several groups at once, such as pupils who attend more than one school. Here, each wave belongs to every genre played in it, with membership weights equal to each genre's share of the wave's attributed playtime. A wave consisting mostly of Shooter play is governed mostly by the Shooter slope adjustment; a wave divided between Adventure and RPG draws on both adjustments in proportion.

Each genre's slope adjustment is drawn from a common distribution, and the standard deviation of that distribution, σ~s~, is this model's answer to H2: it quantifies how much the playtime–wellbeing slope varies with the genres being played, after partial pooling. Three specification choices require comment. First, the model moderates only the playtime slope and includes no genre-specific intercepts; whether, for example, habitual RPG players report higher baseline wellbeing than habitual Shooter players is a question about self-selection, not about genre moderation. Second, the Half-Normal(0, 0.3) hyperprior on σ~s~ is wider than M2's, because the multi-membership posterior samples poorly under a tighter prior; this scale is likewise stress-tested in Appendix D. Third, waves with no recorded play receive uniform weights across genres, a technical requirement of the implementation with little consequence, because such waves carry almost no information about genre-specific effects.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\
\mu_{ij} &= \alpha + \beta_W \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} + \beta_B \text{Time}_{\text{between},j} + u_{0j} + u_{1j} \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} \\
&\quad + \sum_{g=1}^{G} w_{g,ij}(s_{W,g} \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} + s_{B,g} \text{Time}_{\text{between},j}) \\
\begin{pmatrix} u_{0j} \\ u_{1j} \end{pmatrix} &\sim \text{Normal}\left(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\right) \\
s_{W,g} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_s) \\
s_{B,g} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_{s,\text{between}}) \\
\alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 3, 2) \\
\beta_W, \beta_B &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 0, 0.5) \\
\sigma_s, \sigma_{s,\text{between}} &\sim \text{Half-Normal}(0, 0.3)
\end{aligned}$$

Because this use of multi-membership is unconventional (every wave carries all 14 genre labels and only the weights vary), we validated the specification by parameter recovery before fitting it to real data. Synthetic datasets with known genre-slope heterogeneity were fit with identical model code; every population-level parameter, including σ~s~, was recovered within its 95% credible interval, with no divergent transitions (simulation report in the supplementary materials). A simulation-based precision analysis for the pre-registered design is part of the Stage 1 protocol [@ballou2024psychological]. An exploratory daily-timescale analysis, specified after the registered analyses were complete, is described in the Exploratory Daily-Timescale Analysis subsection below and reported at the end of the Results.

## Missing Data

```{r}
#| label: missing-data-stats
#| include: false

biw_md <- read_csv(here("data/clean/survey_biweekly.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(wemwbs_md = rowMeans(across(starts_with("wemwbs_")), na.rm = FALSE))

n_wave7_rows <- sum(biw_md$wave > 6)

biw_md6 <- biw_md |> filter(wave >= 1, wave <= 6)
md_pids <- biw_md6 |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs_md)) |> distinct(pid) |> pull(pid)

n_md_pids       <- length(md_pids)
n_md_grid       <- n_md_pids * 6
n_md_submitted  <- biw_md6 |> filter(pid %in% md_pids) |> nrow()
n_md_item_miss  <- biw_md6 |> filter(pid %in% md_pids, is.na(wemwbs_md)) |> nrow()
n_md_valid      <- n_md_submitted - n_md_item_miss
n_md_wave_miss  <- n_md_grid - n_md_valid
pct_md_wave_miss <- round(100 * n_md_wave_miss / n_md_grid, 1)

wave_response <- biw_md6 |>
  filter(pid %in% md_pids) |>
  count(wave) |>
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / n_md_pids))

# Observed within-person SD of SWEMWBS (used to contextualise the SESOI)
wemwbs_within_sd <- biw_md6 |>
  filter(pid %in% md_pids, !is.na(wemwbs_md)) |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  filter(n() > 1) |>
  mutate(dev = wemwbs_md - mean(wemwbs_md)) |>
  pull(dev) |>
  sd()
wemwbs_total_sd <- sd(biw_md6$wemwbs_md, na.rm = TRUE)
# Guard for the fixed prose ("roughly a third of a within-person SD")
stopifnot(wemwbs_within_sd > 0.28, wemwbs_within_sd < 0.45)
```

Missingness in the outcome takes two forms, of markedly different sizes. Among submitted surveys, item-level missingness is rare and all-or-nothing: `r n_md_item_miss` submitted responses lack SWEMWBS, every one missing all seven items. The dominant form is wave nonresponse: survey completion declined from `r wave_response$pct[1]`% at wave 1 to `r wave_response$pct[6]`% at wave 6, leaving `r formatC(n_md_wave_miss, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` of the `r formatC(n_md_grid, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` analytic person-waves (`r pct_md_wave_miss`%) without an observed SWEMWBS. Telemetry-derived playtime is unaffected: tracking was continuous and automatic, so within linked platforms an absence of recorded play is a recorded absence rather than missing data, and exposures exist for every person-wave.

The primary Bayesian models are fit to the observed outcomes; their mixed-effects likelihood is valid provided outcome missingness is at random given the modelled covariates and random effects. To test the burden that assumption carries, we multiply imputed SWEMWBS on the complete participant × wave grid, following the protocol of the programmatic registered report's other Stage 2 outputs: hierarchical two-level multiple imputation by chained equations \[`mice` and `miceadds`; @vanbuuren2011mice; @robitzsch2024miceadds\] with predictive mean matching (`2l.pmm`), participants as random-intercept clusters [@vanbuuren2018flexible], and m = 100 imputations set from the pilot fraction of missing information by von Hippel's [-@vonhippel2020] two-stage rule. Because predictive mean matching donates observed values, imputed scores respect the 1–5 scale. As can be seen in Appendix D (@tbl-sensitivity-imputation), the results from the multiple imputed analyses do not meaningfully differ from the complete-case analyses.

## Smallest Effect Size of Interest

Establishing the absence of a practically significant effect requires committing in advance to a smallest effect size of interest (SESOI): the threshold below which an association is too small to matter. By practically significant, we mean the smallest change in wellbeing that a player would themselves notice, known as a minimally important difference. Following @ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024, our SESOI of 0.06 SWEMWBS item-mean points per hour of daily play is built from two quantities. The first is how large a change in wellbeing must be before a person notices it: approximately 0.3 points on the 1–5 scale, a value @ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024 anchored within the range implied by WEMWBS responsiveness studies (important change of 3 to 8 points on the 14–70 summed scale, i.e. roughly 0.2 to 0.6 points per item; @maheswaranEvaluatingResponsivenessWarwick2012) and that converges with anchor-based estimates for related depression and positive-affect measures [@anvari2021anchor]. The second is how large a change in playtime is realistically available: UK and US adults average approximately 5 hours of daily leisure time [@sturmFreeTimePhysical2019], an upper bound on how much daily play could plausibly rise or fall. The SESOI is the ratio of the two: 0.3 ÷ 5 = 0.06 points per hour. An association smaller than this means that even a person who shifted their entire daily leisure time into or out of gaming would not experience a noticeable change in wellbeing; there are not enough hours in the day for such an effect to matter.

We evaluate all coefficients against the Region of Practical Equivalence [ROPE; @kruschke2018rejecting], defined as the interval \[−0.06, +0.06\]. Each coefficient receives one of four verdicts from where its 95% credible interval (CrI) falls: entirely inside the ROPE, practically null, meaning even the largest plausible effect is too small to matter; entirely above +0.06, practically positive, or entirely below −0.06, practically negative (meaningfully associated with higher and lower wellbeing, respectively). A CrI straddling either edge of the ROPE is inconclusive: the effect could be practically null or practically meaningful.

## Exploratory Daily-Timescale Analysis

```{r}
#| label: daily-setup
#| include: false
#| eval: true

# Exploratory daily-timescale extension. Unregistered; the analysis plan
# (notes/analysis_plan_daily.md, local working docs) fixed the equivalence
# threshold transfer, exposure window, model set, priors, and the coverage
# amendment BEFORE any exposure-outcome model was estimated. Fits are
# produced by R/fit_daily_models.R and cached under models/daily/.

daily_frame_raw <- read_csv(here("data/processed/daily/daily_model_frame.csv"),
                            show_col_types = FALSE)
d_gh_cols <- sort(grep("^gh_", names(daily_frame_raw), value = TRUE))
stopifnot(length(d_gh_cols) == 14, "covered" %in% names(daily_frame_raw))

d_decompose <- function(df) {
  df |>
    group_by(pid) |>
    mutate(
      total_within  = total_hours_today - mean(total_hours_today, na.rm = TRUE),
      total_between = habitual_daily_hours
    ) |>
    ungroup()
}
# Analysed sample: telemetry-covered responses from participants with reliable
# timezone inference, excluding degenerate same-day windows (< 1 h).
daily_frame <- d_decompose(
  daily_frame_raw |>
    filter(covered, !tz_unreliable, window_hours >= 1,
           !is.na(habitual_daily_hours))
)

# Sample and compliance quantities for the prose
d_n_resp_all   <- nrow(daily_frame_raw)
d_n_pid_all    <- n_distinct(daily_frame_raw$pid)
d_n_resp       <- nrow(daily_frame)
d_n_pid        <- n_distinct(daily_frame$pid)
d_days_per_pid <- daily_frame |> count(pid) |> pull(n)
d_median_days  <- median(d_days_per_pid)
d_zero_share   <- mean(daily_frame$total_hours_today == 0)
d_wh_med       <- median(daily_frame$window_hours)
d_n_tz_unrel   <- daily_frame_raw |> filter(tz_unreliable) |> distinct(pid) |> nrow()
d_day1_n       <- sum(daily_frame_raw$day == 1)
d_day30_n      <- sum(daily_frame_raw$day == 30)
d_n_no_tel_pid <- daily_frame_raw |> filter(!has_telemetry) |>
  distinct(pid) |> nrow()
d_n_uncov_resp <- sum(!daily_frame_raw$covered)

# The daily outcome is a 0-100 slider; the biweekly life-satisfaction item
# used by the bridge model is the 0-10 Cantril ladder. Each therefore gets
# its own equivalence benchmark, both built like the registered SESOI: a
# minimally important difference divided by the roughly five hours of daily
# leisure realistically available.
d_mid_daily  <- 5     # slider points (see text for the convergent anchors)
d_primary    <- d_mid_daily / 5
d_mid_bridge <- 0.5   # Cantril ladder rungs
d_bridge_th  <- d_mid_bridge / 5

# Guard the item descriptions the Measures text relies on: the daily slider
# takes far more than 11 values, the biweekly ladder exactly 11.
stopifnot(
  n_distinct(daily_frame_raw$life_sat[!is.na(daily_frame_raw$life_sat)]) > 11,
  max(daily_frame_raw$life_sat, na.rm = TRUE) > 10
)

# Within-person SDs (used descriptively for the cross-timescale standardised
# comparison in the reading paragraph, and the bridge's s_w).
sesoi_d <- readRDS(here("models/daily/sesoi.rds"))
d_within_sd <- function(x, id) {
  d <- tibble(x = x, id = id) |> filter(!is.na(x)) |>
    group_by(id) |> filter(n() >= 2) |> mutate(dev = x - mean(x)) |> ungroup()
  sd(d$dev)
}
stopifnot(
  abs(d_within_sd(daily_frame_raw$life_sat, daily_frame_raw$pid) -
        sesoi_d$s_w_ls) < 1e-6
)

# Correlation between the daily outcome and the momentary valence slider
# (both outcomes; no exposure involved). Quoted in the limitations.
d_ls_av <- daily_frame_raw |> filter(!is.na(life_sat), !is.na(affective_valence))
d_ls_av_r <- cor(d_ls_av$life_sat, d_ls_av$affective_valence)
d_ls_av_rw <- d_ls_av |>
  group_by(pid) |> filter(n() >= 2) |>
  mutate(ls = life_sat - mean(life_sat),
         av = affective_valence - mean(affective_valence)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  summarise(r = cor(ls, av)) |>
  pull(r)

# Positive control 1: self-reported play (past 24 h) vs telemetry in a
# MATCHED 24-hour window; the control keeps the 24 h base precisely because
# the analysis window does not match the self-report item's recall frame.
d_ctrl <- daily_frame_raw |>
  filter(covered24, played24hr %in% c("Yes", "No")) |>
  mutate(self = played24hr == "Yes", tele = total_hours_24h > 0)
d_ctrl_agree <- mean(d_ctrl$self == d_ctrl$tele)
d_ctrl_phi   <- cor(d_ctrl$self, d_ctrl$tele)

# Positive control 2: shooter-gender d in the diary subsample (biweekly
# pipeline exposures; self-contained recode mirroring the Methods recode)
d_intake_g <- read_csv(here("data/clean/survey_intake.csv.gz"),
                       show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(pid, gender = case_when(
    gender %in% c("Man", "Male")     ~ "Man",
    gender %in% c("Woman", "Female") ~ "Woman",
    gender == "Prefer not to say"    ~ NA_character_,
    is.na(gender)                    ~ NA_character_,
    TRUE                             ~ "Non-binary/Other"
  ))
d_shooter <- read_csv(here("data/processed/genre_wave_long.csv"),
                      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(genre == "Shooter") |>
  group_by(pid, wave) |>
  summarise(sh = sum(hours_per_day), .groups = "drop")
d_shooter_pid <- read_csv(here("data/processed/total_playtime.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(pid %in% daily_frame_raw$pid) |>
  distinct(pid) |>
  left_join(d_shooter |> group_by(pid) |> summarise(sh = mean(sh), .groups = "drop"),
            by = "pid") |>
  mutate(sh = replace_na(sh, 0)) |>
  inner_join(d_intake_g, by = "pid") |>
  filter(gender %in% c("Man", "Woman"))
d_sh_m <- d_shooter_pid |> filter(gender == "Man")   |> pull(sh)
d_sh_w <- d_shooter_pid |> filter(gender == "Woman") |> pull(sh)
d_pool_sd   <- sqrt(((length(d_sh_m) - 1) * var(d_sh_m) +
                     (length(d_sh_w) - 1) * var(d_sh_w)) /
                    (length(d_sh_m) + length(d_sh_w) - 2))
d_shooter_d <- (mean(d_sh_m) - mean(d_sh_w)) / d_pool_sd

```

The daily extension is unregistered; an analysis plan fixed the exposure window, sample criteria, model set, priors, and equivalence benchmark before any exposure–outcome model was estimated. US participants were asked to complete daily surveys for the first 30 study days, including a life-satisfaction item ("I was satisfied with my life today") answered on a 0–100 slider [@ballou2025openplay], which serves as the outcome. Exposure is console and PC playtime from 4:00 a.m. local time of the response's waking day up to the survey completion timestamp, computed from the same session-level telemetry and full-attribution genre assignment as the main analysis, with local time taken from each participant's reported timezone; Xbox sessions recorded with date-only timestamps (8% of sessions) have their minutes spread uniformly over the recorded day. A response is analysed when its same-day window overlaps the participant's telemetry coverage, the participant's local time can be reliably established, the window is at least one hour long, and the participant's telemetry span supports a habitual full-day playtime estimate. Of `r print_num(d_n_resp_all)` diary responses from `r print_num(d_n_pid_all)` participants, `r print_num(d_n_resp)` responses (`r round(100 * d_n_resp / d_n_resp_all, 1)`%) from `r print_num(d_n_pid)` participants meet these criteria; exclusions are dominated by windows without telemetry coverage (`r print_num(d_n_uncov_resp)` responses, among them all responses from the `r print_num(d_n_no_tel_pid)` participants with no linked console or PC telemetry). Excluded responses enter an all-responses sensitivity refit that retains every response and scores unobserved play as zero.

The within-between decomposition is hybrid: within-person terms are deviations from a person's own same-day average, and between-person terms are habitual full-day hours (a participant's total telemetry over their observed diary period divided by days, with genre analogues), which keeps habitual contrasts in daily-hour units directly comparable with the registered analysis. Because the pre-registered SESOI is defined on the SWEMWBS item-mean scale, an equivalence benchmark for the slider is constructed the same way, dividing a minimally important difference by the roughly five hours of daily leisure realistically available [@sturmFreeTimePhysical2019]. We adopt a minimally important difference of 5 slider points, below both a distribution-based half within-person standard deviation (`r round(0.5 * sesoi_d$s_w_ls, 1)` points) and the registered minimally important difference expressed as a share of its scale range (7.5%, or 7.5 slider points); the benchmark is therefore 1 slider point per hour of daily play, a deliberately conservative choice, since a smaller minimally important difference makes practical equivalence harder to claim rather than easier. The registered model specifications (M0–M3) are refit at the daily level; because the analysis is unregistered, each parameter's posterior share inside the benchmark region is reported descriptively (@tbl-daily-summary) and no formal equivalence conclusions are drawn. Robustness refits (autocorrelated residuals with a day trend, adjustment for window length, exclusion of the date-only Xbox sessions, and the all-responses sample) and a same-instrument comparison model on the biweekly life-satisfaction ladder are reported in Appendix D.

# Results

Our analytic sample comprised `r formatC(n_participants, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` participants with valid SWEMWBS responses in at least one biweekly wave, yielding `r formatC(n_observations, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` person-wave observations (M = `r round(mean_waves, 1)` of 6 waves per participant; survey response declined from `r wave_response$pct[1]`% at wave 1 to `r wave_response$pct[6]`% at wave 6, see Missing Data and Appendix D). Playtime is measured from linked Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam telemetry, with zero hours recorded for participants and waves without play on these platforms. Participants played an average of `r round(mean_playtime, 2)` hours per day (SD = `r round(sd_playtime, 2)`) on Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam combined. The most played genres were `r genre_means$genre[1]` and `r genre_means$genre[2]`.

## Data Quality Controls

```{r}
#| label: dqc1
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

survey_with_trace <- survey |>
  left_join(
    aggregated_playtime |> select(pid, wave, total_time_all_platforms),
    by = c("pid", "wave")
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(self_reported_biweekly_play), !is.na(total_time_all_platforms))

dqc1_result <- cor.test(
  survey_with_trace$self_reported_biweekly_play,
  survey_with_trace$total_time_all_platforms,
  alternative = "greater"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: dqc2
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

xbox_raw <- read_csv(here("data/clean/xbox.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)
nintendo_raw <- read_csv(here("data/clean/nintendo.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)
steam_raw <- read_csv(here("data/clean/steam.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)

overlapping_sessions <- function(df, start_col = "session_start", end_col = "session_end") {
  df |>
    arrange(pid, .data[[start_col]]) |>
    group_by(pid) |>
    mutate(prev_end = lag(.data[[end_col]])) |>
    ungroup() |>
    filter(!is.na(prev_end), .data[[start_col]] < prev_end)
}

n_xbox_overlaps <- nrow(overlapping_sessions(xbox_raw))

nintendo_overlaps <- nintendo_raw |>
  arrange(pid, session_start) |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  mutate(
    prev_end    = lag(session_end),
    prev_title  = lag(title_id),
    prev_device = lag(device_type)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(!is.na(prev_end), session_start < prev_end) |>
  mutate(overlap_min = pmin(
    as.numeric(difftime(prev_end, session_start, units = "mins")), duration
  ))
n_nintendo_overlaps   <- nrow(nintendo_overlaps)
n_nintendo_sessions   <- nrow(nintendo_raw)
pct_nintendo_overlaps <- 100 * n_nintendo_overlaps / n_nintendo_sessions
pct_nintendo_overlap_min <- 100 * sum(nintendo_overlaps$overlap_min, na.rm = TRUE) /
  sum(nintendo_raw$duration, na.rm = TRUE)
median_nintendo_overlap_min <- median(nintendo_overlaps$overlap_min, na.rm = TRUE)
n_nintendo_overlap_pids <- n_distinct(nintendo_overlaps$pid)
n_nintendo_pids <- n_distinct(nintendo_raw$pid)
n_nintendo_overlaps_diff_title <- sum(
  nintendo_overlaps$title_id != nintendo_overlaps$prev_title, na.rm = TRUE
)
# device_type records the console model (e.g., Lite, OLED), not a device serial,
# so differing models across an overlapping pair are direct evidence of two
# consoles on one account; same-model pairs cannot be distinguished.
n_nintendo_overlaps_diff_device <- sum(
  nintendo_overlaps$device_type != nintendo_overlaps$prev_device, na.rm = TRUE
)
n_nintendo_overlaps_top2 <- nintendo_overlaps |>
  count(pid, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 2) |>
  summarise(n = sum(n)) |>
  pull(n)

# Steam clean data contain reconstructed sessions (not hourly buckets), so the
# pre-registered "no more than 60 minutes between hourly measurements" check
# translates to: no session's recorded minutes may exceed its elapsed duration
# (1-minute tolerance for rounding).
steam_elapsed <- as.numeric(difftime(
  steam_raw$approximate_session_end, steam_raw$approximate_session_start,
  units = "mins"
))
n_steam_rate_violations <- sum(steam_raw$minutes > steam_elapsed + 1, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: dqc3
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

shooter_col <- grep("time_shooter", genre_vars, value = TRUE)
stopifnot(length(shooter_col) == 1)

shooter_by_gender <- aggregated_playtime |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  summarise(shooter_time = mean(.data[[shooter_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(intake |> select(pid, gender), by = "pid") |>
  filter(gender %in% c("Man", "Woman"))

dqc3_test <- t.test(shooter_time ~ gender, data = shooter_by_gender)

men_mean <- mean(shooter_by_gender$shooter_time[shooter_by_gender$gender == "Man"], na.rm = TRUE)
women_mean <- mean(shooter_by_gender$shooter_time[shooter_by_gender$gender == "Woman"], na.rm = TRUE)
pooled_sd <- sqrt(
  ((sum(shooter_by_gender$gender == "Man") - 1) * var(shooter_by_gender$shooter_time[shooter_by_gender$gender == "Man"], na.rm = TRUE) +
   (sum(shooter_by_gender$gender == "Woman") - 1) * var(shooter_by_gender$shooter_time[shooter_by_gender$gender == "Woman"], na.rm = TRUE)) /
  (nrow(shooter_by_gender) - 2)
)
dqc3_d <- (men_mean - women_mean) / pooled_sd
```

Prior to hypothesis testing, we conducted the three pre-registered positive data quality controls (DQCs) to validate expected patterns in the data. First, self-reported biweekly playtime correlated positively with digital trace playtime (*r* = `r round(dqc1_result$estimate, 3)`, one-sided 95% lower bound = `r round(dqc1_result$conf.int[1], 3)`, *p* \< .001). Second, session integrity largely held: Xbox contained `r n_xbox_overlaps` overlapping sessions and no Steam session's recorded playtime exceeded its elapsed wall-clock duration (`r n_steam_rate_violations` violations. Nintendo retained a small number of overlapping session pairs: `r formatC(n_nintendo_overlaps, format="d", big.mark=",")` of `r formatC(n_nintendo_sessions, format="d", big.mark=",")` sessions (`r round(pct_nintendo_overlaps, 2)`%), spread across `r n_nintendo_overlap_pids` of `r formatC(n_nintendo_pids, format="d", big.mark=",")` participants, with a median overlap of `r round(median_nintendo_overlap_min, 1)` minutes and accounting for `r round(pct_nintendo_overlap_min, 2)`% of total Nintendo playtime. These pairs reflect concurrent use of multiple consoles linked to one account: `r n_nintendo_overlaps_diff_title` of the `r n_nintendo_overlaps` pairs involved two different games recorded as running at once, and `r n_nintendo_overlaps_diff_device` involved two distinct console models (e.g., a Switch Lite overlapping an OLED model), which requires two physical devices; because the device identifier records the model rather than the individual console, some same-model pairs likely also reflect two consoles. The overlaps were also concentrated in a few accounts, with two participants alone contributing `r n_nintendo_overlaps_top2` pairs. Given their rarity and their small share of playtime, we judged these overlaps too small to materially influence the wave-level aggregates. Third, men played more shooter games than women (M = `r round(men_mean, 3)` vs. `r round(women_mean, 3)` hrs/day, *t*(`r round(dqc3_test$parameter, 1)`) = `r round(dqc3_test$statistic, 2)`, *p* \< .001, Cohen's *d* = `r round(dqc3_d, 2)`), meeting the pre-registered criterion of a significant difference in the expected direction and consistent with population studies of gendered genre preferences [@rehbeinVideoGamePlaying2016], although the effect was somewhat smaller than the *d* = .3 assumed in the Stage 1 power analysis. We therefore proceeded with the confirmatory analyses.

```{r}
#| label: model-data
#| include: false

options(mc.cores = max(1L, parallel::detectCores() - 1L))
dir.create(here("models"), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# --- Genre hours per (pid, wave) from full-attribution long file ---
# Since R/01_preprocess.R now produces genre_wave_long.csv with full
# attribution (each genre on a multi-genre game gets the full session
# duration, not 1/n_genres splitting), we read that file directly and
# pivot to wide format. The gh_* columns no longer sum to total playtime;
# instead, each gh_genre column represents "hours of exposure to games
# carrying that genre label." Total playtime is tracked separately via
# total_playtime.csv (no double-counting).

genre_hours_wide <- genre_wave_long |>
  mutate(col = {
    clean <- gsub("[^a-z0-9]+", "_", tolower(genre))
    clean <- gsub("^_+|_+$", "", clean)
    clean <- gsub("__+", "_", clean)
    paste0("gh_", clean)
  }) |>
  select(pid, wave, col, hours_per_day) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = col, values_from = hours_per_day, values_fill = 0)

gh_vars <- sort(setdiff(names(genre_hours_wide), c("pid", "wave")))

# Build (pid, wave) analysis frame
# Both H1 and H2 use Nintendo/Xbox/Steam only (total_hours_per_day, not total_time_all_platforms).  Mobile platforms provide only daily aggregates without game-level data; including them for H1 but not H2 would make "total playtime" mean different things across hypotheses.  The pre-registered frequentist sensitivity analysis retains the all-platform total.
analysis_data <- survey |>
  select(pid, wave, wemwbs) |>
  left_join(
    total_playtime |> select(pid, wave, total_hours_per_day),
    by = c("pid", "wave")
  ) |>
  left_join(genre_hours_wide, by = c("pid", "wave")) |>
  mutate(
    total_hours_per_day = replace_na(total_hours_per_day, 0),
    across(all_of(gh_vars), ~ replace_na(.x, 0))
  ) |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  mutate(
    # H1: total playtime (console/PC only, consistent with H2 scope)
    total_within  = total_hours_per_day -
                      mean(total_hours_per_day, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_between = mean(total_hours_per_day, na.rm = TRUE),
    # H2: genre-specific hours (same platforms)
    across(
      all_of(gh_vars),
      list(
        within  = ~ .x - mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        between = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
      ),
      .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

gh_within  <- paste0(gh_vars, "_within")
gh_between <- paste0(gh_vars, "_between")

n_analysis_obs  <- nrow(analysis_data |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs)))
n_analysis_pids <- n_distinct(analysis_data$pid[!is.na(analysis_data$wemwbs)])
n_genres        <- length(gh_vars)
```

```{r}
#| label: mm-data-setup
#| include: false

# --- Multi-membership data setup ---
# Transform genre hours into the format brms::mm() needs:
#   K constant genre-label columns (g_1 ... g_K)
#   K weight columns (w_1 ... w_K) = proportion of this wave's genre hours

genre_labels <- sort(gh_vars)
K <- length(genre_labels)

mm_data <- analysis_data |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(gh_row_total = sum(c_across(all_of(gh_vars)))) |>
  ungroup()

# Weights: proportion of playtime in each genre.
# For zero-playtime waves, use uniform 1/K (mm() needs nonzero weights).
for (i in seq_along(genre_labels)) {
  w_col <- paste0("w_", i)
  gh_col <- genre_labels[i]
  mm_data[[w_col]] <- ifelse(
    mm_data$gh_row_total > 0,
    mm_data[[gh_col]] / mm_data$gh_row_total,
    1 / K
  )
}

# Constant genre-label columns (strip "gh_" prefix)
for (i in seq_along(genre_labels)) {
  g_col <- paste0("g_", i)
  mm_data[[g_col]] <- sub("^gh_", "", genre_labels[i])
}

g_cols <- paste0("g_", seq_len(K))
w_cols <- paste0("w_", seq_len(K))

# Verify weights sum to ~1
w_sums <- mm_data |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(w_sum = sum(c_across(all_of(w_cols)))) |>
  pull(w_sum)
stopifnot(all(abs(w_sums - 1) < 0.001))

# Verify genre labels are constant across rows
for (col in g_cols) {
  stopifnot(n_distinct(mm_data[[col]]) == 1)
}

message(sprintf("mm() setup: %d genres, %d observations", K, nrow(mm_data)))
```

```{r}
#| label: mm-formula-setup
#| include: false

# Build mm() formula
mm_term <- paste0(
  "mm(", paste(g_cols, collapse = ", "),
  ", weights = cbind(", paste(w_cols, collapse = ", "), "))"
)

# Full mm() formula: BOTH within and between genre random slopes (28 random effects).
# Computationally demanding: requires adapt_delta = 0.999 and iter = 8000.
# The fit is cached in models/h2_mm_model_full.rds via brms's file argument.
h2_mm_formula <- bf(paste0(
  "wemwbs ~ total_within + total_between + ",
  "(1 + total_within | pid) + ",
  "(0 + total_within + total_between | ", mm_term, ")"
))

# Discover auto-generated mm group name
mm_priors_check <- get_prior(
  h2_mm_formula,
  data = mm_data |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs))
)

mm_groups <- mm_priors_check |>
  filter(grepl("^mm", group)) |>
  pull(group) |>
  unique()

if (length(mm_groups) == 0) stop("No mm() group found in get_prior() output.")
mm_group_name <- mm_groups[1]
message(sprintf("mm() group name: %s", mm_group_name))

# Priors (use set_prior so group name is evaluated, not deparsed).
# Rescaled for the 1-5 outcome scale (see h1_model comment). sigma_s (the
# multi-membership sd) hyperprior set to normal(0, 0.3), looser than the
# hierarchical prior model's normal(0, 0.1) to avoid extreme sampling
# difficulty in the multi-membership posterior geometry.
mm_model_priors <- c(
  set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 0.5)", class = "b"),
  set_prior("student_t(3, 3, 2)",   class = "Intercept"),
  set_prior("normal(0, 0.3)", class = "sd", group = mm_group_name)
)

# Readable genre display names (column slug → label)
genre_display <- c(
  "adventure"                 = "Adventure",
  "arcade"                    = "Arcade",
  "fighting"                  = "Fighting",
  "hack_and_slash_beat_em_up" = "Hack & Slash / Beat 'em Up",
  "platform"                  = "Platform",
  "point_and_click"           = "Point-and-Click",
  "puzzle"                    = "Puzzle",
  "racing"                    = "Racing",
  "role_playing_rpg"          = "Role-Playing (RPG)",
  "shooter"                   = "Shooter",
  "simulator"                 = "Simulator",
  "sport"                     = "Sport",
  "strategy"                  = "Strategy",
  "visual_novel"              = "Visual Novel"
)

prettify_genre <- function(slug) {
  out <- genre_display[slug]
  # Fallback for any unrecognised slugs
  out[is.na(out)] <- str_replace_all(slug[is.na(out)], "_", " ") |> str_to_title()
  unname(out)
}
```

The analysis data comprise `r formatC(n_analysis_obs, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` observations from `r formatC(n_analysis_pids, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` participants, with playtime distributed across `r n_genres` genres.

```{r}
#| label: h1-fit
#| eval: true

h1_model <- brm(
  bf(wemwbs ~ total_within + total_between +
       (1 + total_within | pid)),
  data    = analysis_data |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs)),
  # Priors rescaled for the 1-5 outcome scale (wemwbs is rowMeans on 1-5).
  # Intercept centred at 3 (midpoint of 1-5); coefficient scale tightened
  # from 2.5 to 0.5 to be weakly informative on the 1-5 outcome range.
  prior   = prior(student_t(3, 0, 0.5), class = "b") +
            prior(student_t(3, 3, 2),   class = "Intercept"),
  family  = gaussian(),
  chains  = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 8675309,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file    = here("models/h1_rewb_model")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: h1-diagnostics
#| include: false
#| eval: true

h1_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(h1_model), na.rm = TRUE)
h1_divs <- sum(subset(brms::nuts_params(h1_model),
                       Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)
stopifnot(h1_rhat < 1.05)
```

```{r}
#| label: h2-fit
#| eval: true

h2_formula <- bf(paste(
  "wemwbs ~",
  paste(c(gh_within, gh_between), collapse = " + "),
  "+ (1 | pid)"
))

h2_model <- brm(
  formula = h2_formula,
  data    = analysis_data |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs)),
  # Priors rescaled for the 1-5 outcome scale (see H1 comment).
  prior   = prior(student_t(3, 0, 0.5), class = "b") +
            prior(student_t(3, 3, 2),   class = "Intercept"),
  family  = gaussian(),
  chains  = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 8675309,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file    = here("models/h2_genre_model")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: h2-diagnostics
#| include: false
#| eval: true

h2_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(h2_model), na.rm = TRUE)
h2_divs <- sum(subset(brms::nuts_params(h2_model),
                       Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)
stopifnot(h2_rhat < 1.05)
```

```{r}
#| label: h2-hier-fit
#| eval: true

# Two learned hyperparameters: tau_genre_within (H2a) and tau_genre_between (H2b).
# Each genre's within-person coefficient is drawn from Normal(0, tau_within);
# each genre's between-person coefficient from Normal(0, tau_between).
# Both receive Half-Normal(0, 0.1) hyperpriors scaled for the 1-5 outcome.
sv_hier <- stanvar(
  scode = "real<lower=0> tau_genre_within;\nreal<lower=0> tau_genre_between;",
  block = "parameters"
) +
stanvar(
  scode = paste(
    "target += normal_lpdf(tau_genre_within | 0, 0.1) - normal_lccdf(0 | 0, 0.1);",
    "target += normal_lpdf(tau_genre_between | 0, 0.1) - normal_lccdf(0 | 0, 0.1);",
    sep = "\n"
  ),
  block = "model"
)

# Hierarchical priors on BOTH within and between genre coefficients
hier_priors_within <- do.call(c, lapply(gh_within, function(g) {
  set_prior("normal(0, tau_genre_within)", class = "b", coef = g)
}))
hier_priors_between <- do.call(c, lapply(gh_between, function(g) {
  set_prior("normal(0, tau_genre_between)", class = "b", coef = g)
}))

h2_hier_priors <- c(
  # Default weakly informative prior for any genre coefficients not covered
  # by the explicit hierarchical priors below
  set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 0.5)", class = "b"),
  set_prior("student_t(3, 3, 2)",   class = "Intercept"),
  hier_priors_within,
  hier_priors_between
)

# Same genre-exposure structure as M1, but with hierarchical priors on
# genre coefficients. No total_within/total_between: genre exposure columns
# are non-exclusive (full attribution), so partialing out total playtime
# would leave only multi-genre inflation artifacts.
h2_hier_formula <- bf(paste(
  "wemwbs ~",
  paste(c(gh_within, gh_between), collapse = " + "),
  "+ (1 | pid)"
))

h2_hier_model <- brm(
  formula  = h2_hier_formula,
  data     = analysis_data |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs)),
  prior    = h2_hier_priors,
  stanvars = sv_hier,
  family   = gaussian(),
  chains   = 4, iter = 8000, warmup = 4000, seed = 2025,
  control  = list(adapt_delta = 0.999, max_treedepth = 15),
  file     = here("models/h2_hier_model_v2")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: h2-hier-diagnostics
#| include: false
#| eval: true

h2_hier_divs <- sum(subset(brms::nuts_params(h2_hier_model),
                            Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)
h2_hier_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(h2_hier_model), na.rm = TRUE)

message(sprintf("Hierarchical model - Divergent transitions: %d", h2_hier_divs))
message(sprintf("Hierarchical model - Max R-hat: %.3f", h2_hier_rhat))

# With adapt_delta = 0.999 (practical ceiling), residual divergences in this
# model arise from Neal's funnel geometry: tau_genre_within and
# tau_genre_between approach zero, making the posterior ill-conditioned near
# the boundary.  The proper long-term fix is non-centered reparameterisation
# (z_raw ~ Normal(0,1); beta = z_raw * tau).  A small number of divergences
# (<=10 out of 16,000 post-warmup samples) does not materially affect
# inferences when R-hat is healthy; we warn rather than abort so the
# manuscript can render, and document this in the text.
if (h2_hier_divs > 10) {
  stop(sprintf(
    "Unacceptable number of divergent transitions in h2_hier_model: %d. ",
    h2_hier_divs
  ))
} else if (h2_hier_divs > 0) {
  warning(sprintf(
    paste0(
      "h2_hier_model has %d divergent transition(s) out of 16,000 ",
      "post-warmup samples (adapt_delta = 0.999). ",
      "This reflects funnel geometry near tau ~ 0; ",
      "inferences are not materially affected (max R-hat = %.4f). ",
      "Non-centered reparameterisation is the recommended fix."
    ),
    h2_hier_divs, h2_hier_rhat
  ))
}
stopifnot(h2_hier_rhat < 1.05)
```

```{r}
#| label: h2-mm-fit
#| eval: true

h2_mm_model <- brm(
  formula = h2_mm_formula,
  data    = mm_data |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs)),
  prior   = mm_model_priors,
  family  = gaussian(),
  chains  = 4,
  iter    = 8000,
  warmup  = 4000,
  seed    = 8675309,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.999, max_treedepth = 15),
  file    = here("models/h2_mm_model_full")
)
```

```{r}

#| include: false
#| eval: true
```
