```{r}
                          Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)
h2_mm_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(h2_mm_model), na.rm = TRUE)

message(sprintf("MM model - Divergent transitions: %d", h2_mm_divs))
message(sprintf("MM model - Max R-hat: %.3f", h2_mm_rhat))

stopifnot(h2_mm_divs == 0)
stopifnot(h2_mm_rhat < 1.05)
```

## H1: Total Playtime and Wellbeing

```{r}
#| label: h1-rope
#| include: false
#| eval: true

h1_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(h1_model)

# H1a: within-person
beta1_draws   <- h1_draws$b_total_within
beta1_mean    <- mean(beta1_draws)
beta1_ci      <- quantile(beta1_draws, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
beta1_in_rope <- mean(beta1_draws > -0.06 & beta1_draws < 0.06)

# H1b: between-person
beta2_draws   <- h1_draws$b_total_between
beta2_mean    <- mean(beta2_draws)
beta2_ci      <- quantile(beta2_draws, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
beta2_in_rope <- mean(beta2_draws > -0.06 & beta2_draws < 0.06)

# Person-level heterogeneity in the within-person slope (random-slope SD).
# Bounds how much person-specific playtime associations vary; reported here
# and interpreted in the Discussion (individual-susceptibility escape hatch).
sd_slope_draws   <- h1_draws$sd_pid__total_within
sd_slope_mean    <- mean(sd_slope_draws)
sd_slope_ci      <- quantile(sd_slope_draws, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
sd_slope_p_above <- mean(sd_slope_draws > 0.06)
stopifnot(sd_slope_mean < 0.06, sd_slope_p_above < 0.10)

# Guards for the dose-inversion prose (Discussion): the play change
# required to reach the 0.3-point MID is several times a full day at the
# within-person point estimate (> 72 h/day), exceeds the waking day within
# persons (> 16 h/day) and available daily leisure between persons
# (> 5 h/day), even at the credible-interval bounds most favourable.
stopifnot(0.3 / beta1_mean > 72, 0.3 / beta1_ci[2] > 16, 0.3 / abs(beta2_ci[1]) > 5)

# Guards for the life-events comparison (Discussion): on the total-SD scale
# the SESOI-dose threshold sits below the marriage benchmark (0.26 SD), and
# the observed 2 h/day within-person shift is at least 10x below the
# threshold's 0.12 points.
stopifnot(0.12 / wemwbs_total_sd < 0.26, abs(beta1_mean) * 2 < 0.012)
```

```{r}
#| label: h2-mm-h1
#| include: false
#| eval: true

# H1 from the mm model: the fixed effects total_within and total_between
h2_mm_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(h2_mm_model)

mm_beta1_draws   <- h2_mm_draws$b_total_within
mm_beta1_mean    <- mean(mm_beta1_draws)
mm_beta1_ci      <- quantile(mm_beta1_draws, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
mm_beta1_in_rope <- mean(mm_beta1_draws > -0.06 & mm_beta1_draws < 0.06)

mm_beta2_draws   <- h2_mm_draws$b_total_between
mm_beta2_mean    <- mean(mm_beta2_draws)
mm_beta2_ci      <- quantile(mm_beta2_draws, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
mm_beta2_in_rope <- mean(mm_beta2_draws > -0.06 & mm_beta2_draws < 0.06)
```

```{r}
#| label: h1-all-models-extract
#| include: false
#| eval: true

# Only M0 and M3 contribute to H1. M1 and M2 use non-exclusive genre
# exposure columns without a separate total playtime predictor, so they
# cannot estimate the overall dose-response.
h1_comparison_draws <- bind_rows(
  tibble(
    model = "M0: Total playtime only",
    effect = "Within-person (H1a)",
    value = posterior::as_draws_df(h1_model)$b_total_within
  ),
  tibble(
    model = "M0: Total playtime only",
    effect = "Between-person (H1b)",
    value = posterior::as_draws_df(h1_model)$b_total_between
  ),
  tibble(
    model = "M3: Multi-membership",
    effect = "Within-person (H1a)",
    value = posterior::as_draws_df(h2_mm_model)$b_total_within
  ),
  tibble(
    model = "M3: Multi-membership",
    effect = "Between-person (H1b)",
    value = posterior::as_draws_df(h2_mm_model)$b_total_between
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    # Reversed so the lowest model (M0) displays at the top
    model = factor(model, levels = c(
      "M3: Multi-membership", "M0: Total playtime only"
    )),
    effect = factor(effect, levels = c(
      "Within-person (H1a)", "Between-person (H1b)"
    ))
  )
```

@fig-h1-all-models summarises the H1 results; the underlying posterior summaries for all hypothesis tests are tabulated in Appendix E (@tbl-hypothesis-summary). For the within-person effect (H1a), the posterior mean was `r round(beta1_mean, 3)` SWEMWBS item-mean points per hour/day (95% CrI: \[`r round(beta1_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(beta1_ci[2], 3)`\]), with `r round(beta1_in_rope * 100, 1)`% of the posterior inside the ROPE, above the 95% posterior-mass criterion adopted in Deviation D4 (the pre-registered decision rule, based on 90% CI bounds, is applied in the supplement and in the multiple-imputation analysis (Appendix D), and agrees). H1a is therefore supported: when a participant plays more than their own average in a given wave, their wellbeing does not change to any practically meaningful degree. For the between-person effect (H1b), the posterior mean was `r round(beta2_mean, 3)` (95% CrI: \[`r round(beta2_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(beta2_ci[2], 3)`\]), with `r round(beta2_in_rope * 100, 1)`% of the posterior inside the ROPE, likewise establishing practical equivalence. The between-person estimate leans negative (its credible interval extends just to zero), but its magnitude is far below the SESOI: even a 2 hour/day difference in habitual playtime would correspond to only `r round(beta2_mean * 2, 3)` points on the 1–5 scale (about `r abs(round(beta2_mean * 2 / 4 * 100, 1))`% of the 4-point range).

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-h1-all-models
#| fig-cap: "*Posterior Distributions for Total Playtime Effects (H1).* M0 is the standalone H1 model; M3 adds genre information through multi-membership weights while still estimating overall playtime effects. M1 and M2 have no separate total-playtime predictor and are excluded. Green band: pre-registered ROPE (±0.06); panels share an x-axis."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

ggplot(h1_comparison_draws, aes(x = value, y = model)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -0.06, xmax = 0.06,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.10) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-0.06, 0.06), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_halfeye(aes(fill = model_family(model)), .width = c(0.66, 0.95),
               alpha = 0.7, point_interval = "median_qi") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = model_palette, guide = "none") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "solid", alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ effect) +
  labs(x = "Effect on SWEMWBS item-mean (per hour/day)", y = NULL,
       caption = "Green band: ROPE (\u00b10.06). Thick: 66% CrI. Thin: 95% CrI.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```
:::

Both components of H1 are therefore supported. The model also bounds person-to-person variation in the within-person association: the random-slope SD was `r round(sd_slope_mean, 3)` (95% CrI: \[`r round(sd_slope_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(sd_slope_ci[2], 3)`\]), with `r round(sd_slope_p_above * 100, 1)`% of its posterior above the SESOI; we return to this bound, and to the practical magnitude of the estimates, in the Discussion.

The multi-membership model also provides H1 estimates via its fixed effects. @fig-h1-all-models confirms that M0 and M3 yield consistent H1 estimates: the inclusion of genre-level terms in M3 does not alter the overall playtime–wellbeing association.

## H2: Genre-Specific Effects

H2 asks whether genres differ in how playtime relates to wellbeing. We answer it in two steps. First, we report the genre heterogeneity parameters, which provide the direct test of H2: how much do genre-specific playtime slopes vary? The primary evidence comes from the multi-membership model (M3), corroborated by the hierarchical prior model (M2) and the pre-registered fixed-effects specification (M1). Second, we examine the per-genre estimates the three specifications produce. A complementary predictive comparison, asking whether genre information improves out-of-sample prediction at all, is reported in Appendix D.

### Genre Heterogeneity

```{r}
#| label: h2-mm-sigma
#| include: false
#| eval: true

# sigma_s_within: SD of genre random slopes on total_within
sigma_sw_col <- names(h2_mm_draws)[grepl(
  paste0("sd_", mm_group_name, ".*total_within"),
  names(h2_mm_draws)
)]
if (length(sigma_sw_col) == 0) {
  sigma_sw_col <- names(h2_mm_draws)[grepl("sd_mm.*total_within", names(h2_mm_draws))]
}
stopifnot(length(sigma_sw_col) >= 1)
sigma_sw_col <- sigma_sw_col[1]

sigma_sw_draws       <- h2_mm_draws[[sigma_sw_col]]
sigma_sw_mean        <- mean(sigma_sw_draws)
sigma_sw_ci          <- quantile(sigma_sw_draws, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
sigma_sw_above_sesoi <- mean(sigma_sw_draws > 0.06)

# sigma_s_between: SD of genre random slopes on total_between (the full mm()
# formula includes both total_within and total_between in the mm() term)
sigma_sb_col <- names(h2_mm_draws)[grepl(
  paste0("sd_", mm_group_name, ".*total_between"),
  names(h2_mm_draws)
)]
if (length(sigma_sb_col) == 0) {
  sigma_sb_col <- names(h2_mm_draws)[grepl("sd_mm.*total_between", names(h2_mm_draws))]
}
stopifnot(length(sigma_sb_col) >= 1)
sigma_sb_col         <- sigma_sb_col[1]

sigma_sb_draws       <- h2_mm_draws[[sigma_sb_col]]
sigma_sb_mean        <- mean(sigma_sb_draws)
sigma_sb_ci          <- quantile(sigma_sb_draws, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
sigma_sb_above_sesoi <- mean(sigma_sb_draws > 0.06)
```

The primary test of H2 comes from the multi-membership model's genre heterogeneity parameters. For the within-person dimension (H2a), the posterior mean of $\sigma_{s,\text{within}}$ was `r round(sigma_sw_mean, 3)` (95% CrI: \[`r round(sigma_sw_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(sigma_sw_ci[2], 3)`\]). Because a standard deviation cannot be negative, the informative benchmark is the SESOI rather than zero: `r round(sigma_sw_above_sesoi * 100, 1)`% of the posterior exceeds 0.06. The data are thus most consistent with genre-to-genre variation in within-person slopes that is smaller than the smallest effect of interest, though the wide interval means heterogeneity of up to roughly 0.1 points per hour/day cannot be ruled out. For the between-person dimension (H2b), $\sigma_{s,\text{between}}$ = `r round(sigma_sb_mean, 3)` (95% CrI: \[`r round(sigma_sb_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(sigma_sb_ci[2], 3)`\]), with only `r round(sigma_sb_above_sesoi * 100, 1)`% of the posterior above the SESOI: between-person genre heterogeneity is practically negligible.

The two corroborating specifications answer the same question through different machinery and reach the same verdict more decisively.

```{r}
#| label: h2-hier-tau
#| include: false
#| eval: true

h2_hier_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(h2_hier_model)

# H2a: within-person genre heterogeneity
tau_draws <- h2_hier_draws$tau_genre_within
tau_mean  <- mean(tau_draws)
tau_ci    <- quantile(tau_draws, c(0.025, 0.975))
tau_in_rope <- mean(tau_draws > -0.06 & tau_draws < 0.06)

# H2b: between-person genre heterogeneity
tau_between_draws <- h2_hier_draws$tau_genre_between
tau_between_mean  <- mean(tau_between_draws)
tau_between_ci    <- quantile(tau_between_draws, c(0.025, 0.975))
tau_between_in_rope <- mean(tau_between_draws > -0.06 & tau_between_draws < 0.06)
```

Under the hierarchical prior model, τ~within~ = `r round(tau_mean, 3)` (95% CrI: \[`r round(tau_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(tau_ci[2], 3)`\]), with `r round(tau_in_rope * 100, 1)`% of the posterior inside the pre-registered ROPE (±0.06): the between-genre variation in within-person slopes is practically negligible under this specification. For the between-person dimension (H2b), τ~between~ = `r round(tau_between_mean, 3)` (95% CrI: \[`r round(tau_between_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(tau_between_ci[2], 3)`\]), with `r round(tau_between_in_rope * 100, 1)`% of the posterior inside the ROPE. The between-person parameter describes whether individuals who habitually favour certain genres differ in average wellbeing from those who favour others.

```{r}
#| label: h2-joint-test
#| include: false
#| eval: true

# Bayesian analogue of the pre-registered joint Wald test: "are all genre
# within-person coefficients equal?"
# For each MCMC draw, compute the SD of genre within-person effects.  If this
# heterogeneity SD is clearly > 0, at least one genre pair differs.
h2_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(h2_model)

# brms names fixed effects as b_{varname}
within_cols <- paste0("b_", gh_within)
within_mat  <- as.matrix(h2_draws[, within_cols, drop = FALSE])

genre_effect_sd   <- apply(within_mat, 1, sd)
genre_sd_mean     <- mean(genre_effect_sd)
genre_sd_ci       <- quantile(genre_effect_sd, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

# Same for between-person effects
between_cols      <- paste0("b_", gh_between)
between_mat       <- as.matrix(h2_draws[, between_cols, drop = FALSE])
genre_between_sd  <- apply(between_mat, 1, sd)
genre_bsd_mean    <- mean(genre_between_sd)
genre_bsd_ci      <- quantile(genre_between_sd, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
```

Finally, the pre-registered fixed-effects specification (M1) provides the simplest version of the test: the Bayesian analogue of the pre-registered joint Wald test. We computed the standard deviation of the 14 genre-specific within-person coefficients at each MCMC draw. The posterior mean of this heterogeneity SD was `r round(genre_sd_mean, 3)` (95% CrI: \[`r round(genre_sd_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(genre_sd_ci[2], 3)`\]), an interval that lies entirely below the SESOI of 0.06. For between-person effects the heterogeneity SD was `r round(genre_bsd_mean, 3)` (95% CrI: \[`r round(genre_bsd_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(genre_bsd_ci[2], 3)`\]), the only statistic among the three specifications to exceed the SESOI; as discussed below, this raw SD includes sampling error and should be read as an upper bound. The pre-registered primary-genre joint Wald tests in the supplement do not reject the hypothesis that all genre coefficients are equal, for either dimension; on the full-attribution exposures used here, the complete-case joint test detects a statistically significant but practically negligible departure from exact within-person equality, which the multiple-imputation analysis (Appendix D) reports and contextualises against the SESOI.

@fig-h2-heterogeneity shows the posterior distributions for the genre heterogeneity statistics from all three H2 models. M1's statistic is the standard deviation of the 14 independent within-person genre coefficients (computed per posterior draw); M2's is τ~genre~ from the learned hierarchical prior; M3's is σ~s~ from the multi-membership random effects. All three are in the same units (SWEMWBS item-mean per hour/day) and represent how much genre-specific playtime slopes vary across genres.

```{r}
#| label: h2-heterogeneity-extract
#| include: false
#| eval: true

# Reuse draws already extracted in this section:
#   M1: genre_effect_sd / genre_between_sd   (h2-joint-test)
#   M2: tau_draws / tau_between_draws        (h2-hier-tau)
#   M3: sigma_sw_draws / sigma_sb_draws      (h2-mm-sigma)
m1_sd_within_per_draw  <- genre_effect_sd
m1_sd_between_per_draw <- genre_between_sd

h2_het_draws <- bind_rows(
  # Within-person (H2a)
  tibble(dimension = "Within-person (H2a)", model = "M1: SD of fixed-effect coefs", value = m1_sd_within_per_draw),
  tibble(dimension = "Within-person (H2a)", model = "M2: τ_within (hierarchical)",  value = tau_draws),
  tibble(dimension = "Within-person (H2a)", model = "M3: σ_s (multi-membership)",  value = sigma_sw_draws),
  # Between-person (H2b)
  tibble(dimension = "Between-person (H2b)", model = "M1: SD of fixed-effect coefs", value = m1_sd_between_per_draw),
  tibble(dimension = "Between-person (H2b)", model = "M2: τ_between (hierarchical)", value = tau_between_draws),
  tibble(dimension = "Between-person (H2b)", model = "M3: σ_s_between (multi-membership)", value = sigma_sb_draws)
) |>
  mutate(
    # Reversed so the lowest model (M1) displays at the top
    model = factor(model, levels = c(
      "M3: σ_s_between (multi-membership)",
      "M3: σ_s (multi-membership)",
      "M2: τ_between (hierarchical)",
      "M2: τ_within (hierarchical)",
      "M1: SD of fixed-effect coefs"
    )),
    dimension = factor(dimension, levels = c(
      "Within-person (H2a)", "Between-person (H2b)"
    ))
  )
```

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-h2-heterogeneity
#| fig-cap: "*Genre Heterogeneity Across H2 Model Specifications.* Left: within-person (H2a); right: between-person (H2b). Green band: SESOI region (0 to 0.06). A posterior falling entirely inside the band indicates practically negligible genre heterogeneity."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

ggplot(h2_het_draws, aes(x = value, y = model)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 0.06,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.10) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.06, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_halfeye(aes(fill = model_family(model)), .width = c(0.66, 0.95),
               alpha = 0.7, point_interval = "median_qi") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = model_palette, guide = "none") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "solid", alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ dimension, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Genre heterogeneity (SWEMWBS item-mean per hour/day)", y = NULL,
       caption = sprintf("Green band: heterogeneity < SESOI (%.2f). Constrained ≥ 0 by definition.", 0.06)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```
:::

The H2 heterogeneity estimates converge on a consistent qualitative picture: genre-to-genre variation in per-hour wellbeing slopes is at most small. All three statistics are positive by construction, so their posteriors cannot include zero; the informative benchmark in @fig-h2-heterogeneity is the SESOI band. On the within-person dimension, M2's τ (`r round(tau_mean, 3)`) and M1's raw SD (`r round(mean(m1_sd_within_per_draw), 3)`) both fall entirely below 0.06, while M3's σ~s~ (`r round(sigma_sw_mean, 3)`) straddles the boundary with about a fifth of its posterior above it. On the between-person dimension, the two pooled estimates (M2, M3) fall below the SESOI while M1's raw SD exceeds it, the expected signature of sampling-noise inflation. M1's SD is the empirical standard deviation of 14 independently estimated coefficients and therefore includes estimation error, especially from rare genres with wide posteriors; M2's τ and M3's σ~s~ are model-estimated pooling parameters that separate signal from noise. The two pooled parameters operate on different quantities: τ is a hyperprior scale on genre *fixed effects* under Half-Normal(0, 0.1), while σ~s~ is the standard deviation of genre *random-slope deviations* under Half-Normal(0, 0.3), so their posterior medians need not coincide; σ~s~ can exceed τ because it absorbs genre-to-genre variation in the slope of total playtime, a quantity M2 does not directly parameterise. Overall, the pooled specifications place genre heterogeneity below the pre-registered equivalence threshold on both dimensions, and no specification provides positive evidence of practically meaningful genre differences.

The heterogeneity estimates and convergence diagnostics for all three specifications are tabulated in Appendix E (@tbl-hypothesis-summary). Full posterior summaries for all four models are provided in the supplementary materials.

### Per-Genre Estimates

@fig-integrated-coefs compares per-genre exposure coefficients across the three H2 specifications, with the within-person and between-person dimensions in side-by-side panels. Each genre row shows three estimates, distinguished by shape: M1 (circle, no pooling), M2 (square, hierarchical prior), and M3 (diamond, multi-membership). M1 and M2 use the same non-exclusive genre exposure columns; M2 adds partial pooling via τ~genre~. M3 uses a different operationalisation: composition-weighted deviations from the overall playtime slope, with the overall fixed effect added back so all three sit on the same absolute scale.

```{r}
#| label: integrated-coefs-extract
#| include: false
#| eval: true

# --- M1 (fixed-effects): extract within and between ---
m1_within <- broom.mixed::tidy(h2_model, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(grepl("^gh_.*_within$", term), effect == "fixed") |>
  mutate(
    genre = prettify_genre(sub("^gh_(.*)_within$", "\\1", term)),
    model = "M1: Fixed effects"
  ) |>
  select(model, genre, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high)

m1_between <- broom.mixed::tidy(h2_model, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(grepl("^gh_.*_between$", term), effect == "fixed") |>
  mutate(
    genre = prettify_genre(sub("^gh_(.*)_between$", "\\1", term)),
    model = "M1: Fixed effects"
  ) |>
  select(model, genre, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high)

# --- M3 (multi-membership): extract random slopes + add overall fixed effect ---
# M3's random slopes are deviations from the overall total_within fixed effect.
# To make them comparable to M1/M2's absolute genre coefficients, we add the
# overall total_within fixed effect back to each genre adjustment.
mm_total_within_fe <- fixef(h2_mm_model)["total_within", "Estimate"]

# Note: variable named m2_re from legacy code; this is M3's ranef output
m3_re <- ranef(h2_mm_model)
mm_key <- names(m3_re)[grepl("^mm", names(m3_re))][1]

m3_mm_within <- as.data.frame(m3_re[[mm_key]][, , "total_within"]) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("genre_slug") |>
  mutate(
    genre = prettify_genre(genre_slug),
    model = "M3: Multi-membership",
    # Add overall fixed effect to convert adjustment → absolute
    estimate  = Estimate + mm_total_within_fe,
    std.error = Est.Error,
    conf.low  = Q2.5 + mm_total_within_fe,
    conf.high = Q97.5 + mm_total_within_fe
  ) |>
  select(model, genre, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high)

# M3 (multi-membership) between-person: extract random slopes + add overall total_between FE
mm_total_between_fe <- fixef(h2_mm_model)["total_between", "Estimate"]

m3_mm_between <- as.data.frame(m3_re[[mm_key]][, , "total_between"]) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("genre_slug") |>
  mutate(
    genre = prettify_genre(genre_slug),
    model = "M3: Multi-membership",
    estimate  = Estimate + mm_total_between_fe,
    std.error = Est.Error,
    conf.low  = Q2.5 + mm_total_between_fe,
    conf.high = Q97.5 + mm_total_between_fe
  ) |>
  select(model, genre, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high)

# --- M2 (hierarchical prior): extract within and between ---
m2_hier_within <- summary(h2_hier_model)$fixed |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("term") |>
  filter(grepl("^gh_.*_within$", term)) |>
  mutate(
    genre = prettify_genre(sub("^gh_(.*)_within$", "\\1", term)),
    model = "M2: Hierarchical prior",
    estimate  = Estimate,
    std.error = Est.Error,
    conf.low  = `l-95% CI`,
    conf.high = `u-95% CI`
  ) |>
  select(model, genre, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high)

m2_hier_between <- summary(h2_hier_model)$fixed |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("term") |>
  filter(grepl("^gh_.*_between$", term)) |>
  mutate(
    genre = prettify_genre(sub("^gh_(.*)_between$", "\\1", term)),
    model = "M2: Hierarchical prior",
    estimate  = Estimate,
    std.error = Est.Error,
    conf.low  = `l-95% CI`,
    conf.high = `u-95% CI`
  ) |>
  select(model, genre, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high)

# --- Combine ---
# Within-person: all three models (M1 FE, M2 Hier, M3 MM)
all_within  <- bind_rows(m1_within, m2_hier_within, m3_mm_within)
# Between-person: all three models (M3 now has full within + between)
all_between <- bind_rows(m1_between, m2_hier_between, m3_mm_between)

# Sport: named descriptively in the Discussion as the largest positive
# between-person point estimate (not interpreted, per the pre-registration).
sport_b <- m2_hier_between |> filter(genre == "Sport")
sport_w <- m2_hier_within  |> filter(genre == "Sport")
stopifnot(
  nrow(sport_b) == 1, nrow(sport_w) == 1,
  sport_b$estimate == max(m2_hier_between$estimate),
  sport_b$conf.low < 0, sport_b$conf.high > 0.06,        # straddles zero AND the ROPE bound
  sport_w$conf.low < 0, sport_w$conf.high > 0,           # within-person counterpart is null
  abs(sport_w$estimate) < 0.02
)

# Guard for the Discussion's per-genre paragraph: all 14 within-person
# point estimates lie within a third of the SESOI (|estimate| < 0.02).
stopifnot(max(abs(m2_hier_within$estimate)) < 0.02)

# Order genres by the M2 (hierarchical prior) within-person estimate; the
# shared y-axis requires a single ordering across both facets.
genre_order_within <- m2_hier_within |> arrange(estimate) |> pull(genre)

all_coefs <- bind_rows(
  all_within  |> mutate(dimension = "Within-person (H2a)"),
  all_between |> mutate(dimension = "Between-person (H2b)")
) |>
  mutate(dimension = factor(dimension, levels = c(
    "Within-person (H2a)", "Between-person (H2b)"
  )))
```

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-integrated-coefs
#| fig-cap: "*Per-Genre Exposure Coefficients Across Three Model Specifications.* Left: within-person (H2a); right: between-person (H2b), on a common x-axis. Each genre row shows M1 (circle, no pooling), M2 (square, hierarchical prior), and M3 (diamond, multi-membership, with the overall fixed effect added back to place all three on an absolute scale). Genres ordered by the M2 within-person estimate. Green band: pre-registered ROPE (±0.06)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

# Factor order: M1 top within each genre row, M3 bottom.
# position_dodge with a vertical y-axis places the LAST level at the top,
# so we reverse the desired visual order in the factor levels.
model_levels <- c("M3: Multi-membership", "M2: Hierarchical prior", "M1: Fixed effects")

ggplot(all_coefs |>
         mutate(genre = factor(genre, levels = genre_order_within),
                model = factor(model, levels = model_levels)),
       aes(x = estimate, y = genre, shape = model, colour = model)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -0.06, xmax = 0.06,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.10) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-0.06, 0.06), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "solid", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
                 linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.5,
                 position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = estimate - std.error, xmax = estimate + std.error),
                 linewidth = 1,
                 position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("M1: Fixed effects" = 16,
                                 "M2: Hierarchical prior" = 15,
                                 "M3: Multi-membership" = 18),
                     breaks = c("M1: Fixed effects", "M2: Hierarchical prior", "M3: Multi-membership")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("M1: Fixed effects" = unname(model_palette["M1"]),
                                  "M2: Hierarchical prior" = unname(model_palette["M2"]),
                                  "M3: Multi-membership" = unname(model_palette["M3"])),
                      breaks = c("M1: Fixed effects", "M2: Hierarchical prior", "M3: Multi-membership")) +
  facet_wrap(~ dimension) +
  labs(x = "Genre coefficient (SWEMWBS item-mean per hour/day)",
       y = NULL, shape = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```
:::

The three model specifications converge on a consistent per-genre pattern for both within- and between-person effects. The primary visible difference is that M2 and M3 produce narrower credible intervals for rare genres (Visual Novel, Fighting, Point-and-Click) relative to M1's wider independent estimates, reflecting the partial pooling that each achieves through different mechanisms. For common genres, the three specifications produce near-identical point estimates and interval widths.

```{r}
#| label: h2-hier-genre-coefs
#| include: false
#| eval: true

hier_within_coefs <- summary(h2_hier_model)$fixed |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("term") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(grepl("^gh_.*_within$", term)) |>
  mutate(genre = prettify_genre(sub("^gh_(.*)_within$", "\\1", term)))

hier_between_coefs <- summary(h2_hier_model)$fixed |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("term") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(grepl("^gh_.*_between$", term)) |>
  mutate(genre = prettify_genre(sub("^gh_(.*)_between$", "\\1", term)))

n_hier_within_in_rope <- sum(
  hier_within_coefs[["l-95% CI"]] > -0.06 & hier_within_coefs[["u-95% CI"]] < 0.06
)
hier_between_max_genre <- hier_between_coefs$genre[which.max(hier_between_coefs$Estimate)]
```

Under the hierarchical prior (M2), `r n_hier_within_in_rope` of the 14 within-person genre coefficients have 95% CrIs that fall entirely within the pre-registered ROPE band (±0.06). The between-person coefficients are wider but show a similar pattern, with `r hier_between_max_genre` as the genre whose point estimate sits closest to the upper ROPE boundary.

Taken together, the H2 results do not support the pre-registered prediction that genres differ meaningfully in their association with wellbeing. The pooled heterogeneity estimates fall below the smallest effect size of interest on both the within- and between-person dimensions, genre terms do not improve out-of-sample prediction (Appendix D), and the wide credible intervals for rare genres preclude confident inference about any specific genre–wellbeing pair.

## Robustness

Three sensitivity analyses probe the conclusions' dependence on analytic choices; all three leave every conclusion intact. Adjusting for age, gender, and ethnicity shifts the H1 coefficients by less than 0.01 points and changes no ROPE verdict (@tbl-sensitivity-demo). Halving or doubling the heterogeneity hyperprior scales leaves the H2 parameters essentially unchanged (@tbl-prior-sensitivity). Refitting on multiply imputed data (m = 100) reproduces the H1 equivalence under the pre-registered 90% CI rule and rejects genre-coefficient equality in neither pooled dimension (@tbl-sensitivity-imputation). Full specifications, results, and diagnostics for all three analyses, together with the predictive model comparison and a description of the pre-registered frequentist analysis supplement, are reported in Appendix D.

```{r}
#| label: abstract-claims-guard
#| include: false

# The abstract is static YAML text and cannot compute its numbers inline.
# Since it now reports findings in plain language (APA style), the only values
# it still quotes are the sample descriptors, which the first two assertions
# pin directly. The rest are retained as a regression check on the headline
# posterior quantities: those are reported via inline R in the Results and
# Discussion, so a refit that shifts a printed digit fails the render loudly
# rather than drifting through unnoticed.
# Tolerance = half a rounding unit at the reported precision.
stopifnot(
  n_participants == 1838,
  n_observations == 6680,
  abs(beta1_mean - 0.003)     < 5e-4,
  abs(beta1_ci[1] - (-0.008)) < 5e-4,
  abs(beta1_ci[2] - 0.014)    < 5e-4,
  beta1_in_rope > 0.9995,
  abs(beta2_mean - (-0.017))  < 5e-4,
  abs(beta2_ci[1] - (-0.035)) < 5e-4,
  abs(beta2_ci[2] - 0.001)    < 5e-4,
  abs(tau_mean - 0.014)       < 5e-4,
  abs(sigma_sw_mean - 0.044)  < 5e-4,
  genre_sd_mean > tau_mean, genre_sd_mean < sigma_sw_mean,
  abs(sd_slope_mean - 0.035)  < 5e-4,
  abs(sd_slope_ci[1] - 0.005) < 5e-4,
  abs(sd_slope_ci[2] - 0.062) < 5e-4
)
```

## Exploratory Results: The Daily Timescale

```{r}
#| label: daily-fits
#| include: false
#| eval: true

# ---- Fits ------------------------------------------------------------------
d_m0_ls   <- readRDS(here("models/daily/m0_daily_ls.rds"))
d_m0_full <- readRDS(here("models/daily/m0_daily_ls_full.rds"))
d_m0_ar   <- readRDS(here("models/daily/m0_daily_ls_ar.rds"))
d_m0_wh   <- readRDS(here("models/daily/m0_daily_ls_wh.rds"))
d_m0_xfl  <- readRDS(here("models/daily/m0_daily_ls_xfl.rds"))
d_xfl_dr  <- posterior::as_draws_df(d_m0_xfl)
d_rx_b1    <- mean(d_xfl_dr$b_xfl_within)
d_rx_b1_ci <- quantile(d_xfl_dr$b_xfl_within, c(.025, .975))
d_m2_ls   <- readRDS(here("models/daily/m2_daily_ls_v2.rds"))
d_m3_ls   <- readRDS(here("models/daily/m3_daily_mm_ls.rds"))

stopifnot(nobs(d_m0_ls) == sum(!is.na(daily_frame$life_sat)))

d_extract_m0 <- function(fit, sesoi) {
  dr <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit)
  w <- dr$b_total_within
  b <- dr$b_total_between
  s <- dr$sd_pid__total_within
  list(
    b1 = mean(w), b1_ci = quantile(w, c(.025, .975)),
    b1_rope = mean(abs(w) < sesoi),
    b2 = mean(b), b2_ci = quantile(b, c(.025, .975)),
    b2_rope = mean(abs(b) < sesoi),
    sd_slope = mean(s), sd_slope_ci = quantile(s, c(.025, .975)),
    sd_slope_above = mean(s > sesoi),
    rhat = max(brms::rhat(fit), na.rm = TRUE),
    divs = sum(subset(brms::nuts_params(fit), Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)
  )
}
d_extract_m2 <- function(fit, sesoi) {
  dr <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit)
  tw <- dr$tau_genre_within
  tb <- dr$tau_genre_between
  list(
    tau_w = mean(tw), tau_w_ci = quantile(tw, c(.025, .975)),
    tau_w_rope = mean(tw < sesoi),
    tau_b = mean(tb), tau_b_ci = quantile(tb, c(.025, .975)),
    tau_b_rope = mean(tb < sesoi),
    rhat = max(brms::rhat(fit), na.rm = TRUE),
    divs = sum(subset(brms::nuts_params(fit), Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)
  )
}
d_r0  <- d_extract_m0(d_m0_ls, d_primary)
d_r0f <- d_extract_m0(d_m0_full, d_primary)
d_r0a <- d_extract_m0(d_m0_ar, d_primary)
d_r0w <- d_extract_m0(d_m0_wh, d_primary)
d_ar1_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(d_m0_ar)[["ar[1]"]]
d_ar1 <- mean(d_ar1_draws)
d_r2  <- d_extract_m2(d_m2_ls, d_primary)

# Draw vectors kept for the daily figure

d_dr2 <- posterior::as_draws_df(d_m2_ls)

d_m3_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(d_m3_ls)
d_sw_col <- names(d_m3_draws)[grepl("sd_mm.*total_within", names(d_m3_draws))]
d_sb_col <- names(d_m3_draws)[grepl("sd_mm.*total_between", names(d_m3_draws))]

d_sigma_sw_ci    <- quantile(d_m3_draws[[d_sw_col]], c(.025, .975))

d_sigma_sb_ci    <- quantile(d_m3_draws[[d_sb_col]], c(.025, .975))
d_sigma_sb_below <- mean(d_m3_draws[[d_sb_col]] < d_primary)

# M1-daily: unpooled fixed-effects specification. Its heterogeneity summary
# is the per-draw SD across the 14 genre coefficients, which includes
# estimation error (sampling-noise inflation), as in the registered M1.
d_m1_ls    <- readRDS(here("models/daily/m1_daily_ls.rds"))
d_m1_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(d_m1_ls)
d_m1_wcols <- grep("^b_gh_.*_w$", names(d_m1_draws), value = TRUE)
d_m1_bcols <- grep("^b_gh_.*_b$", names(d_m1_draws), value = TRUE)
stopifnot(length(d_m1_wcols) == 14, length(d_m1_bcols) == 14)
d_m1_sdw_draws <- apply(as.matrix(d_m1_draws[, d_m1_wcols]), 1, sd)
d_m1_sdb_draws <- apply(as.matrix(d_m1_draws[, d_m1_bcols]), 1, sd)
d_m1_sdw       <- mean(d_m1_sdw_draws)
d_m1_sdw_ci    <- quantile(d_m1_sdw_draws, c(.025, .975))
d_m1_sdw_below <- mean(d_m1_sdw_draws < d_primary)
d_m1_sdb       <- mean(d_m1_sdb_draws)
d_m1_sdb_ci    <- quantile(d_m1_sdb_draws, c(.025, .975))
d_m1_sdb_below <- mean(d_m1_sdb_draws < d_primary)
d_m1_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(d_m1_ls), na.rm = TRUE)
d_m1_divs <- sum(subset(brms::nuts_params(d_m1_ls),
                        Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)

# M3-daily H1 estimates via its total-playtime fixed effects (mirrors the
# biweekly M0-vs-M3 consistency check in @fig-h1-all-models)
d_m3_b1      <- mean(d_m3_draws$b_total_within)
d_m3_b1_ci   <- quantile(d_m3_draws$b_total_within, c(.025, .975))
d_m3_b1_rope <- mean(abs(d_m3_draws$b_total_within) < d_primary)
d_m3_b2      <- mean(d_m3_draws$b_total_between)
d_m3_b2_ci   <- quantile(d_m3_draws$b_total_between, c(.025, .975))
d_m3_b2_rope <- mean(abs(d_m3_draws$b_total_between) < d_primary)
d_m3_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(d_m3_ls), na.rm = TRUE)
d_m3_divs <- sum(subset(brms::nuts_params(d_m3_ls), Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)

# Same-instrument bridge: M0 on the biweekly life-satisfaction ladder
# (0-10, registered-style frame). Its leisure-anchored benchmark on that
# scale is 7.5% of the 10-point range over five leisure hours = 0.15/h.
d_bridge_fit  <- readRDS(here("models/daily/m0_biweekly_ls_bridge.rds"))
d_bridge_dr   <- posterior::as_draws_df(d_bridge_fit)
d_bridge_b1   <- mean(d_bridge_dr$b_total_within)
d_bridge_ci   <- quantile(d_bridge_dr$b_total_within, c(.025, .975))
d_bridge_rope <- mean(abs(d_bridge_dr$b_total_within) < d_bridge_th)
d_bridge_b2      <- mean(d_bridge_dr$b_total_between)
d_bridge_b2_ci   <- quantile(d_bridge_dr$b_total_between, c(.025, .975))
d_bridge_b2_rope <- mean(abs(d_bridge_dr$b_total_between) < d_bridge_th)
d_bridge_n    <- nobs(d_bridge_fit)
d_bridge_sw   <- sesoi_d$s_w_bls
```

Participants in the analysed daily sample contribute a median of `r d_median_days` diary days, and participation declines from `r print_num(d_day1_n)` responses on day 1 to `r print_num(d_day30_n)` on day 30. Windows have a median length of `r round(d_wh_med, 1)` hours and close at the survey completion timestamp, so `r round(100 * d_zero_share, 1)`% of person-days record zero console/PC play in the window. Both positive controls pass in this subsample: self-reported past-24-hour play agrees with telemetry in a matched 24-hour window on `r round(100 * d_ctrl_agree, 1)`% of responses (φ = `r round(d_ctrl_phi, 2)`), and men play more Shooter than women (d = `r round(d_shooter_d, 2)`).

At the daily level, the within-person association between same-day playtime and life satisfaction was positive: β = `r round(d_r0$b1, 2)` points per additional hour (95% CrI \[`r round(d_r0$b1_ci[1], 2)`, `r round(d_r0$b1_ci[2], 2)`\]), with the lower credible bound at zero and the entire posterior inside the equivalence region (`r round(100 * d_r0$b1_rope, 1)`%); the interval widens past zero under two of the three robustness refits (Appendix D). Person-to-person variation in this slope was bounded: random-slope SD = `r round(d_r0$sd_slope, 2)` (95% CrI \[`r round(d_r0$sd_slope_ci[1], 2)`, `r round(d_r0$sd_slope_ci[2], 2)`\]), with `r round(100 * (1 - d_r0$sd_slope_above), 1)`% of the posterior below the benchmark. Between persons, with habitual play measured in full-day hours, participants who play more than others reported slightly lower daily life satisfaction: β = `r round(d_r0$b2, 2)` points per habitual daily hour (95% CrI \[`r round(d_r0$b2_ci[1], 2)`, `r round(d_r0$b2_ci[2], 2)`\]), a negative lean whose posterior sits `r round(100 * d_r0$b2_rope, 1)`% inside the equivalence region; the all-responses refit and the multi-membership model's total-playtime fixed effects give materially the same estimates on both dimensions (@tbl-daily-summary).

Genre heterogeneity at the daily level, with between-person genre exposures likewise in habitual daily hours, stayed within the registered pattern. Within persons all three specifications sit inside the benchmark: the unpooled M1 gives a per-draw SD across the 14 genre coefficients of `r round(d_m1_sdw, 2)` (95% CrI \[`r round(d_m1_sdw_ci[1], 2)`, `r round(d_m1_sdw_ci[2], 2)`\]; noise-inflated, as at the biweekly level), the hierarchical prior gives τ~within~ = `r round(d_r2$tau_w, 2)` (95% CrI \[`r round(d_r2$tau_w_ci[1], 2)`, `r round(d_r2$tau_w_ci[2], 2)`\]; `r round(100 * d_r2$tau_w_rope, 1)`% below the benchmark), and the multi-membership model gives σ~s,within~ = `r round(d_sigma_sw, 2)` (95% CrI \[`r round(d_sigma_sw_ci[1], 2)`, `r round(d_sigma_sw_ci[2], 2)`\]; `r round(100 * d_sigma_sw_below, 1)`% below). Between persons the pooled evidence is inconclusive rather than bounded: τ~between~ = `r round(d_r2$tau_b, 2)` (95% CrI \[`r round(d_r2$tau_b_ci[1], 2)`, `r round(d_r2$tau_b_ci[2], 2)`\]) straddles the benchmark with `r round(100 * d_r2$tau_b_rope, 1)`% of its posterior below it, σ~s,between~ = `r round(d_sigma_sb, 2)` (95% CrI \[`r round(d_sigma_sb_ci[1], 2)`, `r round(d_sigma_sb_ci[2], 2)`\]) keeps `r round(100 * d_sigma_sb_below, 1)`% below, and M1's between-person raw SD (`r round(d_m1_sdb, 2)`, 95% CrI \[`r round(d_m1_sdb_ci[1], 2)`, `r round(d_m1_sdb_ci[2], 2)`\]) sits far above with the usual estimation-error inflation. Sampling diagnostics were healthy (all R-hat ≤ `r round(max(d_r0$rhat, d_r0f$rhat, d_r0a$rhat, d_r0w$rhat, d_m1_rhat, d_r2$rhat, d_m3_rhat), 3)`); the hierarchical-prior model retained `r d_r2$divs` divergent transitions of 16,000 post-warmup draws (0.1%), and no other fit had any. Individual genre estimates carry credible intervals many times wider than their point estimates and are not interpreted. @fig-daily-posteriors displays the posteriors against the benchmark.

Right: genre heterogeneity from all three specifications, coloured as in @fig-integrated-coefs: M1 (per-draw SD of the 14 unpooled coefficients; includes estimation error and reads as an upper bound), M2 (hierarchical-prior τ), and M3 (multi-membership σ_s). d_fig_draws <- bind_rows(

```{r}
         param = "M1: SD of coefs, within", value = d_m1_sdw_draws),

         param = "M2: τ within", value = d_dr2$tau_genre_within),

) |>

# Per-panel benchmark geometry: symmetric for the dose panel, one-sided for

d_fig_bands <- tibble(
  panel = factor(levels(d_fig_draws$panel), levels = levels(d_fig_draws$panel)),

d_fig_lines <- bind_rows(

ggplot(d_fig_draws, aes(x = value, y = param)) +

    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

```{r}
stopifnot(

  d_r0$b1_ci[1] >= 0, d_r0$b1_ci[1] < 0.01,

  # Robustness triple: AR and window-length lose the exclusion, exclude-

  abs(d_r0a$b1 - 0.14) < 5e-3, d_r0a$b1_ci[1] < 0,
  abs(d_ar1 - 0.31) < 0.02,
  abs(d_r0w$b1 - 0.15) < 5e-3, d_r0w$b1_ci[1] < 0,
  abs(d_rx_b1 - 0.18) < 5e-3, d_rx_b1_ci[1] > 0,

  abs(d_r0$b2 - (-0.43)) < 5e-3,

  d_r0$b2_rope > 0.92, d_r0$b2_rope < 0.97,

  abs(d_r0f$b2 - (-0.52)) < 5e-3, d_r0f$b2_ci[1] < 0, d_r0f$b2_ci[2] > 0,

  abs(d_r0$sd_slope - 0.64) < 5e-3, (1 - d_r0$sd_slope_above) > 0.97,
  # M3 agreement with M0 on both dimensions
  abs(d_m3_b1 - 0.14) < 5e-3, abs(d_m3_b1 - d_r0$b1) < 0.1,
  abs(d_m3_b2 - (-0.46)) < 5e-3, abs(d_m3_b2 - d_r0$b2) < 0.1,
  # H2-daily within bounded in all three specifications
  abs(d_m1_sdw - 0.61) < 5e-3, d_m1_sdw_below > 0.99,
  abs(d_r2$tau_w - 0.15) < 5e-3, d_r2$tau_w_rope > 0.9995,
  abs(d_sigma_sw - 0.32) < 5e-3, d_sigma_sw_below > 0.95,

      d_r2$tau_w, d_m1_sdw, d_sigma_sw) < d_primary,
  # H2-daily between: tau_b straddles; sigma_sb largely below; M1 noise
  abs(d_r2$tau_b - 0.84) < 5e-3,

  d_m1_sdb > d_primary,

  max(d_r0$rhat, d_r0f$rhat, d_r0a$rhat, d_r0w$rhat, d_m1_rhat,
      d_r2$rhat, d_m3_rhat) < 1.05,

  # Bridge: within practically null; between credibly negative at its scale
  abs(d_bridge_b1 - (-0.031)) < 5e-4, d_bridge_ci[2] < 0.01,
  d_bridge_rope > 0.9995,
  abs(d_bridge_b2 - (-0.117)) < 5e-4, d_bridge_b2_ci[2] < 0,
  d_bridge_b2_rope > 0.15, d_bridge_b2_rope < 0.35,

  # "roughly double" in s_w units
  (d_r0$b1 / sesoi_d$s_w_ls) / (beta1_mean / sesoi_d$s_w_swemwbs) > 1.4,
  (d_r0$b1 / sesoi_d$s_w_ls) / (beta1_mean / sesoi_d$s_w_swemwbs) < 2.5
)
```

# Discussion

This study asked two questions. First, is total playtime meaningfully associated with wellbeing when measured across multiple platforms with digital trace data? Second, does it matter what people play? The answer to the first question is no: both within-person fluctuations and between-person differences in playtime were practically equivalent to zero against the pre-registered threshold, replicating and extending prior findings from single-platform studies [@ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024; @vuorreTimeSpentPlaying2022]. Because playtime was measured jointly across participants' console and PC platforms (the all-platform total, including mobile, reaches the same conclusion in the pre-registered sensitivity analysis), the recurring objection that single-platform nulls could be offset by effects hiding in unmeasured play does not apply here. The answer to the second is also, at this measurement resolution, no. Genre heterogeneity estimates fell at or below the smallest effect size of interest across three model specifications, genre terms did not improve out-of-sample prediction, and individual genre estimates were too imprecise to single out specific genres. One candidate explanation for the field's persistent aggregate null was that large, opposing genre effects cancel when averaged; our results do not support that account at the biweekly timescale. The registration asked whether it is justified to generalise video game effects across genres; for mental wellbeing, the answer is yes: the aggregate null generalises, tested directly rather than assumed [@yarkoniGeneralizabilityCrisis2019]. Disaggregating playtime by genre sharpened the picture without changing its substance, which redirects attention towards finer-grained characterisations of play.

## Total Playtime and Wellbeing (H1)

H1 predicted that total playtime would not be meaningfully associated with wellbeing, and both components of the hypothesis were supported (see @fig-h1-all-models and @tbl-hypothesis-summary). Within persons, when participants played more than their own average in a given two-week wave, their wellbeing barely changed, consistent with previous digital trace studies, which have repeatedly found aggregate playtime to be a poor predictor of wellbeing fluctuations [@ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024; @ballouPerceivedValueVideo2025; @larrieuHowGamingMotives2023]. Between persons, practical equivalence was likewise established. The between-person point estimate leans negative (individuals who play more on average report slightly lower wellbeing), but the association sits far below the threshold of practical significance and, as a between-person quantity, is vulnerable to confounding.

Life-events benchmarks put these magnitudes in context; because meta-analytic life-event effects are standardised on the total, between-person variation in wellbeing, we standardise here on the observed total SD of `r round(wemwbs_total_sd, 2)` rather than the within-person SD used in the Methods. On that scale, an association at the SESOI threshold corresponds to `r round(0.12 / wemwbs_total_sd, 2)` SD for a 2-hour/day change in play. This is below the meta-analytic effect of getting married on cognitive wellbeing (life satisfaction; approximately +0.26 SD \[95% CI 0.17, 0.35\]) and roughly a third of the effect of losing a job (approximately −0.43 SD \[−0.48, −0.38\]); on affective wellbeing, by contrast, marriage's immediate effect is near zero [@luhmann2012subjective]. The threshold thus sits below the typical major life event, as a minimally important difference should. The associations we actually observe fall an order of magnitude below the threshold itself: at the within-person point estimate, a 2-hour/day change corresponds to `r round(beta1_mean * 2, 3)` points, about `r round(abs(beta1_mean) * 2 / wemwbs_total_sd, 2)` SD, a plausible magnitude for a routine daily leisure activity whose cumulative impact is modulated by many other life factors.

Inverting the estimates makes their practical magnitude concrete. For wellbeing to shift by the minimally important difference of 0.3 points (see Smallest Effect Size of Interest), the within-person point estimate implies that a player would need to sustain roughly `r round(0.3 / beta1_mean)` additional hours of play per day, several times more hours than a day contains; even at the credible-interval bound most favourable to an effect, the required dose is `r round(0.3 / beta1_ci[2])` extra hours per day, still more than the waking day contains and more extreme than the 10 additional daily hours that @vuorreTimeSpentPlaying2022 derived from game-level telemetry. Even if within-person effects accumulated across waves, which is an unrealistic assumption [cf. @vuorreTimeSpentPlaying2022], a player adding one hour of play every day would cross the noticeability threshold only after roughly `r round(0.3 / beta1_mean)` biweekly waves, or about `r round(0.3 / beta1_mean * 2 / 52, 1)` years. Between persons, the same inversion at the most favourable bound implies that two otherwise-similar people would need to differ by approximately `r round(0.3 / abs(beta2_ci[1]))` hours of habitual daily play, more than the roughly 5 hours of daily leisure time available, before their expected wellbeing differed noticeably.

The directional pattern, a within-person estimate centred on zero alongside a between-person estimate leaning negative, is the classic signature of selection, individuals with lower baseline wellbeing spending more time gaming rather than gaming causing lower wellbeing [@ballouPerceivedValueVideo2025], and it is not unique to gaming. It is a general feature of observational research with time-invariant confounding, well-documented in the social media and screen time literature and formalised as the ecological fallacy: the principle that between-person correlations do not necessarily reflect within-person processes [@robinson1950ecological; see @kievit2013simpsons for a review in psychological science; @rohrer2023within]. Qualitative evidence from the same dataset supports the selection interpretation: participants reported playing more during periods of illness or grief, consistent with lower wellbeing driving gaming uptake rather than the reverse [@ballou2025confounds]. @egami2024causal illustrate the stakes of this confounding within a single dataset: their preliminary association analysis showed a small negative correlation between gaming and mental health (higher psychological distress) even after covariate adjustment, whereas their causal analysis of the same data, exploiting console lotteries as a natural experiment, showed positive effects of 0.1 to 0.6 standard deviations.

Beyond the average association, the model also bounds how much the person-specific association can vary. A standing objection to aggregate nulls is that a null mean may conceal subpopulations for whom playtime genuinely helps or harms [cf. @karhulahti2025claims]. The random-slope estimate speaks directly to this: person-specific within-person slopes are distributed with SD = `r round(sd_slope_mean, 3)` (95% CrI: \[`r round(sd_slope_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(sd_slope_ci[2], 3)`\]), and only `r round(sd_slope_p_above * 100, 1)`% of the posterior places this spread above the SESOI. Individuals in the tails of that distribution may still exceed the threshold, but the typical person-to-person deviation is smaller than the smallest effect we consider practically meaningful; this is the same conclusion the genre analysis reaches for content categories. At the biweekly timescale, the playtime null is not an artefact of averaging: it holds across persons as well as across genres.

## Genre-Specific Effects (H2)

H2 predicted that genres would differ in their associations with wellbeing, some potentially positive and others potentially negative, with varying strength. The data disconfirmed this registered expectation, and with a magnitude attached rather than a simple failure to support: the primary multi-membership model estimates the between-genre standard deviation of within-person slopes at σ~s~ = `r round(sigma_sw_mean, 3)` (95% CrI: \[`r round(sigma_sw_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(sigma_sw_ci[2], 3)`\]), with the hierarchical prior (τ~genre~ = `r round(tau_mean, 3)`, 95% CrI: \[`r round(tau_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(tau_ci[2], 3)`\]) and the pre-registered fixed-effects specification (coefficient SD = `r round(genre_sd_mean, 3)`, 95% CrI: \[`r round(genre_sd_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(genre_sd_ci[2], 3)`\]) in agreement. All three are estimated at or below the smallest effect size of interest, with `r round(tau_in_rope * 100, 1)`% of the τ~genre~ posterior inside the pre-registered ROPE, although the multi-membership σ~s~ retains roughly a fifth of its posterior mass above the threshold. Consistent with this, the pre-registered primary-genre joint Wald tests in the supplement fail to reject coefficient equality and genre terms do not improve out-of-sample prediction; the complete-case joint test on the full-attribution exposures does detect a departure from exact within-person equality, but of a magnitude well below the SESOI (Appendix D). Whatever genre-to-genre variation exists in the per-hour relationship with wellbeing, it is smaller than the smallest difference we deemed practically meaningful: genres are, in these data, statistically distinguishable yet practically interchangeable.

These estimates are upper bounds rather than failures to detect. Each pooled model estimates how much genre slopes could differ and places the bulk of that posterior below the SESOI, so the evidence constrains the magnitude of genre heterogeneity rather than merely failing to distinguish it from zero; the prior sensitivity analysis (Appendix D) shows the constraint is data-driven rather than an artefact of the hyperprior scale.

This conclusion carries a precision caveat: equivalence claims are bounded by the width of the intervals behind them. Under the hierarchical prior, `r n_hier_within_in_rope` of the 14 within-person genre coefficients have 95% CrIs that fall entirely within the ROPE band, but the intervals for rarely played genres are wide. Our conclusion is therefore not that gaming genre is irrelevant to wellbeing; it is that, at the biweekly timescale and with the present sample, we cannot distinguish between "genre X has a modest practically meaningful effect" and "genre X has no effect at all" for any individual genre, while the pooled evidence bounds genre differences below the threshold of practical significance. The predictive comparison corroborates these bounds rather than independently establishing them: an ELPD comparison of this size is not guaranteed to detect heterogeneity as small as the SESOI, but if genre-specific slopes differed substantially, models encoding genre composition should predict held-out wellbeing better than a model blind to it, and they do not.

The per-genre pattern is one of tight clustering rather than contrast. Under the hierarchical prior, the 14 within-person point estimates span only `r round(min(m2_hier_within$estimate), 3)` (`r m2_hier_within$genre[which.min(m2_hier_within$estimate)]`) to +`r round(max(m2_hier_within$estimate), 3)` (`r m2_hier_within$genre[which.max(m2_hier_within$estimate)]`); no estimate lies more than a third of the SESOI from zero. The most-played genres by total playtime (`r paste(head(rank14, 4), collapse = ", ")`; see @fig-genre-upset) sit inside this same narrow band, so the genres dominating everyday play show no meaningful association with wellbeing fluctuations from wave to wave.

The between-person genre coefficients, more vulnerable to confounding but more directly comparable to the life-events literature, show a qualitatively similar picture: most overlap both zero and the ROPE band, and per the pre-registered analysis plan we do not interpret differences between individual genre coefficients without formal post-hoc tests. Descriptively, the largest positive between-person point estimate belongs to Sport (`r round(sport_b$estimate, 3)`, 95% CrI \[`r round(sport_b$conf.low, 3)`, `r round(sport_b$conf.high, 3)`\] in M2), but its interval straddles both zero and the ROPE bound and is formally inconclusive; its within-person counterpart is null (`r round(sport_w$estimate, 3)`, 95% CrI \[`r round(sport_w$conf.low, 3)`, `r round(sport_w$conf.high, 3)`\]), a divergence consistent with self-selection: people who favour sport games may, for example, be more physically or socially active, rather than the games themselves improving wellbeing.

The imprecision for rare genres is a data sparsity problem, not a theoretical one. Theory suggests these genres could relate to wellbeing through distinct pathways: visual novels prioritise narrative choice and eudaimonic engagement [@cole2021eudaimonic], and competitive genres like fighting games combine the competitive pressure that @adachiEffectViolentVideo2011 identified as the active ingredient in aggression effects with the potential for competence frustration [@ballou2023frustration]. Meaningfully estimating these effects would require either substantially larger samples or finer temporal resolution than the biweekly level used here.

## The Daily Timescale (Exploratory)

The exploratory daily analysis reproduces both registered conclusions at the daily level. Within persons, every estimate lies inside the equivalence region under every specification, and the same-day point estimate is positive, roughly double its biweekly counterpart in within-person standard-deviation units (`r round(d_r0$b1 / sesoi_d$s_w_ls, 3)` versus `r round(beta1_mean / sesoi_d$s_w_swemwbs, 3)` s~w~ per hour); the direction is consistent with the session-level affective uplift reported for this population [@vuorre2024affective] and with the positive causal estimates of @egami2024causal, though its resolution is fragile across the robustness refits and should be read as suggestive rather than resolved. Its practical magnitude is negligible under every reading: shifting daily life satisfaction by one minimally important difference (`r d_mid_daily` points) would require `r round(d_mid_daily / d_r0$b1)` additional hours of same-day play at the point estimate, more hours than the day itself contains, and `r round(d_mid_daily / d_r0$b1_ci[2])` hours even at the credible bound most favourable to an effect, most of the waking day and far beyond the five hours of daily leisure the benchmark assumes. Between persons the daily estimate leans negative inside the equivalence region, as the registered SWEMWBS estimate does at its own scale; the one credibly negative quantity in this family is the biweekly life-satisfaction ladder's between-person estimate (β = `r round(d_bridge_b2, 3)` rungs per hour, 95% CrI \[`r round(d_bridge_b2_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(d_bridge_b2_ci[2], 3)`\], `r round(100 * d_bridge_b2_rope, 1)`% inside its benchmark region), whose within-person counterpart stays practically null (β = `r round(d_bridge_b1, 3)`, 95% CrI \[`r round(d_bridge_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(d_bridge_ci[2], 3)`\]). The between-person dimension is also the least settled: at the credible bound most favourable to an effect the dose reaches one minimally important difference within `r round(d_mid_daily / abs(d_r0$b2_ci[1]))` habitual hours per day, inside the realistic leisure range, and a habitual-play contrast is where selection, that people play more during worse periods of life, is least separable from any effect of play. Whether the negative lean reflects the life-satisfaction construct, the evaluative frame, or selection into habitual play is exactly the between-person question a registered follow-up should settle, and no design at this timescale can.

## Implications for the Field

Beyond the hypothesis tests, the findings speak to the questions the introduction raised: whether genre can serve as a workable scientific category, and where wellbeing effects should be sought if content categories carry so little signal.

The study demonstrates a workflow the genre literature has repeatedly called for but not yet implemented. Systematic reviews report that roughly half of genre studies employ a bespoke classification, one in five never specifies its basis, and labels are typically self-reported by participants or assigned by researchers [@starostaTangledWaysClassify2024]; structured metadata repositories have been proposed as the remedy [@liPreliminaryNetworkAnalysis2020; @starostaTangledWaysClassify2024]. Here, objective telemetry from three platforms was linked to a single crowd-sourced repository taxonomy (IGDB), covering `r round(genre_cov_overall, 1)`% of in-study playtime, with the full pipeline released for reuse [@ballou2025openplay]. These results demonstrate that genre-level media research with digital trace data is practicable. The workflow is a contribution independent of what it found: the coverage and precision figures reported here tell the next team what a design of this size can and cannot resolve.

Our conclusion that genre labels may be too coarse a proxy for the psychologically relevant features of gameplay is supported by converging evidence. Our 13-mechanisms review [@ballouHowVideoGames2025] identifies exposures at three levels: context-centred (when, where, with whom), game-centred (what game, what features, what genre), and player-centred (why, how, what is experienced). Of the 13 proposed mechanisms through which gaming might affect wellbeing, most operate at the feature or player-experience level: need satisfaction depends on autonomy-supportive design features [@ballouBasicNeedsGames2023; @pengNeedSatisfactionSupportive2012], social capital depends on co-play relationships [@depping2018friendship; @vella2015playing], and affect regulation depends on the match between gameplay and current emotional state [@kosa2020escapism]. Genre labels cannot capture any of these, and dedicated taxonomies of structural game features now exist for characterising them directly [@sainiInvestigatingGamingStructural2023]. Recent work demonstrates that even within a single game, behavioural variation in how players engage with mechanics and modes is associated with meaningful wellbeing differences when genre and total playtime are held constant [@hakman2026notallplay]. If within-game variation predicts wellbeing when genre is constant, genre labels are not the relevant unit of analysis.

Together, these findings suggest a hierarchy of disaggregation for the gaming–wellbeing question. Aggregate playtime (the coarsest measure) consistently shows null associations. Genre-level disaggregation (this study) bounds genre heterogeneity below the threshold of practical significance, with individual genre estimates too imprecise to interpret. Within-game playstyle variation shows between-group wellbeing differences at the behavioural level [@hakman2026notallplay]. Session-level mood assessment detects affective uplift at the temporal scale of individual play sessions [@vuorre2024affective]. And causal designs find positive effects [@egami2024causal]. This bears directly on the call to unpack raw playtime into more informative measures [@ballouRegisteredReportEvidence2024]. Genre is the most accessible decomposition available, requiring only a lookup from title to label, and on these data it buys almost no wellbeing signal. The exploratory daily analysis supplies the hierarchy's intermediate step from within the same dataset: temporal proximity alone, without session-level measurement, recovers at most a suggestion of the direction the uplift literature reports. The pattern across the hierarchy is that effects emerge as measurement becomes more proximal to the actual psychological experience of play.

The multi-membership random-effects model represents, to our knowledge, the first application of this model class in media psychology or video game research. Multi-membership models were originally developed for educational data where students attend multiple schools [@fielding2006cross; see @cafri2015introduction for a methodological review]. The core insight, that units can belong to multiple overlapping groups with varying membership weights, maps directly onto the structure of media content with overlapping category labels. The standard multilevel model forces a choice between assignment to a single category and entry as independent fixed effects; the multi-membership approach avoids both compromises, using composition weights for proportional attribution while partial pooling through σ~s~ stabilises sparse-category estimates. Beyond video games, this approach applies to any media effects question where content carries overlapping labels: streaming content with multiple genre tags, news consumption across outlets with overlapping editorial orientations, or social media posts spanning multiple topic categories.

The findings also carry a policy implication. They provide no empirical basis for genre-sensitive gaming policy: genre heterogeneity was bounded below the smallest effect size of interest, and individual genre estimates were too uncertain to support genre-specific regulation. Our ROPE analysis demonstrates the value of equivalence testing for policy-relevant research: rather than claiming absence of evidence, we provide a continuous measure of how much of the posterior is practically negligible [cf. @karhulahti2025claims]. The counterfactual question, "harmful compared to what?" [@magnusson2024harmful], remains unanswered by genre-level analyses, which compare genres to each other but not to the activities gaming displaces.

## Limitations

Several limitations warrant consideration. First, this study is observational and cannot establish causal relationships between gaming and wellbeing. While the within-person design controls for stable individual differences, time-varying confounds (e.g., concurrent life events, seasonal effects) remain possible alternative explanations.

Second, the combination of measurement resolution and effect-size thresholding in the present study creates a high bar for detecting genre-specific effects. The SESOI of ±0.06 SWEMWBS item-mean points per hour/day is deliberately anchored to a minimally important difference (in observed within-person standard-deviation terms it is moderate rather than strict; see Smallest Effect Size of Interest), and the detection problem is compounded by three features of the measurement context: SWEMWBS is a coarse instrument with only four ordinal units on the item-mean scale; gaming is only one of many activities competing for within-person wellbeing variance over a two-week window (sleep, work, social interaction, physical activity, and life events all contribute larger effects than most daily leisure choices); and the biweekly retrospective window (participants are asked to reflect on "the past 2 weeks") aggregates many individual gaming sessions into a single summary judgement and introduces potential recall bias, averaging over acute affective changes that might be detectable at a session-level timescale [@vuorre2024affective]. In combination, any real per-hour effect of genre on wellbeing would have to be large enough to survive aggregation, competition with other life domains, and the coarseness of the scale to clear the practically meaningful threshold. The exploratory daily analysis addresses the first of these features, shortening the window from fourteen days to one, with results consistent with this reading. The remaining features stand: session-level objective telemetry (already available in the Open Play dataset) would place gaming exposure on the same timescale as the wellbeing measurement, and a daily time-use diary would allow gaming effects to be partialled from competing activities rather than attributing all unexplained daily variance to residual noise. We view the present biweekly null as a measurement-resolution finding: at the temporal resolution and instrument sensitivity typical of this literature, gaming genre does not produce detectable wellbeing shifts. The daily extension suggests what finer resolution may recover first: direction, well before practical magnitude.

Third, sample and platform coverage constrain the generalisability of our findings [cf. the constraints-on-generality statement of @simonsConstraintsGeneralityCOG2017]. The pre-registration specified that participants should have at least 75% of their gaming activity on the included platforms; the actual threshold applied during data collection was 50%, which may underrepresent gamers whose activity is concentrated on platforms excluded from our analysis (e.g., PlayStation, mobile-first players). Mobile gaming (iOS, Android) was excluded from the H2 genre analysis because these platforms provide only daily aggregate minutes without game-level metadata; as a result, our genre-level findings speak primarily to console and PC gaming and may not generalise to the substantial proportion of global gaming activity that occurs on mobile devices. Within the included platforms, in-study playtime is itself dominated by Steam (`r round(share_get("Steam"), 1)`% of minutes, versus `r round(share_get("Xbox"), 1)`% Xbox and `r round(share_get("Nintendo"), 1)`% Nintendo), so the genre findings are, in practice, predominantly findings about PC play. The six-wave study window (approximately three months) also captures a limited temporal span; seasonal effects, novelty effects for newly released games, and longer-term habit formation are not addressable with the present data.

Fourth, our full-attribution approach to multi-genre games (deviation from pre-registration; see Appendix B, Deviation D1) assigns each game's full playtime to every one of its IGDB genre labels. While this better reflects the reality that many games genuinely span multiple genres, it also means that games with more genre labels contribute disproportionately to the sum of genre exposures and that each genre coefficient should be interpreted as the association between exposure to games carrying that label rather than the effect of the genre in isolation (see Multi-genre attribution in Measures). The pre-registered primary-genre-only analysis is reported in the supplementary materials and reaches the same conclusions: practical equivalence for both components of H1, and no significant genre differences under the pre-registered joint Wald tests.

Fifth, the exploratory daily analysis carries limits of its own. It is unregistered, and its equivalence benchmark is constructed rather than pre-registered: no anchor-based minimally important difference exists for the daily slider, so the region rests on a distribution-based rule and a proportional comparison to the registered threshold. The outcome is a single, strongly affect-laden item, correlating `r sprintf("%.2f", d_ls_av_r)` with the momentary valence slider across responses (`r sprintf("%.2f", d_ls_av_rw)` within persons), and the diary panel is attrition-shaped, with missingness handled by observed-data likelihood without multiple imputation. Mobile play is unmeasured and dominates disagreement in the self-report positive control, the same-day window closes at the response itself, so evening play is invisible to that day's estimate, and play-so-far and satisfaction-so-far are measured contemporaneously, leaving temporal precedence unestablished within a day. These results are therefore a direction-setting replication at the daily level, not confirmatory equivalence.

## Future Directions

This study is one of the first attempts to examine genre-specific associations between playtime and wellbeing using objective behavioural data at scale. Several directions could strengthen future work. First, the exploratory daily analysis took the first step down the temporal hierarchy; the remaining steps are session-level designs pairing telemetry with momentary assessment, time-use data to partial gaming from competing activities, and a registered daily protocol with imputation for diary attrition. Rare genres remain unresolvable even at the daily level without larger samples. Second, interactions between genres and player characteristics (motivations [@kiralyComprehensiveModelUnderstand2022], personality, social context) may reveal that the experience of play matters for wellbeing beyond what the genre label captures. The H1 random-slope SD places an upper bound on what such moderators can deliver at this timescale: person-specific playtime slopes vary with SD ≈ `r round(sd_slope_mean, 3)`, so moderation studies at the biweekly level should expect to explain subtle rather than dramatic subgroup differences. Third, incorporating additional wellbeing dimensions beyond the SWEMWBS (e.g., affect, sleep quality, social connectedness) could uncover domain-specific associations masked by a global measure.

## Conclusion

Undifferentiated playtime is not meaningfully associated with mental wellbeing, and disaggregating it by genre, even with comprehensive multi-platform telemetry, sharpens the picture without changing its substance. The registered question, whether it is justified to generalise playtime–wellbeing findings across video game genres, thereby receives a direct answer: at this measurement resolution the null generalises, across content categories and, given the bounded person-level slope variation, largely across players as well. Genre labels emerge as a necessary but insufficient step towards the characterisations of play that plausibly do matter: the features games offer, the needs they satisfy or frustrate, the behaviours they elicit, and the momentary experiences they produce. As measurement moves closer to the psychological experience of play, effects emerge; the exploratory daily analysis traces this pattern within the present dataset up to the limit a one-day window can reach. For aggregate playtime, the equivalence tests turn the null into evidence of practical absence. For individual genres they do not, because the intervals remain too wide to separate a small effect from none at all.
