# Appendix A: Genre Mapping {.appendix}

Genre labels from all three platforms resolve to the study taxonomy in two steps: Xbox store labels are first mapped onto IGDB genres (per the pre-registration's Appendix B), and raw IGDB labels (`r n_raw_genre_labels` distinct labels observed in the study metadata) are then collapsed into 14 analysis-level categories. @tbl-genre-mapping presents both steps in one place: each row is an implemented study genre, with the raw IGDB labels it subsumes, the Xbox store labels routed to it, and, where the pre-registered mapping (which would yield `r n_prereg_genres` distinct genres on the observed labels) treated a label differently, the pre-registered assignment. The implemented mapping diverges from the pre-registered one in both directions: it preserves granularity for sub-genres that prior literature treats as distinct (Hack-and-slash/Beat-'em-up, Point-and-click, Visual Novel), collapses more aggressively elsewhere (MOBA into Strategy, Card & Board Game into Puzzle, Pinball and Music into Arcade), and excludes Indie as a non-substantive label (see Appendix B, Deviation D2). Two details sit outside the table: the Xbox label Family + Kids has no IGDB equivalent and is resolved by the title's secondary genre, and IGDB includes no top-level "Action" category, so what is colloquially called "action" is distributed across Shooter, Hack-and-slash, Fighting, and Platform.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-genre-mapping
#| tbl-cap: "Mapping from platform genre labels to the 14 study genres. Xbox store labels map onto IGDB genres, which are then collapsed into the study taxonomy. The final column gives the pre-registered assignment where it differs; blank cells indicate identical treatment."
#| echo: false

genre_map <- tribble(
  ~`Study genre`, ~`IGDB label(s) subsumed`, ~`Xbox store label(s)`, ~`Pre-registered assignment (where different)`,
  "Adventure", "Adventure", "Action + Adventure", "Also subsumes Point-and-click and Visual Novel",
  "Arcade", "Arcade, Pinball, Music", "Classics, Music", "Pinball and Music retained as separate genres",
  "Fighting", "Fighting", "Fighting", "",
  "Hack-and-slash/Beat-'em-up", "Hack and slash/Beat 'em up", "", "Collapsed into Action",
  "Platform", "Platform", "Platformer", "",
  "Point-and-click", "Point-and-click", "", "Collapsed into Adventure",
  "Puzzle", "Puzzle, Quiz/Trivia, Card & Board Game", "Puzzle + Trivia, Card + Board, Casino", "Card & Board Game retained as a separate genre",
  "Racing", "Racing", "Racing + Flying", "",
  "Role-playing (RPG)", "Role-playing (RPG)", "Role Playing", "",
  "Shooter", "Shooter", "Shooter", "",
  "Simulator", "Simulator", "Simulation", "",
  "Sport", "Sport", "Sports", "",
  "Strategy", "Strategy, Turn-based strategy (TBS), Real time strategy (RTS), Tactical, MOBA", "Strategy, Multi-Player Online Battle Arena", "MOBA retained as a separate genre",
  "Visual Novel", "Visual Novel", "", "Collapsed into Adventure",
  "(excluded)", "Indie", "", "Retained as Indie"
)

genre_map |>
  tt(width = 1) |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(j = 1, bold = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(i = nrow(genre_map), j = 1, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.75)
```

# Appendix B: Deviations from Pre-Registration {.appendix}

This appendix documents all known deviations from the Stage 1 pre-registration [@ballou2024psychological] in a single numbered scheme (D1–D9). Every deviation is presented in the structured disclosure format of Willroth and Atherton [-@willroth2024reporting], reporting the type of deviation, the original pre-registered wording, a description of what was done instead, the reason, the timing relative to data access and results, and the potential impact on interpretation. Related decisions are documented together rather than split across entries: prior specification is part of the inference-framework deviation (D4), the H2 model-structure decisions form a single deviation (D5), and the three changes that arose upstream during data collection (outside the authors' control and reported in full by @ballou2025openplay) are consolidated as D9. One unregistered correction, which implements the pre-registered plan more faithfully than the upstream data pipeline did, is documented last in the same format (U1).

| \# | Topic | Type | Timing |
|:----------------|:--------------------|:----------------|:------------------|
| D1 | Genre assignment (full attribution) | Data preparation | After data access, before results known |
| D2 | Genre taxonomy (sub-genre collapsing) | Data preparation | After data access, before results known |
| D3 | Telemetry–survey alignment | Variables | After data access, before results known |
| D4 | Inference framework and priors | Inferential criteria | After data access, before results known |
| D5 | H2 model specifications | Analytic approach | Partly after H2 results known |
| D6 | H1 platform scope | Variables | After data access, before results known |
| D7 | Outcome measure and scoring | Variables | Instrument: during data collection; scoring: after data access |
| D8 | Missing data handling | Analytic approach | Protocol upgraded after complete-case results known |
| D9 | Upstream data-collection changes | Data collection procedures | During data collection, before data access |
| U1 | Xbox genre mapping correction | Data preparation (correction) | After data access, before results known |

## Structured disclosures

### D1: Genre assignment (full attribution)

| Field | Content |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Data preparation |
| **Original wording** | Games are classified by their primary (first) IGDB genre. The pre-registration does not specify how to handle multi-genre games beyond this. |
| **Deviation description** | Each game's full playtime is attributed to every one of its IGDB genre labels (all labels retained; up to `r max_raw_labels` raw labels per game observed in the metadata). A game with 2 hours of play and two genre labels (e.g., Adventure + RPG) contributes 2 hours to each genre. Genre hours therefore represent total exposure to games carrying that label and are not mutually exclusive: summing across genres exceeds total playtime. Total playtime for H1 is computed separately from raw sessions without genre duplication. An earlier draft capped attribution at 3 genres per game; the cap was removed because `r round(pct_games_gt3_labels)`% of games with any genre label carry more than 3 raw IGDB labels and truncation discards classification information. |
| **Reason** | Many games genuinely span multiple genres; restricting to the primary genre discards meaningful classification information and introduces arbitrary dependence on IGDB's label ordering. Full attribution reflects actual exposure to each genre. |
| **Timing** | After data access, before results of the pre-registered approach were known |
| **Reader impact** | Full attribution means genre-level playtime variables cannot be summed to recover total playtime, and each genre coefficient estimates the association with exposure to games carrying that label rather than the effect of the genre in isolation. This is appropriate because a player of an Adventure-RPG is fully exposed to both Adventure and RPG design elements. Total playtime is tracked independently to avoid conflating genre exposure with total gaming time. The pre-registered primary-genre analysis is reported in the supplement. |

### D2: Genre taxonomy (sub-genre collapsing)

| Field | Content |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Data preparation |
| **Original wording** | The pre-registration collapses IGDB sub-genres as follows: Hack and slash/Beat 'em up → Action; Point-and-click and Visual Novel → Adventure; Turn-based strategy, Real-time strategy, and Tactical → Strategy; Quiz/Trivia → Puzzle. |
| **Deviation description** | Hack-and-slash/Beat-'em-up, Point-and-click, and Visual Novel are retained as distinct categories; MOBA is folded into Strategy; Card & Board Game joins Quiz/Trivia under Puzzle; Pinball and Music are folded into Arcade; Indie is excluded as a non-substantive label. The implemented taxonomy comprises 14 analysis-level categories (full mapping in Appendix A of this manuscript). The metadata contain `r n_raw_genre_labels` distinct raw IGDB labels; the pre-registration's body text mentions 19 IGDB genres while its own Appendix A lists all 23, and we report the count as observed in the data. |
| **Reason** | The pre-registered collapsing conflated meaningfully different genres; e.g., Visual Novels and Beat-'em-ups would both disappear into broad categories despite prior literature treating them as psychologically distinct. Retaining them preserves granularity where theory suggests it matters. |
| **Timing** | After data access, before results of the pre-registered approach were known |
| **Reader impact** | Genre-level coefficients refer to different category boundaries than the pre-registration implies, so per-genre estimates are not directly comparable to a hypothetical analysis under the original taxonomy. The retained sub-genres are rarely played, producing wide credible intervals for those categories; the pooled heterogeneity parameters (M2, M3) are designed to remain stable under this sparsity. |

### D3: Telemetry–survey alignment

| Field | Content |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Variables |
| **Original wording** | Not specified; the pre-registration implicitly assumes wave windows counted forward from the baseline day (days 0–83). |
| **Deviation description** | Playtime windows are aligned retrospectively to the survey: each wave's playtime covers the 14 days ending the day before the biweekly survey, so wave 1 covers days −14 to −1 relative to baseline. Pre-baseline telemetry is available for all three platforms because participants linked their accounts at intake. |
| **Reason** | SWEMWBS asks participants to reflect on "the past 2 weeks." The wave 1 survey is completed on the baseline day, so its retrospective window predates the study start; forward-counted windows would misalign every wave's playtime with the period participants were actually reporting on. |
| **Timing** | After data access, before results of the pre-registered approach were known |
| **Reader impact** | Improves measurement validity by matching exposure and outcome windows. Estimates are not directly comparable to an analysis using forward-counted windows, and wave 1 relies on telemetry recorded before the study formally began (over 85% of participants per platform had observable telemetry covering the full wave 1 period). |

### D4: Inference framework and priors (frequentist → Bayesian)

| Field | Content |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Inferential criteria |
| **Original wording** | H1 will be tested via equivalence test with SESOI = ±0.06 SWEMWBS points per 1-hour change in daily playtime, using 90% CIs (TOST procedure). H2 will be tested via a joint Wald test via `car::linearHypothesis()`. The pre-registration specifies no priors (all models frequentist). |
| **Deviation description** | Both H1 and H2 are estimated using Bayesian multilevel models \[`brms`; @burkner2017brms\] rather than frequentist `lmer`. H1 is evaluated via ROPE analysis with bounds identical to the pre-registered SESOI \[−0.06, +0.06\]; if \>95% of the posterior falls within the ROPE, practical equivalence is established [@kruschke2018rejecting]. H2 is evaluated through posterior genre-heterogeneity parameters ($\sigma_s$ in M3, $\tau$ in M2, the SD of coefficients in M1), with magnitude judged against the SESOI. Because the pre-registration specifies no priors, these were chosen as weakly informative on the 1–5 item-mean outcome scale: Student-*t*(3, 0, 0.5) on fixed-effect coefficients, Student-*t*(3, 3, 2) on the intercept, Half-Normal(0, 0.1) on M2's $\tau$ hyperparameters, Half-Normal(0, 0.3) on M3's $\sigma_s$ (looser to accommodate the more challenging multi-membership posterior geometry), and `brms` defaults on remaining variance components. The pre-registered frequentist models (TOST and joint Wald tests) are reported in full in the pre-registered analysis supplement. |
| **Reason** | A Bayesian framework provides richer equivalence testing via ROPE and continuous uncertainty quantification; the priors regularise estimation without strongly constraining the posterior. |
| **Timing** | After data access, before results of the pre-registered approach were known |
| **Reader impact** | The SESOI is unchanged and the ROPE procedure provides a continuous measure of practical equivalence rather than a binary significance decision. Risk of bias is low: the equivalence region is identical and the deviation was decided before results were known. More diffuse priors could permit larger heterogeneity estimates; prior sensitivity could be assessed by varying the prior scales. |

### D5: H2 model specifications

| Field | Content |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Analytic approach |
| **Original wording** | H2 uses genre-specific fixed-effect coefficients with a random intercept and uncorrelated random slopes for all within-person genre predictors (zero-correlation syntax), tested via a joint Wald test. The pre-registration anticipates identifiability issues and specifies dropping random slopes if the model is singular. |
| **Deviation description** | Three related decisions. (a) The pre-registered random slopes (14 genres × 2 dimensions = 28 slope parameters) render the model near-singular; the random-intercept-only contingency was applied, as pre-registered. (b) Two additional specifications were added: M2 replaces the independent priors on genre coefficients with a learned hierarchical prior ($\tau$), and M3 is a multi-membership random-effects model in which genre modulates the total playtime slope via composition weights, adopted as the primary H2 analysis. (c) For M3, each wave's membership weights are that wave's genre shares of total genre-attributed playtime; waves with zero playtime receive uniform weights (1/K), a technical requirement of `brms::mm()`. |
| **Reason** | With 28 independently estimated genre coefficients, the pre-registered specification is overparameterised and rare-genre estimates are dominated by sampling noise. The pooled specifications (M2, M3) separate genuine genre heterogeneity from estimation error and answer H2 through a single interpretable parameter. |
| **Timing** | The random-slope contingency was applied at model fitting. M2 and M3 were added after the fixed-effects (M1) results were known. |
| **Reader impact** | The timing of adding M2 and M3 (after seeing M1 results) increases risk of bias for the choice of primary analysis; readers who prefer the pre-registered specification can rely on the M1 results, reported in full, which lead to the same qualitative conclusion. The M3 specification was validated with a parameter-recovery simulation before being fit to real data. Uniform weights for zero-playtime waves have minimal substantive impact, as those observations contribute little information to genre-specific estimates. |

### D6: H1 platform scope (mobile excluded)

| Field | Content |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Variables |
| **Original wording** | H1 will test the association between total cross-platform playtime and wellbeing, using data from all five platforms (Nintendo, Xbox, Steam, iOS, Android). |
| **Deviation description** | H1 total playtime is computed from Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam only, excluding iOS and Android. Mobile platforms provide only daily aggregate minutes without game-level data (D9). Including mobile for H1 but not H2 would mean "total playtime" refers to different quantities across hypotheses. |
| **Reason** | Internal consistency between H1 and H2. |
| **Timing** | After data access, before results of the pre-registered approach were known |
| **Reader impact** | This reduces the total playtime measure by excluding mobile gaming. However, mobile contributed a small minority of total playtime for most participants. The pre-registered analysis supplement retains the all-platform total, allowing a direct comparison of console/PC-only versus all-platform H1 estimates. Risk of bias is low: the deviation was motivated by internal consistency, not by the data or results. |

### D7: Outcome measure and scoring

| Field | Content |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Variables |
| **Original wording** | General mental wellbeing will be measured with the WEMWBS (Tennant et al., 2007). |
| **Deviation description** | The instrument administered in the Open Play study is the short-form SWEMWBS (7 items, each scored 1–5), an upstream design decision documented by @ballou2025openplay. The score is computed as the **item mean** (`rowMeans` of the 7 items, range 1–5), not the summed score (range 7–35). The pre-registered SESOI of 0.06 per hour/day was derived by Ballou, Sewall, et al. (2024) on the 1–5 item-mean scale (0.3 minimally important difference ÷ 5 hours of realistic daily leisure), and the pre-registration's own precision analysis assumes a within-person SD of 0.7, which is only coherent on the 1–5 scale. An earlier version of this analysis used `rowSums`, which inflated coefficients by a factor of 7 relative to the scale the SESOI was defined on. |
| **Reason** | Item-mean scoring places the coefficients, priors, and SESOI on a single consistent scale. |
| **Timing** | Instrument: during data collection, before data access (upstream). Scoring: after data access, before results were known. |
| **Reader impact** | No change to the underlying data or model specification; only the summary score computation differs from a summed-score reading of the pre-registration. All downstream numbers (coefficients, equivalence tests, ROPE bounds) are on the scale the SESOI was designed for. |

### D8: Missing data handling

| Field | Content |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Analytic approach |
| **Original wording** | Missing data: multiple imputation via `mice` package (predictive mean matching, wide format). Report both complete-case and imputed results. |
| **Deviation description** | Outcome missingness has two components. Among submitted surveys, `r n_md_item_miss` responses (`r round(100 * n_md_item_miss / n_md_submitted, 1)`% of `r formatC(n_md_submitted, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` in the analytic sample) are missing SWEMWBS, all with every item missing. The larger component is wave nonresponse: `r formatC(n_md_wave_miss, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` of `r formatC(n_md_grid, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` person-waves (`r pct_md_wave_miss`%) in the analytic sample were never submitted (response declined from `r wave_response$pct[1]`% at wave 1 to `r wave_response$pct[6]`% at wave 6). Instead of the pre-registered single-level wide-format PMM, we imputed on the complete participant × wave grid with hierarchical two-level MICE (`2l.pmm`, participants as clusters, ±1-wave lag/lead terms, fully observed exposures with explicit person means, intake auxiliaries), the protocol shared with the programmatic RR's other Stage 2 outputs; the number of imputations follows von Hippel's (2020) rule from the pilot fraction of missing information. The primary Bayesian models remain fit to observed outcomes (valid under MAR given the modelled covariates and random effects); pooled frequentist counterparts on the imputed data are reported in Appendix D. The imputation grid covers the analytic sample; `r n_distinct(biw_md6$pid) - n_md_pids` surveyed participants with no valid SWEMWBS in any wave provide no outcome information to anchor imputation and are outside both the analytic sample and the grid. |
| **Reason** | The pre-registered wide-format single-level PMM understates the hierarchical structure, and an initial implementation of it could only address item-level missingness among submitted surveys. The grid protocol addresses the dominant wave-nonresponse component and is consistent with the sibling Stage 2 studies. |
| **Timing** | Complete-case-first decision: after data access, before results known. Grid-imputation protocol: adopted after complete-case results were known, by mirroring the sibling studies' protocol rather than tailoring choices to results. |
| **Reader impact** | The imputation model conditions on all analysis-model exposures, so it is congenial with (indeed richer than) the analysis models. Equivalence and joint-test conclusions are unchanged under imputation (see Sensitivity Analyses); the pooled between-person interval widens because person means are genuinely uncertain for participants with few observed waves (high fraction of missing information), which Rubin's rules propagate. If nonresponse depends on unobserved wellbeing beyond the modelled covariates (MNAR), both complete-case and imputed estimates could be biased in the same direction; the agreement between them rules out bias from the modelled missingness mechanism, not MNAR. |

### D9: Upstream data-collection changes

| Field | Content |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Data collection procedures |
| **Original wording** | Age range 18–75 (UK) and 18–30 (US); ≥75% of gaming time on included platforms; Android telemetry collected as session-level exports via ActivityWatch. |
| **Deviation description** | Three changes made by the Open Play team during data collection, before this study's data access: (a) screening admitted ages 18–40 in both regions; (b) the platform coverage threshold was lowered to ≥50%; (c) Android data were collected as daily aggregate minutes via Digital Wellbeing screenshots rather than session-level exports. All three are reported in full by @ballou2025openplay. |
| **Reason** | Recruitment and data-collection constraints in the upstream Open Play study; outside the authors' control. |
| **Timing** | During data collection, before data access |
| **Reader impact** | The narrower age range limits generalisability to older adults. The lower coverage threshold admits participants with a larger share of unobserved play, adding measurement error to total playtime. The Android granularity change restricts Android to daily totals, contributing to the pre-registered all-platform sensitivity analysis only and excluding it from H2 (see D6). |

## Unregistered correction

### U1: Xbox genre mapping correction

| Field | Content |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| **Type** | Data preparation (correction, consistent with the pre-registration) |
| **Original wording** | Xbox genres are mapped onto the IGDB taxonomy via the mapping table in the pre-registration's Appendix B. |
| **Deviation description** | The upstream Open Play preprocessing pipeline (`label_genres.R`) failed to map approximately `r round(100 - xbox_pct_before)`% of Xbox playtime to IGDB genres due to a string-formatting bug (exact-match against multi-value and inconsistently-formatted genre strings). We applied a corrected mapping in our preprocessing using the `xbox_primary_genre` and `xbox_subgenre` metadata fields, recovering genre information for an additional `r round(xbox_min_rescued / 1e6, 1)` million minutes of Xbox playtime. This is a fix, not a deviation: the pre-registration explicitly specified the Xbox-to-IGDB mapping, and the correction implements it as intended. |
| **Reason** | Implementing the pre-registered mapping faithfully; the upstream bug would otherwise cause systematic genre-data missingness for the largest platform by volume. |
| **Timing** | After data access, before results were known |
| **Reader impact** | Xbox genre coverage increased from `r round(xbox_pct_before)`% to `r round(xbox_pct_after)`% of playtime, substantially reducing systematic missingness in the genre-level analyses. |

# Appendix D: Sensitivity and Supplementary Analyses {.appendix}

This appendix reports the three sensitivity analyses summarised under Robustness in the main text: demographic covariate adjustment, hyperprior-scale sensitivity for the genre heterogeneity parameters, and multiple imputation of wave nonresponse (with distributional diagnostics). It then reports the predictive model comparison (whether genre terms improve out-of-sample prediction), followed by a description of the pre-registered frequentist analysis supplement.

## Demographic Covariates

The pre-registration specified a sensitivity analysis adjusting the primary models for demographic covariates. We refit M0 (total playtime) and M1 (genre fixed effects) with age, gender, and ethnicity added as population-level predictors, using the subset of participants with complete demographic data.

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity-demographics-bayes
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| include: false

demo_data <- analysis_data |>
  left_join(analytic_sample |> select(pid, age, gender, ethnicity), by = "pid") |>
  filter(!is.na(age), !is.na(gender), !is.na(ethnicity), !is.na(wemwbs)) |>
  mutate(
    gender    = factor(gender, levels = c("Man", "Woman", "Non-binary/Other")),
    ethnicity = factor(ethnicity, levels = c("White", "Asian", "Black",
                                              "Mixed/Multiple", "Other"))
  )

n_sens_pids <- n_distinct(demo_data$pid)
n_sens_obs  <- nrow(demo_data)

# H1 with demographics (fit cached; see R/fit_sensitivity_models.R)
h1_demo <- brm(
  bf(wemwbs ~ total_within + total_between + age + gender + ethnicity +
       (1 + total_within | pid)),
  data    = demo_data,
  prior   = prior(student_t(3, 0, 0.5), class = "b") +
            prior(student_t(3, 3, 2),   class = "Intercept"),
  family  = gaussian(),
  chains  = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 8675309,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file    = here("models/h1_demographics")
)

# H2 with demographics
h2_demo_formula <- bf(paste(
  "wemwbs ~ age + gender + ethnicity +",
  paste(c(gh_within, gh_between), collapse = " + "),
  "+ (1 | pid)"
))

h2_demo <- brm(
  formula = h2_demo_formula,
  data    = demo_data,
  prior   = prior(student_t(3, 0, 0.5), class = "b") +
            prior(student_t(3, 3, 2),   class = "Intercept"),
  family  = gaussian(),
  chains  = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 8675309,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file    = here("models/h2_demographics")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity-extract
#| include: false
#| eval: true

# H1 coefficients from the adjusted model
h1_demo_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(h1_demo)
sens_b1_draws   <- h1_demo_draws$b_total_within
sens_b1_mean    <- mean(sens_b1_draws)
sens_b1_ci      <- quantile(sens_b1_draws, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
sens_b1_in_rope <- mean(sens_b1_draws > -0.06 & sens_b1_draws < 0.06)

sens_b2_draws   <- h1_demo_draws$b_total_between
sens_b2_mean    <- mean(sens_b2_draws)
sens_b2_ci      <- quantile(sens_b2_draws, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
sens_b2_in_rope <- mean(sens_b2_draws > -0.06 & sens_b2_draws < 0.06)

# Genre heterogeneity (SD of coefficients per draw) from the adjusted model
h2_demo_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(h2_demo)
sens_within_cols  <- grep("^b_gh_.*_within$",  names(h2_demo_draws), value = TRUE)
sens_between_cols <- grep("^b_gh_.*_between$", names(h2_demo_draws), value = TRUE)
sens_sd_within  <- apply(as.matrix(h2_demo_draws[, sens_within_cols]),  1, sd)
sens_sd_between <- apply(as.matrix(h2_demo_draws[, sens_between_cols]), 1, sd)

sens_diag_rhat <- max(
  max(brms::rhat(h1_demo), na.rm = TRUE),
  max(brms::rhat(h2_demo), na.rm = TRUE)
)
sens_diag_divs <- sum(subset(brms::nuts_params(h1_demo), Parameter == "divergent__")$Value) +
  sum(subset(brms::nuts_params(h2_demo), Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)

sens_h1_max_diff <- max(abs(c(sens_b1_mean - beta1_mean, sens_b2_mean - beta2_mean)))
# Guard for the main-text Robustness claim ("less than 0.01 points").
stopifnot(sens_h1_max_diff < 0.01)
```

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity-demo
#| tbl-cap: "Primary versus demographic-adjusted estimates. H1 rows compare M0's total-playtime coefficients with the same coefficients after adding age, gender, and ethnicity. H2 rows compare M1's genre heterogeneity statistic (SD of the 14 genre coefficients per draw) with its adjusted counterpart. Estimates in SWEMWBS item-mean points per hour/day."
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

tibble(
  Quantity = c(
    "H1a: Within-person total playtime",
    "H1b: Between-person total playtime",
    "H2a: Genre SD (within)",
    "H2b: Genre SD (between)"
  ),
  `Primary` = c(
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", beta1_mean, beta1_ci[1], beta1_ci[2]),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", beta2_mean, beta2_ci[1], beta2_ci[2]),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", genre_sd_mean, genre_sd_ci[1], genre_sd_ci[2]),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", genre_bsd_mean, genre_bsd_ci[1], genre_bsd_ci[2])
  ),
  `Adjusted` = c(
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", sens_b1_mean, sens_b1_ci[1], sens_b1_ci[2]),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", sens_b2_mean, sens_b2_ci[1], sens_b2_ci[2]),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", mean(sens_sd_within),
            quantile(sens_sd_within, 0.025), quantile(sens_sd_within, 0.975)),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", mean(sens_sd_between),
            quantile(sens_sd_between, 0.025), quantile(sens_sd_between, 0.975))
  )
) |> tt()
```
:::

The adjusted models use `r formatC(n_sens_obs, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` observations from `r formatC(n_sens_pids, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` participants with complete demographic data. @tbl-sensitivity-demo compares the primary and covariate-adjusted estimates. The H1 coefficients shift by at most `r round(sens_h1_max_diff, 3)` points after adjustment, and the ROPE conclusions are unchanged: `r round(sens_b1_in_rope * 100, 1)`% of the adjusted within-person posterior falls inside the ROPE (primary: `r round(beta1_in_rope * 100, 1)`%), and `r round(sens_b2_in_rope * 100, 1)`% of the adjusted between-person posterior (primary: `r round(beta2_in_rope * 100, 1)`%). One qualification: the adjusted between-person credible interval (\[`r round(sens_b2_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(sens_b2_ci[2], 3)`\]) excludes zero, unlike the unadjusted interval; this small negative association remains far inside the ROPE and is consistent with the selection account discussed under H1. The genre heterogeneity estimates are likewise essentially unaffected. Both adjusted models converged cleanly (max R-hat = `r round(sens_diag_rhat, 3)`, `r sens_diag_divs` divergent transitions). Demographic composition therefore does not account for the observed associations.

## Prior Sensitivity

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity-priors
#| include: false

ps_path <- here("data/processed/prior_sensitivity_summary.rds")
if (!file.exists(ps_path)) {
  stop(
    "Prior-sensitivity summary not found. Run `Rscript R/03_prior_sensitivity.R` ",
    "before rendering."
  )
}
ps <- readRDS(ps_path)

# Base-fit rows from the draws already extracted in this document
# (h2-hier-tau and h2-mm-sigma chunks), on the same summary scale.
ps_base <- tibble(
  model = c("M2", "M2", "M3", "M3"),
  parameter = c("tau_within", "tau_between", "sigma_s_within", "sigma_s_between"),
  scale = c(0.1, 0.1, 0.3, 0.3),
  mean = c(mean(tau_draws), mean(tau_between_draws),
           mean(sigma_sw_draws), mean(sigma_sb_draws)),
  median = c(median(tau_draws), median(tau_between_draws),
             median(sigma_sw_draws), median(sigma_sb_draws)),
  q2.5 = c(quantile(tau_draws, .025), quantile(tau_between_draws, .025),
           quantile(sigma_sw_draws, .025), quantile(sigma_sb_draws, .025)),
  q97.5 = c(quantile(tau_draws, .975), quantile(tau_between_draws, .975),
            quantile(sigma_sw_draws, .975), quantile(sigma_sb_draws, .975)),
  p_below_sesoi = c(mean(tau_draws < 0.06), mean(tau_between_draws < 0.06),
                    mean(sigma_sw_draws < 0.06), mean(sigma_sb_draws < 0.06))
)

ps_all <- bind_rows(ps_base, ps |> select(all_of(names(ps_base)))) |>
  arrange(model, parameter, scale) |>
  mutate(base = scale %in% c(0.1, 0.3))

# Guards for the fixed prose: across all hyperprior scales, the within-person
# heterogeneity posteriors keep their medians below the SESOI and the M2
# estimates remain essentially unchanged.
ps_w <- ps_all |> filter(parameter %in% c("tau_within", "sigma_s_within"))
stopifnot(all(ps_w$median < 0.06))
stopifnot(all(abs(ps_all$median[ps_all$parameter == "tau_within"] -
                    median(tau_draws)) < 0.01))
```

The heterogeneity hyperpriors are the component of the specification where prior choice could most plausibly shape the H2 conclusion, since the Half-Normal(0, 0.1) prior on M2's τ places its own median near the SESOI. As committed to in Deviation D4, we therefore refit M2 with the hyperprior scale halved and doubled (0.05, 0.20) and M3 with its σ~s~ scale halved and doubled (0.15, 0.60), using otherwise identical specifications (`R/03_prior_sensitivity.R`).

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-prior-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Prior sensitivity for the genre heterogeneity parameters. Each row is a full refit at the hyperprior scale shown; bolded scales are those reported in the main results. P(< SESOI) is the posterior probability that the parameter is below 0.06."
#| echo: false

ps_disp <- ps_all |>
  mutate(
    Model = model,
    Parameter = dplyr::recode(parameter,
      tau_within = "τ (within)", tau_between = "τ (between)",
      sigma_s_within = "σ_s (within)", sigma_s_between = "σ_s (between)"),
    `Hyperprior scale` = sprintf("%.2f", scale),
    `Posterior median [95% CrI]` = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", median, q2.5, q97.5),
    `P(< SESOI)` = sprintf("%.2f", p_below_sesoi)
  ) |>
  select(Model, Parameter, `Hyperprior scale`,
         `Posterior median [95% CrI]`, `P(< SESOI)`, base)

# style_tt(bold=) renders in both HTML and typst; markdown "**" does not
# survive the typst route.
tt(ps_disp |> select(-base)) |>
  style_tt(i = which(ps_disp$base), j = "Hyperprior scale", bold = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.85)
```
:::

@tbl-prior-sensitivity shows that the heterogeneity conclusions are not an artefact of the hyperprior scales. Both parameters are essentially unchanged when their hyperprior scales are halved or doubled: M2's τ estimates agree to the third decimal across the fourfold range of scales, and M3's σ~s~ posterior median and its posterior mass below the SESOI shift only trivially. This is consistent with both posteriors being strongly data-dominated (the posterior SDs are roughly a tenth of the corresponding prior SDs). Across all specifications and scales, the qualitative conclusion is the same as in the main analysis: genre heterogeneity at or below the smallest effect size of interest.

## Multiple Imputation

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity-imputation-load
#| include: false

source(here("R/02_impute_wemwbs.R"))

if (!file.exists(IMP_META_PATH) || !file.exists(IMP_LONG_PATH)) {
  # First render on a fresh clone: produces the cached imputation (~20 min)
  impute_wemwbs()
}

imp_meta     <- readRDS(IMP_META_PATH)
imputed_long <- readRDS(IMP_LONG_PATH)
m_imp        <- length(imputed_long)

miss_wave        <- imp_meta$missingness_by_wave
n_grid_cells     <- imp_meta$n_cells
n_grid_missing   <- imp_meta$n_missing
pct_grid_missing <- round(100 * n_grid_missing / n_grid_cells, 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity-imputation-models
#| include: false
#| cache: true

# --- H1 (console/PC total, same specification as M0) ------------------------
# Complete-case comparator: identical lmer on the observed rows only.
h1_imp_fits <- lapply(imputed_long, function(d) {
  suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
    lmer(wemwbs ~ total_within + total_between + (1 + total_within | pid),
         data = d,
         control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", calc.derivs = FALSE))
  ))
})

h1_cc_data <- imputed_long[[1]] |>
  semi_join(
    analysis_data |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs)) |> select(pid, wave),
    by = c("pid", "wave")
  ) |>
  select(pid, wave, total_hours_per_day) |>
  inner_join(
    analysis_data |> select(pid, wave, wemwbs),
    by = c("pid", "wave")
  ) |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  mutate(
    total_within  = total_hours_per_day - mean(total_hours_per_day),
    total_between = mean(total_hours_per_day)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

h1_cc_fit <- lmer(
  wemwbs ~ total_within + total_between + (1 + total_within | pid),
  data = h1_cc_data, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

h1_imp_pool    <- pool(as.mira(h1_imp_fits))
h1_imp_pool_95 <- summary(h1_imp_pool, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)
h1_imp_pool_90 <- summary(h1_imp_pool, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.90)

eq_verdict <- function(lb, ub, sesoi = 0.06) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    lb > -sesoi & ub <  sesoi ~ "Practically equivalent",
    lb >  sesoi               ~ "Practically positive",
    ub < -sesoi               ~ "Practically negative",
    TRUE                      ~ "Inconclusive"
  )
}

h1_imp_eq <- h1_imp_pool_90 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(term %in% c("total_within", "total_between")) |>
  mutate(verdict = eq_verdict(`5 %`, `95 %`))

h1_cc_ci90 <- confint(h1_cc_fit, parm = c("total_within", "total_between"),
                      level = 0.90, method = "Wald")

# --- H2 (14 genre exposures, same structure as M1; ML for pooled tests) -----
gh_within_f  <- paste(gh_within,  collapse = " + ")
gh_between_f <- paste(gh_between, collapse = " + ")
h2_full_f    <- paste("wemwbs ~", gh_within_f, "+", gh_between_f, "+ (1 | pid)")

fit_h2 <- function(d, f) {
  suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
    lmer(f, data = d, REML = FALSE,
         control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", calc.derivs = FALSE))
  ))
}

h2_imp_fits <- lapply(imputed_long, fit_h2, f = h2_full_f)

# Pooled joint tests of coefficient equality: 13 explicit difference
# constraints per dimension, combined across imputations with the D1
# multivariate Wald statistic (mitml::testConstraints).
d1_h2a <- mitml::testConstraints(
  h2_imp_fits, constraints = paste0(gh_within[-1], " - ", gh_within[1]),
  method = "D1")
d1_h2b <- mitml::testConstraints(
  h2_imp_fits, constraints = paste0(gh_between[-1], " - ", gh_between[1]),
  method = "D1")

d1_row <- function(tm) {
  tt <- as.data.frame(tm$test)
  tibble(F = tt[1, 1], df1 = tt[1, 2], df2 = tt[1, 3], p = tt[1, 4],
         riv = tt[1, 5])
}
d1_h2a_row <- d1_row(d1_h2a)
d1_h2b_row <- d1_row(d1_h2b)

# Complete-case H2 (observed rows; ML) with the classic joint Wald tests
h2_cc_data <- imputed_long[[1]] |>
  select(pid, wave, all_of(gh_vars)) |>
  inner_join(analysis_data |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs)) |> select(pid, wave, wemwbs),
             by = c("pid", "wave")) |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(gh_vars),
                list(within = ~ .x - mean(.x), between = ~ mean(.x)),
                .names = "{.col}_{.fn}")) |>
  ungroup()

h2_cc_fit <- fit_h2(h2_cc_data, h2_full_f)
h2_cc_wald_a <- car::linearHypothesis(
  h2_cc_fit, paste0(gh_within[1], " = ", gh_within[-1]))
h2_cc_wald_b <- car::linearHypothesis(
  h2_cc_fit, paste0(gh_between[1], " = ", gh_between[-1]))

# Genre heterogeneity (SD of the 14 within/between coefficient estimates),
# descriptive analogue of M1's posterior heterogeneity statistic
sd_within_imp <- mean(vapply(h2_imp_fits, function(m)
  sd(lme4::fixef(m)[gh_within]), numeric(1)))
sd_between_imp <- mean(vapply(h2_imp_fits, function(m)
  sd(lme4::fixef(m)[gh_between]), numeric(1)))
sd_within_cc  <- sd(lme4::fixef(h2_cc_fit)[gh_within])
sd_between_cc <- sd(lme4::fixef(h2_cc_fit)[gh_between])

# --- Guards for the fixed prose below (fail the render if violated) ---------
stopifnot(all(h1_imp_eq$verdict == "Practically equivalent"))
stopifnot(d1_h2a_row$p > 0.05, d1_h2b_row$p > 0.05)
# The complete-case joint test on the full-attribution exposures DOES reject
# exact equality for the within-person dimension; the prose reports this.
stopifnot(h2_cc_wald_a$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2] < 0.05, h2_cc_wald_b$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2] > 0.05)
# ...while the heterogeneity magnitude stays below the SESOI in every frame.
stopifnot(sd_within_cc < 0.06, sd_within_imp < 0.06)
```

The pre-registration specified multiple imputation by chained equations with predictive mean matching. We implemented the two-level grid protocol described in Methods (Missing Data): across the `r formatC(n_grid_cells, format = "d", big.mark = ",")`-cell participant × wave grid, `r formatC(n_grid_missing, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` cells (`r pct_grid_missing`%) had no observed SWEMWBS (@tbl-missingness-wave), and m = `r m_imp` imputed datasets were generated. The pilot fractions of missing information for the H1 coefficients were `r round(imp_meta$fmi_pilot$fmi[imp_meta$fmi_pilot$term == "tt_within"], 2)` (within-person) and `r round(imp_meta$fmi_pilot$fmi[imp_meta$fmi_pilot$term == "tt_between"], 2)` (between-person): the between-person coefficient depends on person means that are genuinely uncertain for participants with few observed waves, and Rubin's rules propagate that uncertainty into the pooled intervals. `r if (imp_meta$m_needed > m_imp) sprintf("Von Hippel's rule would require %d imputations for a %.0f%%-stable standard error; with m = %d the achieved coefficient of variation of the pooled standard errors is approximately %.2f, which widens the pooled intervals slightly but does not affect the equivalence verdicts.", imp_meta$m_needed, 100 * 0.05, m_imp, imp_meta$se_cv_achieved) else sprintf("This satisfies von Hippel's requirement of %d imputations.", imp_meta$m_needed)`

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-missingness-wave
#| tbl-cap: "SWEMWBS missingness by wave on the full participant × wave grid (analytic sample). Wave 1 was completed on the baseline day; later waves show progressive nonresponse."
#| echo: false

miss_wave |>
  transmute(
    Wave = wave,
    Possible = n_possible,
    Observed = n_observed,
    Missing = n_missing,
    `% missing` = pct_missing
  ) |>
  tt() |>
  format_tt(digits = 1) |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.85)
```
:::

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity-imputation
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'sprintf("Complete-case versus multiply imputed estimates (m = %d; Rubin-pooled with Barnard-Rubin degrees of freedom). H1 rows: total-playtime coefficients from identical frequentist REWB models, with equivalence verdicts applying the pre-registered rule (90%% CI within a SESOI of 0.06). H2 rows: joint tests of genre-coefficient equality (complete-case Wald chi-square; imputed pooled D1 F-test) and the SD of the 14 genre coefficients.", m_imp)'
#| echo: false

h1_rows <- tibble(
  Quantity = c("H1a: Within-person total playtime", "H1b: Between-person total playtime"),
  `Complete-case` = c(
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", fixef(h1_cc_fit)["total_within"],
            h1_cc_ci90["total_within", 1], h1_cc_ci90["total_within", 2]),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", fixef(h1_cc_fit)["total_between"],
            h1_cc_ci90["total_between", 1], h1_cc_ci90["total_between", 2])
  ),
  `Imputed (pooled)` = c(
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]",
            h1_imp_eq$estimate[h1_imp_eq$term == "total_within"],
            h1_imp_eq$`5 %`[h1_imp_eq$term == "total_within"],
            h1_imp_eq$`95 %`[h1_imp_eq$term == "total_within"]),
    sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]",
            h1_imp_eq$estimate[h1_imp_eq$term == "total_between"],
            h1_imp_eq$`5 %`[h1_imp_eq$term == "total_between"],
            h1_imp_eq$`95 %`[h1_imp_eq$term == "total_between"])
  ),
  Verdict = h1_imp_eq$verdict[match(c("total_within", "total_between"), h1_imp_eq$term)]
)

h2_rows <- tibble(
  Quantity = c("H2a: Joint test, within-person genre coefficients equal",
               "H2b: Joint test, between-person genre coefficients equal",
               "Genre SD (within)", "Genre SD (between)"),
  `Complete-case` = c(
    sprintf("chi2(%d) = %.1f, p = %.3f", h2_cc_wald_a$Df[2],
            h2_cc_wald_a$Chisq[2], h2_cc_wald_a$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]),
    sprintf("chi2(%d) = %.1f, p = %.3f", h2_cc_wald_b$Df[2],
            h2_cc_wald_b$Chisq[2], h2_cc_wald_b$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]),
    sprintf("%.3f", sd_within_cc),
    sprintf("%.3f", sd_between_cc)
  ),
  `Imputed (pooled)` = c(
    sprintf("F(%d, %.0f) = %.2f, p = %.3f", d1_h2a_row$df1, d1_h2a_row$df2,
            d1_h2a_row$F, d1_h2a_row$p),
    sprintf("F(%d, %.0f) = %.2f, p = %.3f", d1_h2b_row$df1, d1_h2b_row$df2,
            d1_h2b_row$F, d1_h2b_row$p),
    sprintf("%.3f", sd_within_imp),
    sprintf("%.3f", sd_between_imp)
  ),
  Verdict = c("See text", "Not rejected (either)",
              "Below SESOI (both)", "Below SESOI (both)")
)

bind_rows(h1_rows, h2_rows) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```
:::

@tbl-sensitivity-imputation compares complete-case and pooled imputed results. The H1 conclusions are unchanged: both pooled 90% confidence intervals fall entirely within the pre-registered equivalence bounds of ±0.06, so practical equivalence holds on the imputed data. The between-person interval widens under imputation, reflecting that person-mean wellbeing is uncertain for participants with few observed waves.

For H2, the comparison surfaces the distinction between statistical and practical significance that motivates the SESOI. On the complete cases, the joint Wald test rejects *exact* equality of the 14 within-person genre coefficients (χ²(`r h2_cc_wald_a$Df[2]`) = `r sprintf("%.1f", h2_cc_wald_a$Chisq[2])`, *p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", h2_cc_wald_a$"Pr(>Chisq)"[2])`); under the pre-registered decision rule this reading is limited to "at least one pair of genres differs", with no pairwise interpretation absent formal post-hoc tests. The magnitude of that departure is the quantity the SESOI governs, and it is small: the SD of the 14 coefficient estimates is `r round(sd_within_cc, 3)` (complete-case) and `r round(sd_within_imp, 3)` (imputed), both well below 0.06 and consistent with M1's posterior heterogeneity estimate. On the imputed data the pooled $D_1$ tests reject neither dimension (within: *p* = `r round(d1_h2a_row$p, 3)`; between: *p* = `r round(d1_h2b_row$p, 3)`), though these tests carry reduced power at this level of missing information (relative increase in variance `r round(d1_h2a_row$riv, 2)` for the within-person constraints). The between-person joint test rejects in neither frame. Distributional diagnostics for the imputation are reported in Appendix D (@fig-imp-density). In sum, accounting for wave nonresponse leaves every conclusion intact: total playtime is practically equivalent to zero, and genre heterogeneity, statistically detectable or not depending on the frame, remains below the smallest effect size of interest.

### Distributional Diagnostics

The central plausibility check for the imputation model is distributional: imputed wellbeing values should occupy the same range as the observed data and differ from it only in ways explicable by which participants are missing, not by model artefacts.

```{r}
#| label: fig-imp-density
#| fig-cap: "*Multiple-Imputation Distributional Diagnostic.* Observed grand-mean-centred SWEMWBS values (black) against imputed values in 20 of the 100 imputed datasets (thin orange); a subset is shown so the observed curve stays visible, and all 100 behave alike."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| echo: false

imp_vals_df <- imp_meta$imp$imp$wemwbs_c
n_imp_show  <- 20
stopifnot(ncol(imp_vals_df) >= n_imp_show, nrow(imp_vals_df) > 0)

obs_dens_df <- tibble(wemwbs_c = na.omit(imp_meta$imp$data$wemwbs_c))
imp_dens_df <- imp_vals_df[, seq_len(n_imp_show)] |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "imputation", values_to = "wemwbs_c")

imp_mean_all <- mean(as.matrix(imp_vals_df))
imp_sd_all   <- sd(as.matrix(imp_vals_df))
obs_sd       <- sd(obs_dens_df$wemwbs_c)

# Guards for the fixed prose: imputed values are distributionally close to
# the observed data (centred scale).
stopifnot(abs(imp_mean_all) < 0.1, abs(imp_sd_all - obs_sd) < 0.1)

ggplot() +
  geom_density(
    data = imp_dens_df,
    aes(x = wemwbs_c, group = imputation, colour = "Imputed"),
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_density(
    data = obs_dens_df,
    aes(x = wemwbs_c, colour = "Observed"),
    linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(NULL, values = c(
    Observed = "black",
    Imputed  = scales::alpha("#D55E00", 0.4)
  )) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(x = "Grand-mean-centred SWEMWBS", y = "Density") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

@fig-imp-density shows the imputed values to be distributionally almost indistinguishable from the observed data: pooled across all `r ncol(imp_vals_df)` imputations, the imputed values have mean `r sprintf("%.3f", imp_mean_all)` and SD `r round(imp_sd_all, 2)` on the centred scale, against an observed mean of 0 (by construction) and SD of `r round(obs_sd, 2)`. The imputation model neither compresses the outcome's variance nor shifts nonresponders' imputed wellbeing to implausible regions of the scale. Convergence traces and strip plots are produced alongside the cached imputation (`output/qc_imputation/`).

## Predictive Model Comparison

A complementary way to ask whether genre matters is through predictive performance: does adding genre-specific terms to the total-playtime-only M0 baseline improve out-of-sample prediction? We assess this using approximate leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) via Pareto-smoothed importance sampling [@vehtari2017practical]. A positive difference in expected log predictive density (ELPD) relative to M0 indicates that genre terms help.

```{r}
#| label: loo-comparison
#| cache: true
#| eval: true
#| include: false

# Compute LOO-IC for each model
# Note: moment_match = TRUE requires a valid compiled Stan object, which
# may not survive caching across sessions. Using standard LOO instead.
# If Pareto-k warnings appear, consider reloo = TRUE as a fallback.
loo_h1     <- loo(h1_model)
loo_h2_fe  <- loo(h2_model)
loo_h2_mm  <- loo(h2_mm_model)
loo_h2_hier <- loo(h2_hier_model)

loo_comp <- loo_compare(loo_h1, loo_h2_fe, loo_h2_mm, loo_h2_hier)

# Pareto-k diagnostics across the four models (reported in the text)
pareto_k_all <- lapply(list(loo_h1, loo_h2_fe, loo_h2_mm, loo_h2_hier),
                       function(l) l$diagnostics$pareto_k)
pareto_pct_bad <- 100 * vapply(pareto_k_all, function(k) mean(k > 0.7), numeric(1))
pareto_n_bad   <- vapply(pareto_k_all, function(k) sum(k > 0.7), numeric(1))

loo_tbl <- as.data.frame(loo_comp) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("model_label") |>
  mutate(
    model = case_when(
      grepl("h1_model", model_label)      ~ "M0: Total playtime only",
      grepl("h2_model$", model_label)      ~ "M1: Fixed effects",
      grepl("h2_hier_model", model_label) ~ "M2: Hierarchical prior",
      grepl("h2_mm_model", model_label)   ~ "M3: Multi-membership",
      TRUE ~ model_label
    )
  ) |>
  select(model, elpd_diff, se_diff, elpd_loo, se_elpd_loo, p_loo, looic) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 1))) |>
  rename(
    Model = model, `dELPD` = elpd_diff, `SE(d)` = se_diff,
    ELPD = elpd_loo, SE = se_elpd_loo, `p_loo` = p_loo, LOOIC = looic
  )
```

::: {.place arguments="auto, scope: \"parent\", float: true"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-loo-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Leave-one-out cross-validation. Models ordered by expected log predictive density (ELPD); negative dELPD indicates worse out-of-sample prediction than the best-fitting model. SE(d) = standard error of the difference."
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

loo_tbl |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```
:::

M0, the model with total playtime only, showed the highest expected log predictive density, and all three genre specifications predicted slightly worse out-of-sample (@tbl-loo-comparison), with ELPD deficits between one and roughly two standard errors of the difference. Adding genre information, in any of the three specifications, therefore does not improve the prediction of wellbeing over total playtime alone. Pareto-$k$ diagnostics flagged `r round(min(pareto_pct_bad), 1)`–`r round(max(pareto_pct_bad), 1)`% of observations per model ($k$ \> 0.7; `r round(min(pareto_n_bad))`–`r round(max(pareto_n_bad))` observations), so the ELPD values are approximate; this affects the precision of the differences, not the ordering. The inferential reach of this comparison is considered in the Discussion.

## Pre-Registered Frequentist Analysis

The full pre-registered analysis (primary-genre attribution, frequentist within-between models fit with `lmer`, TOST equivalence tests for H1, joint Wald tests for H2, and multiple imputation via `mice` alongside complete-case results) is reported in the supplementary materials as a standalone document. It also retains the pre-registered all-platform total playtime measure (including iOS and Android; Appendix B, Deviation D6), providing the comparison between console/PC-only and all-platform H1 estimates.

## Daily-Timescale Sensitivity Analyses

Four sensitivity refits and one comparison model accompany the exploratory daily analysis (see Exploratory Daily-Timescale Analysis in Methods). Allowing first-order autocorrelated residuals with a within-person day trend (estimated AR(1) = `r round(d_ar1, 2)`) widens the within-person interval past zero (β = `r round(d_r0a$b1, 2)`, 95% CrI \[`r round(d_r0a$b1_ci[1], 2)`, `r round(d_r0a$b1_ci[2], 2)`\]), as does adjusting for window length (β = `r round(d_r0w$b1, 2)`, 95% CrI \[`r round(d_r0w$b1_ci[1], 2)`, `r round(d_r0w$b1_ci[2], 2)`\]). Excluding the 8% of Xbox sessions recorded with date-only timestamps, whose start times are floored to midnight and whose minutes are spread uniformly over the recorded day, leaves the within-person interval above zero (β = `r round(d_rx_b1, 2)`, 95% CrI \[`r round(d_rx_b1_ci[1], 2)`, `r round(d_rx_b1_ci[2], 2)`\]). The all-responses refit, which retains every diary response and scores unobserved play as zero, gives the same between-person lean as the analysed sample (β = `r round(d_r0f$b2, 2)`, 95% CrI \[`r round(d_r0f$b2_ci[1], 2)`, `r round(d_r0f$b2_ci[2], 2)`\]). The comparison model fits the registered M0 structure to the biweekly life-satisfaction ladder (0–10), whose leisure-anchored benchmark on that scale is 0.15 rungs per hour (7.5% of the 10-point range over five leisure hours); its within-person estimate is practically null (β = `r round(d_bridge_b1, 3)`, 95% CrI \[`r round(d_bridge_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(d_bridge_ci[2], 3)`\], `r round(100 * d_bridge_rope, 1)`% inside the region), while its between-person estimate is credibly negative (β = `r round(d_bridge_b2, 3)`, 95% CrI \[`r round(d_bridge_b2_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(d_bridge_b2_ci[2], 3)`\], `r round(100 * d_bridge_b2_rope, 1)`% inside). Two qualifications apply to the daily genre-level intervals: they inherit the exchangeable-residual assumption that the autocorrelation refit relaxes for the total-playtime model only, and the hierarchical-prior model's `r d_r2$divs` divergent transitions followed a documented step-size escalation, with estimates stable across both settings.

# Appendix E: Hypothesis Test Summaries {.appendix}

This appendix tabulates the posterior summaries and convergence diagnostics underlying the hypothesis tests reported in the Results; the corresponding posterior distributions are shown in @fig-h1-all-models (H1) and @fig-h2-heterogeneity (H2).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hypothesis-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Main hypothesis tests: posterior estimates, 95% credible intervals, posterior mass inside the ROPE, and convergence diagnostics."
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

h2_rhat_m1 <- max(brms::rhat(h2_model), na.rm = TRUE)
h2_rhat_m2 <- max(brms::rhat(h2_hier_model), na.rm = TRUE)
h2_rhat_m3 <- max(brms::rhat(h2_mm_model), na.rm = TRUE)
h2_divs_m1 <- sum(subset(brms::nuts_params(h2_model), Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)
h2_divs_m2 <- sum(subset(brms::nuts_params(h2_hier_model), Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)
h2_divs_m3 <- sum(subset(brms::nuts_params(h2_mm_model), Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)

tibble(
  Hypothesis = c("H1a", "H1b", "H2a", "H2a", "H2a", "H2b", "H2b", "H2b"),
  Model = c("M0", "M0", "M1", "M2", "M3", "M1", "M2", "M3"),
  Parameter = c(
    "Within-person slope",
    "Between-person slope",
    "SD of genre coefficients",
    "τ (hierarchical-prior scale)",
    "σ_s (random-slope SD)",
    "SD of genre coefficients",
    "τ (hierarchical-prior scale)",
    "σ_s (random-slope SD)"
  ),
  Estimate = round(c(
    beta1_mean, beta2_mean,
    mean(m1_sd_within_per_draw), tau_mean, sigma_sw_mean,
    mean(m1_sd_between_per_draw), tau_between_mean, sigma_sb_mean
  ), 3),
  `95% CrI` = c(
    sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", beta1_ci[1], beta1_ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", beta2_ci[1], beta2_ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", quantile(m1_sd_within_per_draw, 0.025), quantile(m1_sd_within_per_draw, 0.975)),
    sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", tau_ci[1], tau_ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", sigma_sw_ci[1], sigma_sw_ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", quantile(m1_sd_between_per_draw, 0.025), quantile(m1_sd_between_per_draw, 0.975)),
    sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", tau_between_ci[1], tau_between_ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", sigma_sb_ci[1], sigma_sb_ci[2])
  ),
  `% in ROPE` = sprintf("%.1f", 100 * c(
    beta1_in_rope, beta2_in_rope,
    mean(m1_sd_within_per_draw < 0.06), tau_in_rope, 1 - sigma_sw_above_sesoi,
    mean(m1_sd_between_per_draw < 0.06), tau_between_in_rope, 1 - sigma_sb_above_sesoi
  )),
  `R-hat` = sprintf("%.3f", c(
    h1_rhat, h1_rhat,
    h2_rhat_m1, h2_rhat_m2, h2_rhat_m3,
    h2_rhat_m1, h2_rhat_m2, h2_rhat_m3
  )),
  Div. = c(
    h1_divs, h1_divs,
    h2_divs_m1, h2_divs_m2, h2_divs_m3,
    h2_divs_m1, h2_divs_m2, h2_divs_m3
  )
) |>
  tt(
    width = c(0.11, 0.08, 0.24, 0.10, 0.17, 0.11, 0.09, 0.10),
    notes = "All estimates are in SWEMWBS item-mean points per hour/day. ROPE = region of practical equivalence, −0.06 to +0.06; the heterogeneity parameters are non-negative by construction, so their ROPE spans 0 to 0.06. The H1 slopes are the fixed effects of the standalone total-playtime model (M0). The three H2 statistics quantify genre-to-genre variation in exposure effects: M1 reports the raw SD across the 14 independently estimated fixed-effect coefficients (inflated by sampling noise), M2 the learned hierarchical-prior scale τ on genre fixed effects, and M3 σ_s, the SD of genre random-slope deviations under multi-membership weighting. R-hat is the maximum across all parameters of the fitted model; Div. = number of divergent transitions."
  ) |>
  group_tt(i = list(
    "H1: Total playtime, dose–response" = 1,
    "H2a: Genre heterogeneity, within-person" = 3,
    "H2b: Genre heterogeneity, between-person" = 6
  )) |>
  style_tt(i = c(1, 4, 8), bold = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```

The exploratory daily-timescale analogue of this summary is given in @tbl-daily-summary.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-daily-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Exploratory daily-timescale hypothesis tests (see Exploratory Results: The Daily Timescale): posterior estimates, 95% credible intervals, posterior mass inside the equivalence region (±1 slider point per hour; within-person rows are per hour of same-day play, between-person rows per hour of habitual daily play; heterogeneity parameters are non-negative, so shares are mass below 1), and convergence diagnostics. M1 rows are per-draw SDs across the 14 unpooled genre coefficients and include estimation error."
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

tibble(
  Hypothesis = c(
    "H1a-daily", "H1a-daily", "H1b-daily", "H1b-daily",
    "H2a-daily", "H2a-daily", "H2a-daily",
    "H2b-daily", "H2b-daily", "H2b-daily"
  ),
  Model = c(
    "M0", "M3", "M0", "M3",
    "M1", "M2", "M3",
    "M1", "M2", "M3"
  ),
  Parameter = c(
    "Within-person slope", "Within-person slope (fixed effect)",
    "Between-person slope", "Between-person slope (fixed effect)",
    "SD of genre coefficients", "τ (hierarchical-prior scale)",
    "σ_s (random-slope SD)",
    "SD of genre coefficients", "τ (hierarchical-prior scale)",
    "σ_s (random-slope SD)"
  ),
  Estimate = round(c(
    d_r0$b1, d_m3_b1, d_r0$b2, d_m3_b2,
    d_m1_sdw, d_r2$tau_w, d_sigma_sw,
    d_m1_sdb, d_r2$tau_b, d_sigma_sb
  ), 2),
  `95% CrI` = c(
    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", d_r0$b1_ci[1], d_r0$b1_ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", d_m3_b1_ci[1], d_m3_b1_ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", d_r0$b2_ci[1], d_r0$b2_ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", d_m3_b2_ci[1], d_m3_b2_ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", d_m1_sdw_ci[1], d_m1_sdw_ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", d_r2$tau_w_ci[1], d_r2$tau_w_ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", d_sigma_sw_ci[1], d_sigma_sw_ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", d_m1_sdb_ci[1], d_m1_sdb_ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", d_r2$tau_b_ci[1], d_r2$tau_b_ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", d_sigma_sb_ci[1], d_sigma_sb_ci[2])
  ),
  `% within benchmark` = sprintf("%.1f", 100 * c(
    d_r0$b1_rope, d_m3_b1_rope, d_r0$b2_rope, d_m3_b2_rope,
    d_m1_sdw_below, d_r2$tau_w_rope, d_sigma_sw_below,
    d_m1_sdb_below, d_r2$tau_b_rope, d_sigma_sb_below
  )),
  `R-hat` = sprintf("%.3f", c(
    d_r0$rhat, d_m3_rhat, d_r0$rhat, d_m3_rhat,
    d_m1_rhat, d_r2$rhat, d_m3_rhat,
    d_m1_rhat, d_r2$rhat, d_m3_rhat
  )),
  Div. = c(
    d_r0$divs, d_m3_divs, d_r0$divs, d_m3_divs,
    d_m1_divs, d_r2$divs, d_m3_divs,
    d_m1_divs, d_r2$divs, d_m3_divs
  )
) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```
